knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Set Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite set families represented by complete member lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be a finite ground set. An explicit set-family input is a sequence \((S_1,\ldots,S_m)\) with each \(S_j\subseteq V\), where every member of the represented family occurs in the sequence and each set is stored by its incidence vector or its element list. The represented family is \(\mathcal F=\{S_j:1\leq j\leq m\}\); repeated entries may either be removed or retained as separately indexed copies, according to the declared convention. Its natural input size is the total encoding length, for example \(\Theta(nm)\) bits under dense binary incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit family lists every member, using incidence vectors or element lists; input size is measured by the complete list encoding.
assumptions_latex: The representation convention specifies whether repeated listed sets are distinct copies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{S_j:1\leq j\leq m\}\) is completely determined by the input list.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite set-system input model

children.title: Implicit Set-Family Encodings
children.top_down_role: Compact or generative descriptions of set families whose members are not enumerated.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Set-Family Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families specified compactly without listing every member.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An implicit encoding of a set family is a finite string \(e\), together with a fixed interpretation procedure, that determines a predicate \(P_e:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\). The represented family is
\[\mathcal F_e=\{S\subseteq V:P_e(\chi^S)=1\}.\]
The encoding is implicit when its length is measured by \(|e|+n\), independently of \(|\mathcal F_e|\), so the family may contain exponentially many sets. Any claimed computational bound must additionally specify which operations on \(P_e\)—such as evaluation, separation, optimization, or generation—are available and their costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact string and interpretation predicate define the family, possibly with exponentially many members; computational claims must state the supported access operations.
assumptions_latex: The interpretation procedure is fixed independently of the particular encoding \(e\).
Each subset of \(V\) is identified with its binary incidence vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\) represents exactly \(\mathcal F_e=\{S\subseteq V:P_e(\chi^S)=1\}\).

notation.meaning: membership predicate determined by the encoding
binary incidence vector of a subset S

children.title: Membership-Oracle Set Families
children.top_down_role: Representations accessed through tests concerning membership in individual sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Membership-Oracle Set Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box access deciding whether a queried subset belongs to the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\). A membership oracle for \(\mathcal F\) is a black-box procedure \(M_{\mathcal F}\) that, for every query \(S\subseteq V\), returns
\[M_{\mathcal F}(S)=\begin{cases}1,&S\in\mathcal F,\\0,&S\notin\mathcal F.\end{cases}\]
An oracle-model algorithm may learn about \(\mathcal F\) only through such answers unless further access is declared. Its oracle complexity is the number of membership queries, while total running time also counts computation and the encoding and processing of each queried subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A membership oracle answers whether each queried subset belongs to the hidden family; query complexity counts these calls separately from other computation.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and known to the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each query \(S\subseteq V\) reveals precisely the bit \(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal F}(S)\).

notation.meaning: power set of the ground set

children.title: Separation-Oracle Set Families
children.top_down_role: Representations accessed through violated-incidence or feasibility queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Oracle Set Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation access to the convex hull of family incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) be nonempty and let \(P(\mathcal F)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^S:S\in\mathcal F\}\subseteq\mathbb R^V\). A strong separation oracle for the set-family representation receives a rational point \(y\in\mathbb Q^V\). It either certifies \(y\in P(\mathcal F)\), or returns rational \(a\in\mathbb Q^V\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb Q\) satisfying
\[a^{\mathsf T}y>\beta\quad\text{and}\quad a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\ \text{for every }x\in P(\mathcal F).\]
Thus the oracle exposes the family through its incidence polytope rather than by identifying individual members.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle either accepts a point in the incidence polytope or returns a valid inequality strictly separating it.
assumptions_latex: Queries and returned separator coefficients are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned inequality is valid for \(P(\mathcal F)\) and violated by \(y\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of incidence vectors of family members

children.title: Enumeration Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where explicit generation, delayed generation, or oracle access changes navigability.

knowledge_statements.title: Enumeration Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case exact enumeration under membership-oracle access alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) have cardinality \(n\), and suppose an unknown family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) is accessible only through an exact membership oracle. Any deterministic algorithm that must output every member of every possible \(\mathcal F\) and certify that no member was omitted requires \(2^n\) oracle queries in the worst case. Querying every subset of \(V\) gives a matching upper bound, so the worst-case membership-query complexity is exactly \(2^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact enumeration of an arbitrary membership-oracle family needs all 2^n membership queries in the deterministic worst case.
assumptions_latex: The family is arbitrary, with no structural promise.
The algorithm is deterministic and must certify complete exact enumeration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case membership-query complexity is exactly \(2^n\).

children.title: Weighted Incidence Systems
children.top_down_role: Costs, profits, priorities, or penalties attached to incidence-system components.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Incidence Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary incidences carrying numerical costs, profits, or coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A weighted incidence system is a triple \((V,\mathcal E,w)\), where \(V\) is a finite ground set, \(\mathcal E\subseteq2^V\), and \(w:I\to\mathbb R\) assigns a scalar to every incidence in \(I=\{(v,E):v\in E\in\mathcal E\}\). Its weighted incidence matrix \(W\in\mathbb R^{V\times\mathcal E}\) is defined by
\[W_{vE}=\begin{cases}w(v,E),&v\in E,\\0,&v\notin E.\end{cases}\]
Element or set weights are special cases obtained by making \(w(v,E)\) depend only on \(v\) or only on \(E\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted incidence system assigns a real coefficient to each element–set incidence, producing a real matrix supported on the underlying binary incidence pattern.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\) has support contained in the binary incidence relation \(I\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted generalization of a binary incidence matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction is internally coherent, but “weighted incidence system” can instead denote vertex weights, edge weights, or a general weighted matrix. A specific source is needed to support this exact incidence-level convention.

children.title: Multiplicity-Bearing Incidence Systems
children.top_down_role: Repeated incidence requirements or repeated availability represented within a set system.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity-Bearing Incidence Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence systems allowing repeated occurrence of an element within a member.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiplicity-bearing incidence system is a triple \((V,\mathcal E,m)\), where \(V\) and \(\mathcal E\) are finite index sets and \(m:V\times\mathcal E\to\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\). The integer \(m(v,E)\) is the number of occurrences of element \(v\) in indexed member \(E\); hence \(E\) represents a multiset rather than necessarily a subset. Its incidence matrix is \(M=(m(v,E))\). The ordinary set-family regime is recovered exactly when \(m(v,E)\in\{0,1\}\) for all \((v,E)\). Distinct indices in \(\mathcal E\) may encode identical multiplicity columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each element–member pair has a nonnegative integer multiplicity; binary multiplicities recover ordinary set-family incidence.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and the member index set \(\mathcal E\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is an ordinary incidence system exactly when \(M\in\{0,1\}^{V\times\mathcal E}\).

notation.meaning: multiplicity of element v in indexed member E

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: multiset incidence is encoded by a nonnegative integer matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonnegative-integer matrix model is coherent and fits the leaf, but the exact terminology and multiset interpretation have no inspectable supporting source.

children.title: Combined Weight–Multiplicity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Models in which heterogeneous values coexist with repeated incidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Weight–Multiplicity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate multiplicities and per-occurrence weights on one incidence relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((V,\mathcal E,m)\) be a multiplicity-bearing incidence system and let \(w:V\times\mathcal E\to\mathbb R\) assign a per-occurrence weight. The combined weight–multiplicity representation is the pair of matrices \((M,W)\), with \(M_{vE}=m(v,E)\) and \(W_{vE}=w(v,E)\), together with the aggregate coefficient matrix
\[C_{vE}=M_{vE}W_{vE}.\]
For a selected-member vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal E}\), the total weighted contribution at element \(v\) is \((Cx)_v=\sum_{E\in\mathcal E}m(v,E)w(v,E)x_E\). Keeping \(M\) and \(W\) separate preserves information that \(C\) alone may lose.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicity and per-occurrence weight are stored separately; their product gives aggregate incidence coefficients used to evaluate selected members.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is nonnegative integral and \(W\) is real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((Cx)_v=\sum_{E\in\mathcal E}m(v,E)w(v,E)x_E\) for every selection vector \(x\).

notation.meaning: aggregate coefficient matrix given entrywise by M times W

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: aggregate contribution equals multiplicity times per-occurrence weight

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and aggregate formula are internally correct and the content kind fits, but no source supports this particular separation of per-occurrence weights from multiplicities.

knowledge_statements.title: Hyperedge-Selection Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-variable representation of selecting members of a finite hypergraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a finite hypergraph with incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{V\times\mathcal E}\). A hyperedge selection is represented by \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal E}\), where \(x_E=1\) exactly when edge \(E\) is selected. The vector
\[Ax\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^{V}\]
counts, for each vertex, the number of selected incident hyperedges. Consequently, covering, packing, and exact-incidence requirements are expressed respectively by coordinatewise constraints \(Ax\geq b\), \(Ax\leq b\), and \(Ax=b\); a linear selection objective has the form \(c^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables select hyperedges, and multiplying by the incidence matrix counts selected edges at each vertex, enabling covering, packing, or exact constraints.
assumptions_latex: Selection is binary, so each indexed hyperedge is chosen at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((Ax)_v=\sum_{E\ni v}x_E\) counts selected hyperedges incident with each \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: prescribed vertexwise incidence bound or target

children.title: Clutter Set Families
children.top_down_role: Antichain set families viewed as incidence structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Clutter Set Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite antichains of subsets under inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite ground set. A clutter on \(V\) is a family \(\mathcal C\subseteq2^V\) satisfying
\[C,D\in\mathcal C\ \text{and}\ C\subseteq D\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C=D.\]
Thus no distinct member of \(\mathcal C\) contains another. The definition permits \(\mathcal C=\varnothing\); if \(\varnothing\in\mathcal C\), then necessarily \(\mathcal C=\{\varnothing\}\). Equivalently, a clutter is an antichain in the Boolean lattice \((2^V,\subseteq)\), and it may be viewed as a simple hypergraph whose edges are inclusion-incomparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clutter is a family of subsets in which no distinct member contains another—equivalently, an antichain in the Boolean lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct \(C,D\in\mathcal C\) satisfy neither \(C\subseteq D\) nor \(D\subseteq C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clutters and minimal-member hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines minimal-member reduction, upward closure, and clutters for finite hypergraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a hypergraph $H=(V,\mathcal E)$, define $H^{\min}=(V,\{F\in\mathcal E:\nexists E\in\mathcal E\text{ with }E\subsetneq F\})$ and $H^{\uparrow}=(V,\{F\subseteq V:\exists E\in\mathcal E\text{ with }E\subseteq F\})$. The hypergraph $H$ is a clutter if no two distinct edges contain one another. Consequently, $H^{\min}$ is a clutter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal-member hypergraph retains precisely the inclusionwise minimal edges, and the upward closure consists of all vertex subsets containing an edge. A clutter has no two distinct edges comparable by inclusion; therefore every minimal-member hypergraph is a clutter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is a clutter}\iff \forall E,F\in\mathcal E,\ E\subseteq F\Rightarrow E=F,\qquad H^{\min}\text{ is a clutter}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clutters and Their Blocking Clutters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines antichain set families and their inclusion-minimal transversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set system $(E,\mathcal F)$ is a clutter if
\[
X,Y\in\mathcal F\text{ and }X\subseteq Y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X=Y.
\]
For a clutter $(E,\mathcal F)$, its blocking clutter is
\[
BL(E,\mathcal F)=\left(E,\left\{X\subseteq E:\ X\cap Y\neq\varnothing\ \forall Y\in\mathcal F,\text{ and }X\text{ is inclusion-minimal with this property}\right\}\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clutter is a set family in which no distinct member contains another. Its blocking clutter consists of the inclusion-minimal sets intersecting every member of the original clutter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl((E,\mathcal F)\text{ is a clutter}\iff\forall X,Y\in\mathcal F,\ X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow X=Y\bigr),\quad BL(E,\mathcal F)\text{ is the family of inclusion-minimal transversals when }(E,\mathcal F)\text{ is a clutter}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypergraphs and clutters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite set-system terminology underlying clutter representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hypergraph \(H\) is a finite set of finite sets. Its node set is \(\bigcup H\), and its members are called edges. It is a clutter if no edge properly contains another; equivalently, \[\forall E,F\in H,\quad E\subseteq F\Longrightarrow E=F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hypergraph is a finite family of finite sets, whose members are edges and whose elements are nodes. It is a clutter when no edge properly contains another.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is a clutter}\iff \forall E,F\in H,\ E\subseteq F\Rightarrow E=F

children.title: Minimal-Member Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations retaining inclusion-minimal members of a set family.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Member Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical clutter representation of an upward-closed finite family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite and let \(\mathcal U\subseteq2^V\) be upward closed: whenever \(S\in\mathcal U\) and \(S\subseteq T\subseteq V\), one has \(T\in\mathcal U\). Define
\[\min(\mathcal U)=\{S\in\mathcal U:\text{no }T\in\mathcal U\text{ satisfies }T\subsetneq S\}.\]
Then \(\min(\mathcal U)\) is a clutter and
\[\mathcal U=\{T\subseteq V:\text{there exists }C\in\min(\mathcal U)\text{ with }C\subseteq T\}.\]
Moreover, \(\min(\mathcal U)\) is the unique clutter whose upward closure equals \(\mathcal U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every upward-closed finite family is uniquely determined by its inclusion-minimal members, which form a clutter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal U=\uparrow\min(\mathcal U)\), and \(\min(\mathcal U)\) is its unique clutter generator.

children.title: Redundancy Elimination by Inclusion
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of removing members that contain smaller members.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy Elimination by Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deleting containing hyperedges preserves hitting sets and transversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal E\subseteq 2^V\) be finite, and let \(\mathcal C\) consist of its inclusion-minimal members. A set \(T\subseteq V\) is a transversal of \(\mathcal E\) when \(T\cap E
eq\varnothing\) for every \(E\in\mathcal E\). Then \[\{T\subseteq V:T\cap E
eq\varnothing\ 	ext{for every }E\in\mathcal E\}=\{T\subseteq V:T\cap C
eq\varnothing\ 	ext{for every }C\in\mathcal C\}.\] Thus every nonminimal hyperedge is redundant for transversal feasibility, and deleting all such edges preserves both all transversals and all inclusion-minimal transversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For hitting-set feasibility, any edge containing another edge is redundant; retaining only inclusion-minimal edges preserves all transversals and minimal transversals.
assumptions_latex: Transversals are defined by nonempty intersection with every indexed hyperedge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transversal families of \(\mathcal E\) and its minimal-member clutter \(\mathcal C\) are equal.

notation.meaning: inclusion-minimal members of the original family

children.title: Clutter Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where minimal-member reduction does not preserve the intended optimization semantics.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Min}(\mathcal F)\) determines \(\mathcal F^{\uparrow}\), but not multiplicities or nonmonotone membership data.

notation.meaning: Inclusion-minimal members of a set family.
Upward closure of a set family.

review_flags: Exact supporting textbook locator for the representation boundary is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of representing a finite set family solely by its inclusion-minimal members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\), define \(\operatorname{Min}(\mathcal F)=\{F\in\mathcal F: \nexists G\in\mathcal F\text{ with }G\subsetneq F\}\) and \(\mathcal F^{\uparrow}=\{X\subseteq V:\exists F\in\mathcal F,\ F\subseteq X\}\). Then \(\operatorname{Min}(\mathcal F)\) is a clutter and uniquely determines \(\mathcal F^{\uparrow}\). Conversely, every clutter \(\mathcal C\subseteq 2^V\) is the minimal-member family of \(\mathcal C^{\uparrow}\). This representation does not determine the original non-upward-closed family \(\mathcal F\), repeated members, or incidence multiplicities; distinct families can therefore have the same clutter representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimal members uniquely encode an upward-closed family, but they cannot recover nonmonotone membership, repeated sets, or incidence multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.title: Clutter Representation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no source or inspectable locator supports the representation claims.

children.title: Transversal Hypergraphs
children.top_down_role: Hypergraphs formed from transversal structures of a source family.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Tr}(H)=\min_{\subseteq}\{T\subseteq V:\forall e\in E,\ T\cap e\ne\varnothing\}\).

notation.meaning: Hypergraph of minimal transversals of the hypergraph.
The vertex set and edge family of the hypergraph.

review_flags: Exact supporting textbook definition is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite simple or nonsimple hypergraphs; the output is always reduced to its inclusion-minimal transversal clutter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(T\subseteq V\) is a transversal of \(H=(V,E)\) when \(T\cap e\ne\varnothing\) for every \(e\in E\). The transversal hypergraph of \(H\) is \[\operatorname{Tr}(H)=\left\{T\subseteq V: (\forall e\in E,\ T\cap e\ne\varnothing)\ \text{and}\ (\forall T'\subsetneq T,\ \exists e\in E,\ T'\cap e=\varnothing)\right\}.\] Thus its edges are exactly the inclusion-minimal transversals of \(H\), and consequently \(\operatorname{Tr}(H)\) is a clutter even when \(E\) contains inclusions or duplicate edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transversal hypergraph has as edges precisely the inclusion-minimal vertex sets meeting every edge of the original hypergraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Transversal Hypergraphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and appropriate for transversal hypergraphs, but it has no cited source or definition locator.

children.title: Minimal Hitting Sets
children.top_down_role: Inclusion-minimal hitting objects distinguished from minimum-size solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,E)\) is a finite hypergraph and \(T\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is minimal hitting exactly when every \(v\in T\) has an edge hit uniquely by \(v\).

notation.meaning: An edge witnessing the necessity of a selected vertex.

review_flags: Exact supporting textbook proposition is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local minimality under set inclusion, not minimum cardinality or minimum weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(T\) is a minimal hitting set of \(H\) if and only if \[\bigl(\forall e\in E,\ T\cap e\ne\varnothing\bigr)\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl(\forall v\in T,\ \exists e_v\in E,\ e_v\cap T=\{v\}\bigr).\] The first predicate says that \(T\) hits every edge. The second supplies a private edge for each \(v\in T\), so deleting that vertex leaves some edge unhit. Hence it is equivalent to requiring that no proper subset of \(T\) be a hitting set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hitting set is inclusion-minimal exactly when every selected vertex is the unique selected vertex in some edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Hitting Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The private-edge characterization correctly concerns inclusion-minimal hitting sets and the condition content kind fits, but no supporting proposition is cited.

children.title: Transversal–Hitting Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The representational relationship between transversal hyperedges and minimal hitting objects.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Tr}(H)=\mathcal M(H)\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Tr}(H))=\operatorname{cl}(H)\).

notation.meaning: Clutter obtained by deleting nonminimal edges.

review_flags: Exact supporting blocker-duality theorem locator is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite hypergraph blocker correspondence, with redundant edges removed before involution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M(H)\) denote the family of inclusion-minimal hitting sets of \(H\). By definition, \(\mathcal M(H)=\operatorname{Tr}(H)\). Moreover, transversalization is an involution on clutters: \[\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Tr}(H))=\operatorname{cl}(H).\] In particular, if \(H\) is already a clutter, then \(\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Tr}(H))=H\). Thus the minimal-hitting-set description and the transversal-hypergraph description encode the same incidence dual, while redundant supersets among the original edges are invisible to that dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimal hitting sets are the edges of the transversal hypergraph, and applying transversalization twice recovers the original clutter.
knowledge_statements.title: Transversal–Hitting Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The blocker involution is stated with the necessary minimal-edge reduction and fits the correspondence leaf, but it lacks a theorem citation and locator.

children.title: Transversal Enumeration Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Output-size and representation regimes affecting access to all minimal transversals.

assumptions_latex: \(m\ge 1\) and \(H_m\) has pairwise disjoint two-vertex edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\operatorname{Tr}(H_m)|=2^m\), so explicit enumeration can require exponential output.
review_flags: Exact supporting enumeration-complexity source is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-size boundary for explicit enumeration; it does not assert hardness of output-polynomial generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_m=\{a_i,b_i:1\le i\le m\}\) and \(E_m=\{\{a_i,b_i\}:1\le i\le m\}\), and set \(H_m=(V_m,E_m)\). Every minimal transversal contains exactly one vertex from each pair \(\{a_i,b_i\}\), and every such choice is a minimal transversal. Therefore \[|\operatorname{Tr}(H_m)|=2^m.\] Since \(H_m\) has \(2m\) incidences, the explicit list of all minimal transversals may be exponential in the input size. Consequently, no total-time polynomial bound in the input size alone is possible for explicit transversal enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hypergraph of disjoint pairs has two choices per edge and therefore exponentially many minimal transversals.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning–Exact-Cover Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between combinatorial exact covers and binary set-partitioning equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Index the elements of \(U\) by the rows of \(A\), and define \(A_{uj}=1\) exactly when \(u\in S_j\). For \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(x^J_j=1\) if and only if \(j\in J\). Then \[(Ax^J)_u=\sum_{j\in J}\mathbf 1_{S_j}(u).\] Consequently, \(J\) is an exact cover of \(U\) if and only if \(Ax^J=\mathbf 1\). This gives a bijection between exact covers in the indexed family and feasible binary solutions of the corresponding set-partitioning system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact covers correspond bijectively to binary solutions of the incidence-matrix equation Ax equals one.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite, \(S_1,\ldots,S_n\subseteq U\), and \(A\in\{0,1\}^{|U|\times n}\) is defined by \(A_{uj}=1\) if and only if \(u\in S_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J\) is an exact cover of \(U\) if and only if its incidence vector \(x^J\) satisfies \(Ax^J=\mathbf 1\).

Replacing \(A\) by its support matrix \(B=\mathbf 1[A>0]\) can change feasibility. For example, with \(A=[2]\), no \(x\in\{0,1\}\) satisfies \(Ax=1\), whereas for \(B=[1]\), the choice \(x=1\) satisfies \(Bx=1\). Thus an ordinary set-family representation loses information essential to multiplicity-sensitive exact incidence.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(X=\{j:x_j=1\}\), \[Ax\ge\mathbf 1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall i,\ X\cap R_i\ne\varnothing.\] Hence a column cover is exactly a hitting set of the row-neighborhood hypergraph. Transposition replaces \(A\) by \(A^{\mathsf T}\), exchanging the families \(\{R_i\}\) and \(\{C_j\}\) and interchanging the two incidence ground sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A column cover is a hitting set of row neighborhoods, and matrix transposition exchanges row and column incidence systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Packing–Conflict Transposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transposes pairwise-disjoint packing in a finite set family into stable-set optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\). Define the conflict graph \(G_{\mathcal F}\) with vertex set \(\mathcal F\) and edge set \(\{\{A,B\}:A,B\in\mathcal F,\ A\ne B,\ A\cap B\ne\varnothing\}\). A subfamily \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F\) is a packing, meaning its members are pairwise disjoint, if and only if \(\mathcal P\) is a stable vertex set of \(G_{\mathcal F}\). Thus, for weights \(w:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\), maximum-weight packing and maximum-weight stable set on \(G_{\mathcal F}\) have identical feasible solutions and objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conflict graph joins intersecting sets. Pairwise-disjoint subfamilies are exactly its stable sets, so weighted packing transposes directly to weighted stable-set optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\text{ is a packing}\iff \mathcal P\text{ is stable in }G_{\mathcal F}\).

notation.meaning: intersection-conflict graph of the set family

children.title: Blocker Duality

knowledge_statements.title: Blocker Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite clutter blocker duality through inclusion-minimal transversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal C\subseteq 2^E\) be a clutter, so no member properly contains another. Its blocker is \[b(\mathcal C)=\min_{\subseteq}\{B\subseteq E:B\cap C\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }C\in\mathcal C\}.\] Then \(b(\mathcal C)\) is a clutter and \(b(b(\mathcal C))=\mathcal C\). Consequently, a set \(B\subseteq E\) belongs to \(b(\mathcal C)\) exactly when it is an inclusion-minimal transversal of \(\mathcal C\), while the members of \(\mathcal C\) are precisely the inclusion-minimal transversals of \(b(\mathcal C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The blocker consists of the minimal hitting sets of a finite clutter. Taking minimal hitting sets again recovers the original clutter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(b(\mathcal C))=\mathcal C\).

notation.meaning: clutter of inclusion-minimal transversals of the clutter

children.title: Antiblocker Duality

knowledge_statements.title: Antiblocker Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antiblocker involution for convex corners in the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex corner is a nonempty compact convex set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R_+^n\) with nonempty interior relative to \(\mathbb R_+^n\) that is lower-comprehensive: \(0\le z\le x\in P\) implies \(z\in P\). Define \[\operatorname{abl}(P)=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^n:y^{\mathsf T}x\le1\text{ for every }x\in P\}.\] Then \(\operatorname{abl}(P)\) is a convex corner and the antiblocker operation is involutive: \[\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(P))=P.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex corner, the nonnegative vectors having scalar product at most one with every point form another convex corner, whose antiblocker is the original corner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(P))=P\).

children.title: Blocker Involution Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Blocker Involution Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when double blocking is literal and when it first removes redundant members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite family \(\mathcal A\subseteq2^E\), let \(\min(\mathcal A)\) denote its inclusion-minimal members and define \(b(\mathcal A)\) as the inclusion-minimal sets meeting every member of \(\mathcal A\). Provided \(\varnothing\notin\mathcal A\), blocking ignores redundant supersets and satisfies \[b(\mathcal A)=b(\min(\mathcal A)),\qquad b(b(\mathcal A))=\min(\mathcal A).\] Hence double blocking is a literal involution exactly on clutters; on arbitrary finite families it returns their clutter reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double blocking recovers a finite family only when it is a clutter. In general it deletes members containing other members and returns the minimal-member reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(b(\mathcal A))=\min(\mathcal A)\), and this equals \(\mathcal A\) exactly when \(\mathcal A\) is a clutter.

children.title: Discrete–Geometric Duality Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete–Geometric Duality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that blocker transposition alone does not guarantee an integral covering polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(\mathcal C=\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\},\{1,3\}\}\). Its blocker consists of the three two-element subsets of \(E\). Nevertheless, the covering polyhedron \[Q(\mathcal C)=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^3:x_1+x_2\ge1,\ x_2+x_3\ge1,\ x_1+x_3\ge1\}\] has the fractional extreme point \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\). Thus discrete blocker involution does not imply that incidence inequalities describe the convex hull of integral transversals; an idealness or integrality hypothesis is additionally required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The triangle clutter has exact blocker duality but a fractional covering-polyhedron vertex. Discrete blocker involution therefore does not by itself provide integral geometric duality.
assumptions_latex: The covering polyhedron uses nonnegative real variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\in Q(\mathcal C)\) is fractional and extreme, so blocker involution does not imply integrality.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cardinality Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted finite set cover with every chosen set counted once.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite universe \(U\) and a family \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\) with \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal S}S=U\), minimum-cardinality set cover is \[\min\left\{|\mathcal C|:\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S,\ \bigcup_{S\in\mathcal C}S=U\right\}.\] Equivalently, with one binary variable per set, it is \[\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}x_S:\sum_{S\ni u}x_S\ge1\ \text{for every }u\in U,\ x_S\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose as few sets as possible so that every universe element belongs to at least one chosen set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is the minimum number of members of \(\mathcal S\) whose union equals \(U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite set cover with a nonnegative cost assigned to each available set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\), and costs \(c_S\ge0\), weighted set cover is \[\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S:\sum_{S\ni u}x_S\ge1\ \text{for every }u\in U,\ x_S\in\{0,1\}\ \text{for every }S\in\mathcal S\right\}.\] A feasible solution selects sets covering every element, and its value is the sum of their costs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted and Unweighted Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines weighted set cover and its unit-weight specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite ground set \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}\), subsets \(S_j\subseteq E\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\), and nonnegative weights \(w_j\ge 0\), the weighted set cover problem is \[\min_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}}\sum_{j\in I}w_j\quad\text{subject to}\quad\bigcup_{j\in I}S_j=E.\] If \(w_j=1\) for every \(j\), this is the unweighted set cover problem, equivalently minimum-cardinality set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a finite ground set, a family of its subsets, and a nonnegative weight for each subset, weighted set cover seeks a covering subfamily of minimum total weight. When every weight equals one, it becomes unweighted, or minimum-cardinality, set cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{j\in I}w_j:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\},\ \bigcup_{j\in I}S_j=E\right\};\qquad (\forall j,\ w_j=1)\Rightarrow\text{minimum-cardinality set cover}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted set cover and the vertex-cover specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines weighted set cover through its binary incidence formulation and identifies vertex cover as the row-frequency-two specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $I=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ be a universe, let $S_j\subseteq I$ have weight $w_j$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$ satisfy $a_{ij}=1$ exactly when $i\in S_j$. Weighted set cover is $\min\{w^Tx:Ax\geq\mathbf e,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}$. Vertex cover is the specialization in which every universe element belongs to exactly two sets: elements represent graph edges and their two containing sets represent the endpoint vertices. Thus set cover strictly generalizes vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted set cover chooses minimum-total-weight sets covering every universe element. Vertex cover is the case in which each element occurs in exactly two sets corresponding to the endpoints of an edge, so set cover strictly generalizes vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{SetCover}(A,w)=\min\{w^Tx:Ax\geq\mathbf e,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\},\qquad \text{vertex cover is its row-frequency-two special case.}

children.title: Uniform-Cost Specialization
children.top_down_role: The specialization linking weighted objectives to cardinality objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Cost Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates weighted and minimum-cardinality set cover when all costs coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite feasible set-cover instance \((U,\mathcal S)\), let \(X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal S}:\sum_{S\ni u}x_S\ge1\text{ for every }u\in U\}\). If \(c_S=\lambda>0\) for every \(S\in\mathcal S\), then every \(x\in X\) has weighted objective \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S=\lambda\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}x_S\). Consequently, \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}x_S\] and \[\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{weighted}}=\lambda\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{card}}.\] Unit costs therefore recover minimum-cardinality set cover without rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every available set has the same positive cost, minimizing total cost over the feasible covers selects exactly the minimum-cardinality covers, and the weighted optimum is the common cost times the cardinality optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(\mathcal S\) are finite and the set-cover instance is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}x_S\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{weighted}}=\lambda\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{card}}\).

notation.meaning: common feasible set of binary set-cover selections

children.title: Weight-Sensitive Approximation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions caused by nonuniform set costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Sensitive Approximation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy approximation guarantee for nonnegative weighted set cover on a nonempty finite universe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\ne\varnothing\) be finite, let \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\) be finite, and suppose the weighted set-cover instance is feasible with costs \(c_S\ge0\). Starting with \(R=U\), repeatedly choose a set \(S\in\mathcal S\) with \(S\cap R\ne\varnothing\) that minimizes \(c_S/|S\cap R|\), and then remove \(S\cap R\) from \(R\). Let \(d=\max_{S\in\mathcal S}|S|\ge1\) and \(H_d=\sum_{i=1}^d1/i\). The resulting cover \(\mathcal C_g\) satisfies \[\sum_{S\in\mathcal C_g}c_S\le H_d\operatorname{OPT}\le(1+\ln d)\operatorname{OPT}.\] When incidences and costs are explicitly represented, this greedy procedure has a polynomial-time implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a feasible weighted set-cover instance with a nonempty universe, greedy selection by minimum cost per newly covered element produces a cover costing at most the harmonic number of the largest set size times optimum and can be implemented in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: The instance is feasible and \(c_S\ge0\) for every \(S\in\mathcal S\).
Incidences and costs are explicitly represented for the implementation claim.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(\mathcal C_g)\le H_d\operatorname{OPT}\le(1+\ln d)\operatorname{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: maximum cardinality of an available set
cover returned by the weighted greedy procedure

knowledge_statements.title: Set Multicover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary finite set selection with element-specific integer coverage demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\), costs \(c_S\ge0\), and integer demands \(r_u\ge0\), set multicover is \[\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S:\sum_{S\ni u}x_S\ge r_u\ \text{for every }u\in U,\ x_S\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\] Thus each available set may be selected at most once, while every element \(u\) must occur in at least \(r_u\) selected sets. Feasibility requires \(r_u\le|\{S\in\mathcal S:u\in S\}|\) for all \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a minimum-cost subfamily so that each element is covered at least its prescribed number of times, with each available set usable once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible selection satisfies \(\sum_{S\ni u}x_S\ge r_u\) for each \(u\in U\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-Feasible Multicover Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multicover-specific residual-cost algorithm that outputs selected columns and dual variables, with an explicit infeasibility test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\), \(\mathbf b\), and \(\mathbf w\), initialize \(v_j=0\), \(y_i=0\), and \(\mathrm{COVER}=\varnothing\). While the active row set \(I\) is nonempty, choose \(i\in I\) and an unselected column \(k\) satisfying \(a_{ik}=1\) with minimum current weight. If no such column exists, stop and declare the instance infeasible. Set \(y_i\leftarrow y_i+w_k\), add \(k\) to \(\mathrm{COVER}\), and, for every \(j\) with \(a_{ij}=1\), set \(w_j\leftarrow w_j-w_k\); if the result is negative, set \(v_j\leftarrow v_j-w_j\) and \(w_j\leftarrow0\). Decrease every residual demand by one, remove rows whose demand is zero, and repeat until \(I=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly select an active row and its cheapest currently unselected covering column, update the dual variables and residual column weights, decrease the residual demands, and remove satisfied rows. If an active row has no available covering column, report infeasibility; otherwise return the selected columns and the dual vector.
assumptions_latex: A=(a_{ij})\text{ is the multicover incidence matrix, }\mathbf b\text{ is its demand vector, and }\mathbf w\text{ is its weight vector.}
I\text{ and }J\text{ denote the active row and column index sets.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure either detects an active row with no available covering column or outputs }\mathrm{COVER}\text{ and }(\mathbf y,\mathbf v).

children.title: Partial Set Cover
children.top_down_role: Coverage models requiring service for only a prescribed portion of demand.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost coverage of at least a prescribed number of universe elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\), nonnegative costs \(c_S\), and a quota \(q\in\{0,\ldots,|U|\}\), partial set cover minimizes \[\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S\] over \(x_S\in\{0,1\}\) subject to \[\left|\bigcup_{S:x_S=1}S\right|\ge q.\] Equivalently, binary variables \(y_u\) may record covered elements, with \(y_u\le\sum_{S\ni u}x_S\) for every \(u\) and \(\sum_{u\in U}y_u\ge q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost sets whose union contains at least the prescribed quota of universe elements; covering every element is unnecessary unless the quota is full.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected union has cardinality at least \(q\) and minimum total set cost.

notation.meaning: binary indicator that element u is counted as covered

children.title: Prize-Collecting Set Cover

knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Collecting Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set cover allowing uncovered elements in exchange for explicit penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\), set costs \(c_S\ge0\), and penalties \(\pi_u\ge0\), prize-collecting set cover is \[\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S+\sum_{u\in U}\pi_uz_u:\sum_{S\ni u}x_S+z_u\ge1\ \text{for every }u\in U,\ x_S,z_u\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\] Here \(z_u=1\) pays the penalty for leaving \(u\) uncovered; an optimal solution may take \(z_u=0\) whenever a selected set covers \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose sets and pay a penalty for each uncovered element, minimizing the combined selection cost and uncovered-element penalties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective minimizes selected-set costs plus penalties for elements not covered by the selection.

notation.meaning: penalty for leaving element u uncovered

children.title: Quota-Based Coverage
children.top_down_role: Partial-coverage regimes controlled by aggregate service targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota-Based Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted quota-cover formulation on a finite set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be finite, let \(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^U\), assign costs \(c_S\ge 0\) to sets and weights \(w_e\ge 0\) to elements, and fix \(Q\in[0,\sum_{e\in U}w_e]\). For \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S\), define its covered weight by \(g(\mathcal C)=\sum_{e\in\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal C}S}w_e\). The quota-based coverage problem is
\[\min_{\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S}\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal C}c_S:g(\mathcal C)\ge Q\right\}.\]
It is infeasible precisely when \(Q>g(\mathcal S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost sets whose union covers element weight at least the prescribed quota; infeasibility occurs when all available sets miss the quota.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(Q)=\min\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal C}c_S:g(\mathcal C)\ge Q\}\).

notation.meaning: total weight of elements covered by the chosen sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite weighted quota-cover formulation is standard and unambiguous
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Penalty–Quota Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between penalty-based and quota-based treatments of uncovered elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty–Quota Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supported-solution correspondence between quota constraints and uncovered-weight penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite feasible family, with cost \(c(x)\), covered weight \(g(x)\), and total weight \(W\). For \(\lambda\ge0\), let \(x_\lambda\) minimize \(c(x)+\lambda(W-g(x))\) over \(X\). Then \(x_\lambda\) solves the quota problem \(\min\{c(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\ge g(x_\lambda)\}\). Conversely, a quota optimum \(x^*\) is optimal for some penalty \(\lambda\ge0\) exactly when \((g(x^*),c(x^*))\) is supported by a line of slope \(\lambda\) among attainable coverage-cost pairs. Thus unsupported quota optima need not arise from any scalar penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each penalty optimum is optimal for its attained quota, while only supported quota optima are recoverable by varying the penalty multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\lambda\in\arg\min\{c(x):g(x)\ge g(x_\lambda)\}\), with the converse holding exactly for supported attainable pairs.

notation.meaning: penalty per unit of uncovered weight

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite Lagrangian scalarization gives the stated supported-Pareto correspondence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Capacitated Set Cover
children.top_down_role: Set-cover models with limits on service supplied by selected sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment formulation with one capacity bound per selected set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be finite, let \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\), and give each element demand \(d_e\ge0\), each set capacity \(u_S\ge0\), and each set cost \(c_S\ge0\). Capacitated set cover minimizes
\[\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S\]
over \(x_S\in\{0,1\}\) and \(y_{eS}\in\{0,1\}\) for incidences \(e\in S\), subject to
\[\sum_{S\ni e}y_{eS}=1\quad(e\in U),\qquad \sum_{e\in S}d_ey_{eS}\le u_Sx_S\quad(S\in\mathcal S).\]
Thus every element is assigned to one selected incident set, whose assigned demand cannot exceed its capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select minimum-cost sets and assign every element to a selected containing set without exceeding any selected set's capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\min\{\sum_Sc_Sx_S:\sum_{S\ni e}y_{eS}=1,\ \sum_{e\in S}d_ey_{eS}\le u_Sx_S\}\).

notation.meaning: indicator that set S is selected
indicator that element e is assigned to set S

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assignment model is a coherent hard-capacitated set-cover definition and fits the leaf, but capacitated set cover has variant-dependent conventions. A direct source must substantiate this particular unsplittable, single-assignment formulation.

children.title: Side-Constrained Set Cover
children.top_down_role: Set-cover models with additional budgets, quotas, conflicts, or resource restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Side-Constrained Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set cover augmented by an explicit linear feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be finite, let \(\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_m\}\subseteq2^U\), let \(c\in\mathbb R_+^m\), and let \(D\in\{0,1\}^{U\times m}\) be the incidence matrix. Given \(B\in\mathbb R^{r\times m}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^r\), side-constrained set cover is
\[\min\{c^\top x:Dx\ge\mathbf1,\ Bx\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^m\}.\]
The system \(Bx\le b\) may encode budgets, partition limits, conflicts, or other restrictions, but it is part of the instance and must be satisfied together with coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a minimum-cost set cover whose selection vector also satisfies a specified system of side constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) and \(b\) are explicitly supplied instance data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\{0,1\}^m\) is feasible exactly when \(Dx\ge\mathbf1\) and \(Bx\le b\).

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Hard-Capacity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Capacity models where selected sets cannot be replicated.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonreplicable capacities coupled to binary set selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a hard-capacity set-cover regime, each set \(S\in\mathcal S\) can be selected at most once. With selection variables \(x_S\in\{0,1\}\), assignment variables \(y_{eS}\in\{0,1\}\) defined only when \(e\in S\), demands \(d_e\ge0\), and capacities \(u_S\ge0\), feasibility requires
\[\sum_{S\ni e}y_{eS}=1\quad(e\in U),\qquad \sum_{e\in S}d_ey_{eS}\le u_Sx_S\quad(S\in\mathcal S).\]
No additional copy of \(S\) may be purchased to enlarge \(u_S\); overload therefore makes that assignment infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each set may be opened only once, and its assigned demand must fit within one fixed, nonreplicable capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_S\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\sum_{e\in S}d_ey_{eS}\le u_Sx_S\) enforce a nonreplicable capacity for every \(S\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: binary opening variables distinguish hard from replicable capacities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly expresses nonreplicable, single-copy capacities and fits the hard-capacity leaf. A direct source is still required because hard-capacitated covering conventions and assignment assumptions are variant-sensitive.

children.title: Soft-Capacity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Capacity models permitting replicated or expanded service at additional cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Soft-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replicable set capacities purchased in integral copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a soft-capacity set-cover regime, an arbitrary nonnegative integer number \(z_S\) of copies of each set \(S\in\mathcal S\) may be purchased. If one copy costs \(c_S\) and supplies capacity \(u_S\), the assignment formulation minimizes \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sz_S\) subject to
\[\sum_{S\ni e}y_{eS}=1\quad(e\in U),\qquad \sum_{e\in S}d_ey_{eS}\le u_Sz_S\quad(S\in\mathcal S),\]
where \(z_S\in\mathbb Z_+\) and \(y_{eS}\in\{0,1\}\). Capacity can therefore be enlarged by buying additional copies, each incurring its stated cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set's capacity may be replicated by purchasing integral copies, with cost and available capacity scaling by the copy count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_S\in\mathbb Z_+\) gives total cost \(c_Sz_S\) and total capacity \(u_Sz_S\) for set \(S\).

notation.meaning: number of purchased copies of set S
replicated capacity available at set S

children.title: Minimum-Cardinality Hitting Set
children.top_down_role: Hitting-set instances minimizing the number of selected elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cardinality Hitting Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted transversal optimization for a finite set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite ground set and let \(\mathcal E\subseteq2^V\) contain no empty member. A hitting set is a subset \(H\subseteq V\) satisfying \(H\cap E\ne\varnothing\) for every \(E\in\mathcal E\). The minimum-cardinality hitting-set problem is
\[\tau(\mathcal E)=\min\{|H|:H\subseteq V,\ H\cap E\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }E\in\mathcal E\}.\]
Equivalently, with \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\), it minimizes \(\sum_{v\in V}x_v\) subject to \(\sum_{v\in E}x_v\ge1\) for every \(E\in\mathcal E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose as few ground elements as possible so that every member of the set system contains a chosen element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(\mathcal E)=\min\{\sum_{v\in V}x_v:\sum_{v\in E}x_v\ge1\ (E\in\mathcal E),\ x\in\{0,1\}^V\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite hitting-set and transversal formulations are canonical
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-cardinality hitting-set definition and binary formulation are standard, precise, and appropriate for the leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative citation or locator.

children.title: Weighted Hitting Set
children.top_down_role: Hitting-set instances with heterogeneous element costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Hitting Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost transversal with nonnegative vertex weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite, let \(\mathcal E\subseteq2^V\) contain no empty member, and assign each \(v\in V\) a weight \(w_v\ge0\). The weighted hitting-set problem is
\[\tau_w(\mathcal E)=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in H}w_v:H\subseteq V,\ H\cap E\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }E\in\mathcal E\right\}.\]
Equivalently, it minimizes \(\sum_{v\in V}w_vx_v\) over \(x\in\{0,1\}^V\) subject to \(\sum_{v\in E}x_v\ge1\) for every \(E\in\mathcal E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a minimum-total-weight collection of ground elements intersecting every member of the set system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_w(\mathcal E)=\min\{\sum_vw_vx_v:\sum_{v\in E}x_v\ge1\ (E\in\mathcal E),\ x\in\{0,1\}^V\}\).

notation.meaning: cost of selecting ground element v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonnegative vertex costs give the canonical weighted hitting-set formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted hitting-set definition is internally consistent and matches the terminal container, but it has no source reference with a specific definition, section, or page locator.

children.title: Uniform-Cost Hitting Regime
children.top_down_role: The specialization connecting weighted hitting sets to cardinality minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Cost Hitting Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of uniform-cost and minimum-cardinality hitting sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a finite hitting-set instance \((V,\mathcal E)\) in which every selectable element has the same positive cost \(\alpha\). For every hitting set \(H\subseteq V\), its weighted cost is
\[\sum_{v\in H}\alpha=\alpha|H|.\]
Consequently, a hitting set minimizes total cost if and only if it has minimum cardinality, and the optimum values satisfy \(\tau_w(\mathcal E)=\alpha\tau(\mathcal E)\). In particular, normalizing \(\alpha=1\) changes neither the feasible solutions nor the set of optimal hitting sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every selectable element has the same positive cost, weighted hitting set and minimum-cardinality hitting set have exactly the same optimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\min_H\sum_{v\in H}w_v=\arg\min_H|H|\) and \(\tau_w(\mathcal E)=\alpha\tau(\mathcal E)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a constant positive objective coefficient scales cardinality without changing minimizers
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-positive-cost scaling property is mathematically precise, and property is the correct role for this leaf. Nevertheless, no cited source with an inspectable locator supports the stated equivalence.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Transversal Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum vertex transversals of finite hypergraphs, with weighted and unweighted objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite hypergraph \(\mathcal H=(V,\mathcal E)\) with no empty hyperedge, a transversal is a set \(T\subseteq V\) such that \(T\cap E\ne\varnothing\) for every \(E\in\mathcal E\). Given weights \(w:V\to\mathbb R_+\), the minimum transversal problem is
\[\min\left\{\sum_{v\in T}w_v:T\subseteq V,\ T\cap E\ne\varnothing\text{ for all }E\in\mathcal E\right\}.\]
The unweighted minimum transversal problem is obtained by taking \(w_v=1\) for all \(v\in V\); its optimum is the transversal number \(\tau(\mathcal H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum transversal is a least-cost vertex subset meeting every hyperedge; unit weights yield the minimum-cardinality version.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_w(\mathcal H)=\min\{\sum_{v\in T}w_v:T\cap E\ne\varnothing\text{ for all }E\in\mathcal E\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: hypergraph transversals are canonically identical to hitting sets
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record accurately presents weighted and unweighted finite hypergraph transversal problems and is suitable as a topic-level definition, but no authoritative transversal reference with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Hitting Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hitting sets for incidence ranges induced by geometric objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a finite set of candidate points in a geometric space \(X\), and let \(\mathcal R\) be a finite family of geometric regions in \(X\). A geometric hitting set is a subset \(H\subseteq P\) satisfying \(H\cap R
e\varnothing\) for every \(R\in\mathcal R\) with \(P\cap R
e\varnothing\). Given costs \(w_p\ge0\), the optimization problem is
\[\min\left\{\sum_{p\in H}w_p:H\subseteq P,\ H\cap R
e\varnothing	ext{ for every }R\in\mathcal Right\}.\]
It is the hitting-set instance induced by the range system \(\{P\cap R:R\in\mathcal R\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost candidate points that intersect every geometric region; the regions induce an ordinary finite range-space hitting-set instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P,\{P\cap R:R\in\mathcal R\})\) is the induced finite hitting-set instance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set packing and conflict-graph equivalence to independent set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the binary set-packing formulation and the reductions establishing polynomial equivalence with independent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a zero-one incidence matrix $A$, weights $w$, and the all-ones vector $\mathbf e$, set packing is $\max\{w^Tx:Ax\leq\mathbf e,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}$. Construct the derived graph having one vertex for each column of $A$ and an edge between two vertices exactly when the corresponding columns have nonzero dot product. Feasible set packings are precisely independent sets in this graph. Conversely, independent set is a special case of set packing; therefore the problems are polynomially equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set packing selects a maximum-weight collection of pairwise disjoint sets. Turning sets into vertices and joining overlapping sets produces a conflict graph whose independent sets are exactly the feasible packings. Independent set is also a set-packing special case, so the problems are polynomially equivalent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{w^Tx:Ax\leq\mathbf e,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\text{ is polynomially equivalent to maximum-weight independent set.}

children.title: Maximum-Cardinality Set Packing
children.top_down_role: Set-packing instances maximizing the number of selected sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Cardinality Set Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Largest pairwise-disjoint subfamily of a finite set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be finite and let \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\) be a finite family. A set packing is a subfamily \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal S\) whose distinct members are pairwise disjoint. The maximum-cardinality set-packing problem is
\[\nu(\mathcal S)=\max\{|\mathcal P|:\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal S,\ S\cap T=\varnothing\text{ for all distinct }S,T\in\mathcal P\}.\]
Equivalently, with \(x_S\in\{0,1\}\), it maximizes \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}x_S\) subject to \(\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\le1\) for every \(e\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select the largest possible subfamily of sets such that no ground element belongs to two selected sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(\mathcal S)=\max\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}x_S:\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\le1\ (e\in U),\ x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal S}\}\).

notation.meaning: indicator that set S is packed

children.title: Weighted Set Packing
children.top_down_role: Set-packing instances maximizing heterogeneous selection value.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Set Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite weighted set packing with arbitrary real profits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be a finite ground set, let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) be a finite family, and assign each \(S\in\mathcal F\) a profit \(w_S\in\mathbb R\). A weighted set packing is a subfamily \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F\) whose members are pairwise disjoint. The optimization problem is
\[\max_{\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F}\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal P}w_S: S\cap T=\varnothing\text{ for all distinct }S,T\in\mathcal P\right\}.\]
Equivalently, for the incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{U\times\mathcal F}\), it is \(\max\{w^Tx:Ax\leq\mathbf1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose pairwise disjoint sets maximizing their total assigned profit; equivalently, solve the binary incidence formulation with element-capacity one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\max\{w^Tx:Ax\leq\mathbf1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite incidence formulation of weighted set packing
source_gap: supplied locators concern graph matching rather than general set packing

children.title: Uniform-Profit Specialization
children.top_down_role: The specialization linking weighted packing to cardinality packing.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Profit Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive uniform profits reduce weighted packing to maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) be finite, and suppose \(w_S=\alpha\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), where \(\alpha>0\). For every feasible packing \(\mathcal P\), its profit is \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal P}w_S=\alpha|\mathcal P|\). Consequently,
\[\operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathcal P\text{ packing}}\sum_{S\in\mathcal P}w_S=\operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathcal P\text{ packing}}|\mathcal P|,\]
and the optimal weighted value equals \(\alpha\) times the maximum packing cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every set has the same positive profit, maximizing total profit is exactly the same as maximizing the number of selected sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_w=\alpha\max\{|\mathcal P|:\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F\text{ is a packing}\}\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Weight-Sensitive Packing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions arising from heterogeneous packing profits.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Sensitive Packing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniform profits can reverse cardinality-based preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximum-profit packing need not have maximum cardinality. For example, take \(U=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(\mathcal F=\{A,B,C\}\), where \(A=\{1,2\}\), \(B=\{1,3\}\), and \(C=\{2,4\}\). The packing \(\{B,C\}\) has cardinality two, whereas \(\{A\}\) has cardinality one. If \(w_A=3\) and \(w_B=w_C=1\), the unique maximum-profit packing is \(\{A\}\). Thus nonuniform weights can make a smaller packing optimal, and changing weights can change the optimizer without changing the incidence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonuniform profits, a smaller packing can outperform every maximum-cardinality packing, so the optimizer depends essentially on the weights.
assumptions_latex: Packing profit is additive: \(w(\mathcal P)=\sum_{S\in\mathcal P}w_S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathcal P}w(\mathcal P)\) need not intersect \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathcal P}|\mathcal P|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit finite counterinstance verifies weight sensitivity
source_gap: no supplied locator directly supports general weighted set packing

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Cardinality Set Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set packing whose available sets have uniformly bounded size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(k\geq1\). A bounded-cardinality, or \(k\)-set, packing instance consists of a finite ground set \(U\), a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^U\) satisfying \(|S|\leq k\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and optionally profits \(w_S\). A feasible solution is a pairwise-disjoint subfamily \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F\). The unweighted objective maximizes \(|\mathcal P|\); the weighted objective maximizes \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal P}w_S\). The bound constrains the size of each available set, not the number of sets selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every available set contains at most a fixed number of elements, and one selects a pairwise-disjoint subfamily of maximum cardinality or profit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\text{ is feasible}\iff \mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F\text{ and }S\cap T=\varnothing\text{ for distinct }S,T\in\mathcal P\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on each available set's cardinality

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of k-set packing

children.title: Graph Matching Specialization
children.top_down_role: Set-packing instances induced by edges of an ordinary graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Matching Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph matching is the two-element specialization of set packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and regard every edge \(e=\{u,v\}\in E\) as a two-element subset of \(V\). A subfamily \(M\subseteq E\) is a set packing precisely when no two edges in \(M\) share an endpoint, which is precisely the definition of a graph matching. Hence maximum-cardinality matching is unweighted two-set packing, and maximum-weight matching is weighted two-set packing:
\[\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq1\ \forall v\in V,\ x\in\{0,1\}^E\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating graph edges as two-element sets makes pairwise-disjoint set packings exactly graph matchings, with cardinality and weighted objectives preserved.
assumptions_latex: Each edge is identified with its endpoint set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\iff M\text{ is a packing in }(V,E)\).

children.title: Three-Dimensional Matching
children.top_down_role: Tripartite packing instances using triples as selectable sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Dimensional Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tripartite three-uniform matching and its perfect decision form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) be finite pairwise-disjoint sets and let \(T\subseteq X\times Y\times Z\). A three-dimensional matching is a subset \(M\subseteq T\) such that distinct triples in \(M\) differ in every coordinate; equivalently, no element of \(X\cup Y\cup Z\) occurs in two selected triples. The maximum problem maximizes \(|M|\). When \(|X|=|Y|=|Z|=q\), a perfect three-dimensional matching is one with \(|M|=q\), so every element of \(X\cup Y\cup Z\) occurs exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select triples from three disjoint coordinate classes so that no coordinate element is reused; a perfect matching covers every element exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is feasible}\iff |M\cap(\{x\}\times Y\times Z)|,|M\cap(X\times\{y\}\times Z)|,|M\cap(X\times Y\times\{z\})|\leq1\) for all \(x,y,z\).

notation.meaning: common coordinate-class size in the perfect case

children.title: Higher-Dimensional Matching
children.top_down_role: Packing specializations using tuples from multiple disjoint domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Dimensional Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-dimensional matching in a multipartite uniform hypergraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(d\geq 3\). Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_d\) be finite pairwise-disjoint sets and let \(T\subseteq X_1\times\cdots\times X_d\). A \(d\)-dimensional matching is a subset \(M\subseteq T\) such that, for every coordinate \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), no two distinct tuples of \(M\) have the same \(i\)-th coordinate. Equivalently, interpreting each tuple as a \(d\)-element subset of \(X_1\cup\cdots\cup X_d\), the selected tuples form a set packing. If \(|X_i|=q\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), a perfect matching has \(|M|=q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select d-tuples so that no value is repeated in any coordinate; equivalently, select disjoint hyperedges in a d-partite d-uniform hypergraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is feasible}\iff t_i\neq t'_i\text{ for all distinct }t,t'\in M\text{ and every }i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\).

children.title: Dimension-Driven Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: The structural transition between graph matching and multidimensional packing.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Driven Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical exact-computation boundary between dimension two and fixed dimensions at least three.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dimension \(d=2\), maximum-cardinality and maximum-weight matching in a finite graph are solvable in time polynomial in the graph encoding length. For every fixed \(d\geq3\), the decision problem asking whether a finite \(d\)-partite, \(d\)-uniform instance with equally sized coordinate classes has a perfect matching is NP-complete. Membership in NP follows because a proposed tuple set can be checked for cardinality and coordinate disjointness in polynomial time. Thus increasing the matching dimension from two to three crosses from polynomial-time exact optimization to NP-hard exact optimization, unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary graph matching is polynomial-time solvable, while perfect d-dimensional matching is NP-complete for every fixed dimension at least three.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is fixed rather than part of the input.
Instances are represented explicitly by their available edges or tuples.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d=2\) admits polynomial-time exact optimization, whereas fixed \(d\geq3\) has an NP-complete perfect-matching decision problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact cover as a binary incidence feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be a finite ground set and \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^U\) a finite family. An exact cover is a subfamily \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal F\) such that every element of \(U\) belongs to exactly one member of \(\mathcal C\). If \(A\in\{0,1\}^{U\times\mathcal F}\) is the incidence matrix, exact covers correspond bijectively to vectors \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\) satisfying
\[Ax=\mathbf1.\]
Thus the selected sets are pairwise disjoint and their union is \(U\); both requirements are necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose sets that partition the ground set: every element must occur in exactly one selected set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\text{ is an exact cover}\iff A\chi^{\mathcal C}=\mathbf1\).

notation.meaning: binary incidence vector of the selected subfamily

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Set Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost exact cover over a finite set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be finite, let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) be finite, and assign each \(S\in\mathcal F\) a cost \(c_S\in\mathbb R\). Weighted set partitioning selects an exact cover of minimum total cost. With incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{U\times\mathcal F}\), its formulation is
\[\min\left\{c^Tx:Ax=\mathbf1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\right\}.\]
If no binary vector satisfies \(Ax=\mathbf1\), the instance is infeasible. Otherwise, every feasible vector selects sets that partition \(U\), and the objective distinguishes among those partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among all exact covers, choose one minimizing the sum of its selected-set costs; if no exact cover exists, the instance is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=\mathbf1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\}\) whenever the feasible set is nonempty.

children.title: Generalized Set Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Partitioning models extending ordinary exact assignment through broader eligibility or assignment structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Set Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact prescribed element multiplicities generalizing ordinary set partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) be finite, let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{U\times\mathcal F}\) be their incidence matrix, and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^{U}\). A generalized set partition is a binary selection vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\) satisfying
\[Ax=b.\]
Thus each element \(u\in U\) must occur in exactly \(b_u\) selected sets. With costs \(c\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal F}\), generalized weighted set partitioning minimizes \(c^Tx\) over this feasible set. Ordinary exact cover is the specialization \(b=\mathbf1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select sets so that each element is covered an individually prescribed nonnegative integer number of times; exact cover is the all-ones case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible}\iff x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\text{ and }Ax=b\).
review_flags: terminology_version: generalized set partitioning is taken to mean exact nonunit multiplicities
source_gap: a specific source is needed to establish this terminology

children.title: Multiplicity-Constrained Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Partitioning models prescribing repeated incidence or assignment counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity-Constrained Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set selection with lower and upper element-multiplicity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) be finite, let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{U\times\mathcal F}\) be their incidence matrix, and choose vectors \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^{U}\) satisfying \(\ell\leq u\) componentwise. A multiplicity-constrained partition is a vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\) satisfying
\[\ell\leq Ax\leq u.\]
Hence every element \(i\in U\) occurs in at least \(\ell_i\) and at most \(u_i\) selected sets. Exact prescribed multiplicities arise when \(\ell=u=b\), and ordinary exact cover arises when \(\ell=u=\mathbf1\). An optional linear objective may optimize selection costs or profits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each element must be covered between specified lower and upper multiplicities; equal bounds give prescribed multiplicities, including exact cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible}\iff x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal F}\text{ and }\ell\leq Ax\leq u\).

children.title: Lower-Multiplicity Regimes
