knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Multiplicity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound multiplicities in a finite binary incidence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite set of requirements, \(J\) a finite family of selectable sets, and \(A\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\) their incidence matrix. Given lower multiplicities \(\ell\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{I}\), the lower-multiplicity regime consists of binary selections \(x\in\{0,1\}^{J}\) satisfying \[\sum_{j\in J}A_{ij}x_j\ge \ell_i\qquad(i\in I).\] An associated optimization problem minimizes or maximizes a specified objective over these selections. The case \(\ell_i=1\) for every \(i\in I\) is ordinary set covering; larger values require repeated coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each requirement must belong to at least its prescribed number of selected sets; multiplicity one recovers ordinary covering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\ge \ell\) componentwise.

notation.meaning: Indicator that selectable set j contains requirement i.
Binary selection variable for set j.
Required minimum multiplicity of requirement i.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Multiplicity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-bound multiplicities in a finite binary incidence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite set of requirements, \(J\) a finite family of selectable sets, and \(A\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\) their incidence matrix. Given upper multiplicities \(u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{I}\), the upper-multiplicity regime consists of binary selections \(x\in\{0,1\}^{J}\) satisfying \[\sum_{j\in J}A_{ij}x_j\le u_i\qquad(i\in I).\] An associated optimization problem optimizes a specified objective over these selections. The case \(u_i=1\) for every \(i\in I\) forbids any requirement from occurring in two selected sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No requirement may occur in more than its prescribed number of selected sets; unit bounds enforce pairwise nonoverlap at each requirement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le u\) componentwise.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted finite maximum coverage under a cardinality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite ground set \(I\), subsets \((S_j)_{j\in J}\), nonnegative element weights \(w_i\), and an integer \(k\ge0\), maximum coverage selects at most \(k\) subsets to maximize the weight of their union. With \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(i\in S_j\), its binary formulation is \[\max\left\{\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i:\ y_i\le\sum_{j\in J}A_{ij}x_j\ (i\in I),\ \sum_{j\in J}x_j\le k,\ x_j,y_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose at most k sets so that the total weight of elements contained in at least one chosen set is maximized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{|X|\le k}\sum_{i\in\bigcup_{j\in X}S_j}w_i\).

notation.meaning: Indicator that subset j is selected.
Indicator that element i is covered.

knowledge_statements.title: Budgeted Maximum Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted maximum coverage with nonuniform set costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite ground set \(I\), subsets \((S_j)_{j\in J}\), element weights \(w_i\ge0\), set costs \(c_j\ge0\), and budget \(B\ge0\), budgeted maximum coverage is \[\max\left\{\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i:\ y_i\le\sum_{j\in J}A_{ij}x_j\ (i\in I),\ \sum_{j\in J}c_jx_j\le B,\ x_j,y_i\in\{0,1\}\right\},\] where \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(i\in S_j\). Unit costs and integral budget \(k\) recover maximum coverage with at most \(k\) selected sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose sets of total cost at most B to maximize the weight of elements covered by their union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{X\subseteq J:\,\sum_{j\in X}c_j\le B}\sum_{i\in\bigcup_{j\in X}S_j}w_i\).

notation.meaning: Indicator that element i is covered.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Multicoverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capped multiplicity version of weighted maximum coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\), budget \(k\), caps \(r_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), and weights \(w_i\ge0\), maximum multicoverage selects \(x\in\{0,1\}^{J}\) with \(\sum_{j\in J}x_j\le k\) and maximizes \[\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min\left\{r_i,\sum_{j\in J}A_{ij}x_j\right\}.\] Equivalently, introduce integer variables \(y_i\) satisfying \(0\le y_i\le r_i\) and \(y_i\le\sum_{j\in J}A_{ij}x_j\), and maximize \(\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each element earns value for multiple selected sets containing it, up to an element-specific cap, under a selection budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{J},\,\sum_jx_j\le k}\sum_iw_i\min\{r_i,(Ax)_i\}\).

notation.meaning: Valued coverage-multiplicity cap for element i.
Number of selected sets containing element i.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The capped-multiplicity objective is internally correct, but “maximum multicoverage” is also used for objectives counting elements that meet prescribed coverage thresholds. An authoritative source with a precise locator is needed to establish that this leaf denotes the capped-sum version.

children.title: Group-Constrained Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage models with requirements or limits indexed by population groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Group-Constrained Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage with explicit lower or upper quotas for designated groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be partitioned or covered by designated groups \((I_g)_{g\in G}\). For coverage indicators \(y_i\) induced by a feasible set selection, define group benefit \(z_g=\sum_{i\in I_g}w_i y_i\). A group-constrained coverage problem maximizes a specified coverage objective subject to \[L_g\le z_g\le U_g\qquad(g\in G),\] together with the underlying cardinality or cost budget and incidence constraints. Either bound may be omitted; overlapping groups are permitted when explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coverage solution must place each designated group's covered weight between prescribed lower and upper quotas.
assumptions_latex: \(I\), \(G\), and the selectable set family are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_g\le\sum_{i\in I_g}w_i y_i\le U_g\) for every \(g\in G\).

notation.meaning: Elements assigned to designated group g.
Covered weight attained by group g.
Admissible interval for group g's covered weight.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct quota-constrained extension of maximum coverage
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quota formulation is coherent, but “group-constrained coverage” is not sufficiently standardized to determine whether the intended quantities are covered weight, coverage rates, selection quotas, or another group statistic. A supporting source is required.

children.title: Fair Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage models balancing service outcomes across designated groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Fair Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Max-min normalized group coverage; other fairness criteria are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let groups \((I_g)_{g\in G}\) have positive total weights \(W_g=\sum_{i\in I_g}w_i>0\). For coverage indicators \(y_i\) induced by a selection satisfying the underlying budget, define the normalized group rate \(q_g=W_g^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_g}w_i y_i\). In the max-min fair-coverage formulation, one solves \[\max t\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_g\ge t\quad(g\in G),\] along with the incidence, integrality, and budget constraints. Thus the objective maximizes the least normalized coverage attained by any group.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a budget-feasible collection of sets to maximize the smallest weighted coverage rate among the designated groups.
assumptions_latex: \(I\), \(G\), and the selectable set family are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max t=\max\min_{g\in G}q_g\).

notation.meaning: Total element weight in group g.
Normalized covered-weight rate of group g.
Guaranteed coverage rate across all groups.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Max-min normalized group coverage is a valid fair-coverage model, but the title admits several incompatible fairness criteria. The immutable context alone does not establish this particular variant; a source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Minimum-Share Coverage
children.top_down_role: Group regimes requiring prescribed service shares.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Share Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum group shares of the total achieved coverage benefit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((I_g)_{g\in G}\) be designated groups and let \(y_i\) indicate whether element \(i\) is covered by a budget-feasible selection. Define total covered benefit \(Z=\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\) and group benefit \(z_g=\sum_{i\in I_g}w_i y_i\). Given shares \(\rho_g\in[0,1]\), minimum-share coverage requires \[z_g\ge \rho_g Z\qquad(g\in G).\] The remaining objective, commonly maximization of \(Z\), is optimized subject to these share, incidence, integrality, and budget constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every designated group must receive at least a prescribed fraction of the total covered benefit.
assumptions_latex: \(I\), \(G\), and the selectable set family are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in I_g}w_i y_i\ge\rho_g\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\) for every \(g\in G\).

notation.meaning: Covered benefit assigned to group g.
Required minimum share for group g.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed achieved-total-benefit share constraints are coherent, but “minimum share” may instead mean a minimum fraction of each group’s own total weight. A source is needed to determine the intended denominator and mathematical version.

children.title: Disparity-Limited Coverage
children.top_down_role: Group regimes limiting differences in coverage outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Disparity-Limited Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise bounds on normalized coverage-rate disparities between groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For groups \((I_g)_{g\in G}\) with positive total weights \(W_g=\sum_{i\in I_g}w_i\), let \(q_g=W_g^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_g}w_i y_i\) be the normalized rate induced by a budget-feasible coverage selection. Given tolerances \(\Delta_{gh}\ge0\), disparity-limited coverage imposes \[|q_g-q_h|\le\Delta_{gh}\qquad(g,h\in G).\] A coverage objective, such as total covered weight, is optimized subject to these inequalities and the underlying incidence, integrality, and budget constraints. A common uniform version uses one tolerance \(\Delta\) for every pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage rates of any two designated groups may differ by no more than their prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(I\), \(G\), and the selectable set family are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|q_g-q_h|\le\Delta_{gh}\) for all \(g,h\in G\).

notation.meaning: Normalized covered-weight rate of group g.
Total element weight in group g.
Allowed rate disparity between groups g and h.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Pairwise absolute differences of normalized coverage rates form a valid disparity constraint, but alternative disparity measures are common. The exact metric and normalization require authoritative source support.

children.title: Graph-Derived Covering-Packing Interface
children.top_down_role: Classical graph specializations are retained as interfaces rather than duplicating their full graph-theoretic chapters.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Cover Set Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex cover represented as covering the edge universe by incident-edge sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), take universe \(E\) and associate with each vertex \(v\in V\) the set \(S_v=\{e\in E:v\in e\}\). A vertex subset \(C\subseteq V\) is a vertex cover exactly when \(\bigcup_{v\in C}S_v=E\). With the edge-vertex incidence matrix \(A\), the weighted minimum vertex-cover problem is therefore \[\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}c_vx_v:Ax\ge\mathbf1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\},\] where \(c_v\ge0\) is the vertex cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treat edges as requirements and each vertex as the set of its incident edges; set covers are exactly vertex covers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is a vertex cover}\iff\bigcup_{v\in C}S_v=E\iff A\mathbf1_C\ge\mathbf1\).

notation.meaning: Set of edges incident with vertex v.
Edge-vertex incidence matrix of the graph.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical reduction of vertex cover to set cover
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Dominating-Set Covering Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominating set represented as covering vertices by closed neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), use universe \(V\) and assign to each vertex \(v\in V\) its closed neighborhood \(N[v]=\{v\}\cup\{u\in V:uv\in E\}\). A set \(D\subseteq V\) is dominating exactly when \(\bigcup_{v\in D}N[v]=V\). If \(A_{uv}=1\) exactly when \(u\in N[v]\), weighted minimum domination has the set-cover formulation \[\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}c_vx_v:Ax\ge\mathbf1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treat vertices as requirements and each vertex as its closed neighborhood; set covers are exactly dominating sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\text{ is dominating}\iff\bigcup_{v\in D}N[v]=V\iff A\mathbf1_D\ge\mathbf1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical reduction of dominating set to set cover
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Packing Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable sets represented by edgewise binary packing constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a subset \(S\subseteq V\) is stable exactly when it contains at most one endpoint of every edge. Hence its incidence vector \(x=\mathbf1_S\) satisfies \[x_u+x_v\le1\qquad(uv\in E),\qquad x\in\{0,1\}^{V}.\] Conversely, every binary vector satisfying these inequalities is the incidence vector of a stable set. Thus the maximum-weight stable-set problem is \[\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}w_vx_v:x_u+x_v\le1\ (uv\in E),\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting vertices with at most one endpoint from each edge is exactly selecting a stable set.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is stable}\iff\mathbf1_S(u)+\mathbf1_S(v)\le1\) for every \(uv\in E\).

notation.meaning: Binary incidence vector of the selected vertices.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical edge-packing formulation of stable set

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Element Frequency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform upper bound on element degrees in a finite incidence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite ground set and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) a family of sets. The frequency of an element \(u\in U\) is \(d_{\mathcal F}(u):=|\{F\in\mathcal F:u\in F\}|\). For an integer \(f\ge 0\), the incidence system \((U,\mathcal F)\) has element frequency bounded by \(f\) when \(d_{\mathcal F}(u)\le f\) for every \(u\in U\). Equivalently, every vertex on the \(U\)-side of the bipartite incidence graph has degree at most \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every ground element belongs to at most f sets; equivalently, every element-side vertex of the incidence graph has degree at most f.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall u\in U,\ d_{\mathcal F}(u)\le f\).

notation.meaning: number of sets containing element u

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Set Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform upper bound on hyperedge sizes in a finite set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite ground set and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\). For an integer \(k\ge 0\), the incidence system \((U,\mathcal F)\) has set cardinality bounded by \(k\) if \(|F|\le k\) for every \(F\in\mathcal F\). Equivalently, every vertex representing a member of \(\mathcal F\) in the bipartite incidence graph has degree at most \(k\). This condition bounds row sums of the set-element incidence matrix independently of element frequencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every member of the set family contains at most k ground elements, equivalently bounding every set-side incidence degree by k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall F\in\mathcal F,\ |F|\le k\).

notation.meaning: family of subsets of the ground set

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Incidence Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hereditary linear sparsity, parameterized through an arboricity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite incidence system \((U,\mathcal F)\), let \(G_I=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathcal F,E_I)\) be its bipartite incidence graph, where \(uF\in E_I\) exactly when \(u\in F\). For an integer \(a\ge 0\), call \(G_I\) \(a\)-sparse when every vertex subset \(W\subseteq V(G_I)\) with \(|W|\ge 2\) satisfies \(|E_I[W]|\le a(|W|-1)\). Thus every induced subgraph has linear edge density, and the condition is equivalent to the arboricity of \(G_I\) being at most \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence graph is uniformly sparse when every induced subgraph has at most a fixed linear number of edges, equivalently bounded arboricity.
assumptions_latex: \((U,\mathcal F)\) is a finite incidence system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall W\subseteq V(G_I),\ |W|\ge2\Rightarrow |E_I[W]|\le a(|W|-1)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Nash-Williams-style inequality is mathematically consistent with arboricity at most a, but “a-sparse” is convention-dependent and the asserted equivalence requires an exact authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Union-of-antichains and chain-partition min-max theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Poset min-max identity relating a union of k antichains to chain partitions with chain sizes truncated at k.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let (S,\leq) be a partially ordered set and let k\in\mathbb Z_{+}. Then
\[
\max_{A_1,\ldots,A_k\,\mathrm{antichains}}\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}A_i\right|=\min_{\mathcal C\,\mathrm{a\ partition\ of}\ S\,\mathrm{into\ chains}}\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}\min\{k,|C|\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a partially ordered set and a positive integer k, the maximum size of the union of k antichains equals the minimum, over all partitions into chains, of the sum of each chain's size truncated at k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{A_1,\ldots,A_k\,\mathrm{antichains}}\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}A_i\right|=\min_{\mathcal C\,\mathrm{a\ chain\ partition\ of}\ S}\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}\min\{k,|C|\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Laminar Set Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise nesting-or-disjointness definition for set families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a set and \(\mathcal L\subseteq 2^U\). The family \(\mathcal L\) is laminar if, for every \(A,B\in\mathcal L\), at least one of \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), \(A\subseteq B\), or \(B\subseteq A\) holds. Equivalently, no two members cross: there do not exist \(A,B\in\mathcal L\) for which each of \(A\setminus B\), \(B\setminus A\), and \(A\cap B\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set family is laminar when any two members are disjoint or one contains the other; crossing pairs are forbidden.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall A,B\in\mathcal L,\ A\cap B=\varnothing\ \lor\ A\subseteq B\ \lor\ B\subseteq A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rooted-Tree Representation of Laminar Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent structural representation of laminar families over a finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family $\mathcal L$ of subsets of a finite set $E$ is laminar if and only if it has a tree representation whose tree is directed toward the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of subsets of a finite ground set is laminar exactly when it has a tree representation directed toward the root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal L\text{ is laminar}\iff\mathcal L\text{ has a tree representation directed toward the root}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Containment forest and endpoint ownership for a laminar family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the containment-forest, cut incidence, degree, and endpoint-ownership terminology used in a laminar counting argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L\) be a laminar family ordered by inclusion. A member not contained in another member is a root set. For each nonroot \(S\in\mathcal L\), its parent is the unique inclusion-minimal \(T\in\mathcal L\) containing \(S\). Descendance is the reflexive transitive closure of the child relation; members without children are leaves, and the subtree rooted at \(S\) consists of its descendants. An edge \(e\) is incident at \(S\) if \(e\in\delta_G(S)\), and the degree of \(S\) is \(|\delta_G(S)|\). A set \(S\) owns an endpoint \(v\) of an edge when \(S\) is the smallest member of \(\mathcal L\) containing \(v\); the subtree rooted at \(S\) owns \(v\) if a descendant of \(S\) owns \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inclusion organizes the laminar family as a rooted forest. The extract also defines cut-edge incidence, set degree, and ownership of an edge endpoint by its smallest containing laminar set or by a subtree containing that owner.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is the graph used to define }\delta_G(S)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal L\text{ carries the stated containment-forest structure and associated incidence, degree, and endpoint-ownership terminology.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cross-free and laminar set systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines both nesting conditions and records the root-complementation equivalence and ground-set dependence boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $U$ be a nonempty finite set and $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U$. The set system $(U,\mathcal F)$ is cross-free if, for every $X,Y\in\mathcal F$, at least one of $X\setminus Y$, $Y\setminus X$, $X\cap Y$, and $U\setminus(X\cup Y)$ is empty. It is laminar if, for every $X,Y\in\mathcal F$, at least one of $X\setminus Y$, $Y\setminus X$, and $X\cap Y$ is empty. For $r\in U$, define $\mathcal F'_r:=\{X\in\mathcal F:r\notin X\}\cup\{U\setminus X:X\in\mathcal F,\ r\in X\}$. Then $(U,\mathcal F)$ is cross-free if and only if $\mathcal F'_r$ is laminar. Laminarity does not depend on unused elements of the ground set, whereas cross-freeness may; if some $r\in U$ belongs to no member of $\mathcal F$, then cross-freeness is equivalent to laminarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family is laminar when every two members are disjoint or one contains the other. It is cross-free when the four regions determined by two members cannot all be nonempty. Complementing every member containing a fixed root turns a cross-free family into a laminar family, and conversely. If the ground set has an element belonging to no family member, cross-freeness and laminarity coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (U,\mathcal F)\text{ is cross-free}\iff \mathcal F'_r\text{ is laminar};\qquad r\notin\bigcup\mathcal F\Rightarrow\bigl((U,\mathcal F)\text{ is cross-free}\iff\mathcal F\text{ is laminar}\bigr).

children.title: Interval Set Systems

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Set Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set systems whose members are intervals of one common linear order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite and let \(\prec\) be a linear order on \(U\). A subset \(F\subseteq U\) is a \(\prec\)-interval if, whenever \(x,z\in F\) and \(x\prec y\prec z\), one has \(y\in F\). A family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) is an interval set system if there exists a linear order \(\prec\) for which every \(F\in\mathcal F\) is a \(\prec\)-interval. The empty set and singleton sets satisfy the interval condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval set system admits one linear ordering of its ground elements in which every member appears as a contiguous block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\prec\ \forall F\in\mathcal F\ \forall x,y,z\in U,\ (x,z\in F\land x\prec y\prec z)\Rightarrow y\in F\).

children.title: Consecutive-Ones Systems

knowledge_statements.title: Consecutive-Ones Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row consecutive-ones property for binary incidence matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\). The matrix \(A\) has the consecutive-ones property for rows if there exists a permutation \(\pi\) of its columns such that, for every row \(i\), the set \(\{j:A_{i,\pi(j)}=1\}\) is empty or equals \(\{\ell_i,\ell_i+1,\ldots,r_i\}\) for some \(1\le \ell_i\le r_i\le n\). A binary incidence system with such a matrix is called a consecutive-ones system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary system has the row consecutive-ones property when its columns can be ordered so that each row's ones form one contiguous block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\pi\ \forall i,\ \{j:A_{i,\pi(j)}=1\}\text{ is an integer interval}\).

notation.meaning: endpoints of the ones in row i

children.title: Interval–Matrix Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Interval–Matrix Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between interval set systems and row-consecutive incidence matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\), let \(\mathcal F=\{F_1,\ldots,F_m\}\), and let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) be defined by \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(u_j\in F_i\). Then \(\mathcal F\) is an interval set system if and only if \(A\) has the consecutive-ones property for rows. More precisely, a linear order of \(U\) makes every \(F_i\) an interval exactly when the corresponding column order makes the ones in every row consecutive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set family is representable by intervals in one element order exactly when its incidence matrix admits a column order with consecutive ones in every row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\text{ is an interval set system}\iff A\text{ has the row consecutive-ones property}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Recognition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A verifiable witness for interval and consecutive-ones recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\), an ordering certificate is a bijection \(p:U\to\{1,\ldots,|U|\}\). It certifies that \(\mathcal F\) is an interval set system when, for every nonempty \(F\in\mathcal F\), one has \(|F|=\max_{u\in F}p(u)-\min_{u\in F}p(u)+1\). Verification computes these extrema and cardinalities for all sets. Under the incidence-matrix correspondence, sorting columns by \(p\) gives a consecutive-ones certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proposed element order is a certificate: every nonempty set must occupy exactly as many positions as the span between its first and last elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\text{ certifies intervality}\iff \forall F\in\mathcal F\setminus\{\varnothing\},\ |F|=\max_{u\in F}p(u)-\min_{u\in F}p(u)+1\).

notation.meaning: candidate position map for ground elements

children.title: Tree-Structured Set Systems
children.top_down_role: Set systems organized by paths, subtrees, or cuts of a tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Structured Set Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set families representable as connected vertex sets of a common host tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\). The system \((U,\mathcal F)\) is tree-structured if there exists a tree \(T=(U,E)\) such that, for every \(F\in\mathcal F\), the induced subgraph \(T[F]\) is connected or \(F=\varnothing\). Equivalently, for any \(x,z\in F\), every vertex on the unique \(x\)-to-\(z\) path in \(T\) also lies in \(F\). The same host tree must witness this condition for all members.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set system is tree-structured when one host tree makes every nonempty member a connected subtree on its elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists T=(U,E)\text{ a tree}\ \forall F\in\mathcal F,\ F=\varnothing\ \lor\ T[F]\text{ is connected}\).

children.title: Hierarchical Set Systems
children.top_down_role: Nested multi-level set families organized by containment or authority.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Set Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted-tree representation of finite laminar families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite and let \(\mathcal H\subseteq 2^U\) be laminar. Form a rooted forest whose nodes are the members of \(\mathcal H\), assigning the parent of each nonmaximal \(A\in\mathcal H\) to be the unique inclusion-minimal \(B\in\mathcal H\) satisfying \(A\subsetneq B\). Then descendants represent nested subsets, incomparable nodes represent disjoint subsets, and roots are the inclusion-maximal members. Conversely, any rooted forest equipped with sets satisfying strict inclusion along parent edges and disjointness between incomparable nodes represents a laminar family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite laminar family has a rooted inclusion forest: descendants are nested sets and incomparable nodes are disjoint; every such forest represents a hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is an ancestor of }B\Rightarrow B\subseteq A\), and \(A,B\text{ incomparable}\Rightarrow A\cap B=\varnothing\).

children.title: Tree Decomposition Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces through which tree structure decomposes incidence-system optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree Decomposition Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separator interface induced by an edge of a tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,(B_t)_{t\in V(T)})\) be a tree decomposition of a finite incidence graph \(G_I\). For an edge \(tt'\in E(T)\), delete \(tt'\) and let \(T_t,T_{t'}\) be the resulting components. Define \(V_t:=\bigcup_{s\in V(T_t)}B_s\), \(V_{t'}:=\bigcup_{s\in V(T_{t'})}B_s\), and the interface \(S_{tt'}:=B_t\cap B_{t'}\). Then \(V_t\cap V_{t'}=S_{tt'}\), and no edge of \(G_I-S_{tt'}\) joins \(V_t\setminus S_{tt'}\) to \(V_{t'}\setminus S_{tt'}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each decomposition-tree edge exposes a bag intersection that separates incidence vertices occurring exclusively on its two sides.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_t\cap V_{t'}=S_{tt'}\) and \(E_{G_I}(V_t\setminus S_{tt'},V_{t'}\setminus S_{tt'})=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: separator interface across tree edge tt'

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated separator interface is a standard tree-decomposition property and is formulated consistently, but no citation or inspectable locator supports it.

children.title: Hierarchy Compatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where overlapping sets fail to respect a common hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy Compatibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossing sets are the exact pairwise obstruction to a common inclusion hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family admits a laminar inclusion hierarchy exactly when it contains no crossing pair. Compatibility can fail even when two subfamilies are separately hierarchical: on \(U=\{1,2,3\}\), the families \(\mathcal H_1=\{\{1,2\}\}\) and \(\mathcal H_2=\{\{2,3\}\}\) are each laminar, but their union is not, because the two sets intersect while neither contains the other. Thus closure under combining hierarchies requires every cross-family pair to be disjoint or nested.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two individually valid hierarchies may be incompatible: their union ceases to be hierarchical precisely when some pair of sets crosses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal H_1\cup\mathcal H_2\text{ is laminar}\iff \forall A\in\mathcal H_1\ \forall B\in\mathcal H_2,\ A\cap B=\varnothing\ \lor\ A\subseteq B\ \lor\ B\subseteq A\).

children.title: Balanced Hypergraphs
children.top_down_role: Hypergraph instances belonging to the balanced structural class.

knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Berge balance defined by exclusion of strong odd cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a finite hypergraph. A strong cycle of length \(k\ge 3\) is a sequence \(v_1,e_1,v_2,e_2,\ldots,v_k,e_k,v_1\) with distinct \(v_i\in V\) and distinct \(e_i\in\mathcal E\), where \(v_i,v_{i+1}\in e_i\) (indices modulo \(k\)) and \(e_i\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}=\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}\). The hypergraph \(H\) is balanced if it has no strong cycle of odd length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite hypergraph is balanced when it contains no odd strong cycle: an odd cycle whose participating edges contain exactly their two consecutive cycle vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is balanced}\iff H\text{ has no strong odd cycle}.\)

notation.meaning: Finite hypergraph with vertex set V and edge family E.
Vertices and hyperedges in a strong cycle.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for the Balanced Hypergraphs leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied for the strong-cycle convention or the balance definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced matrices and balanced hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines balancedness and records equivalent circuit characterizations, closure properties, the graph specialization, and polynomial-time recognizability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A $0$-$1$ matrix $M$ is balanced if it has no submatrix that is the incidence matrix of an odd circuit. A hypergraph $H$ is balanced if its incidence matrix is balanced. If $G_H$ is the incidence bipartite graph of $H=(V,\mathcal E)$, then $H$ is balanced if and only if every chordless circuit in $G_H$ has length divisible by $4$; equivalently, $H$ has no odd circuit as a partial subhypergraph. Balanced hypergraphs are closed under partial subhypergraphs, duality, contractions, restrictions, parallelization, and serialization, and their blockers are closed under parallelization and serialization. For graphs, balancedness is equivalent to bipartiteness. Balancedness can be tested in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-one matrix is balanced when none of its submatrices is an odd-circuit incidence matrix, and a hypergraph is balanced when its incidence matrix is balanced. This is equivalent to the stated circuit conditions. The class has the listed closure properties, coincides with bipartite graphs in the graph case, and is recognizable in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: G_H\text{ is the incidence bipartite graph of }H
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is balanced}\iff M_H\text{ is balanced}\iff\bigl(\text{every chordless circuit of }G_H\text{ has length }0\pmod 4\bigr)\iff\bigl(\text{$H$ has no odd circuit as a partial subhypergraph}\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced hypergraphs and unbalanced circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of balancedness and its coloring and circuit prerequisites, including the failure of essential 2-colorability alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite hypergraph is \(2\)-colorable if its points can be colored with two colors so that every line contains both colors, and it is essentially \(2\)-colorable if deleting its singleton lines leaves a \(2\)-colorable hypergraph. Deleting lines produces a partial hypergraph. For \(U\subseteq V(H)\), the restriction \(H|_U\) has point set \(U\) and lines the nonempty sets \(E\cap U\) for \(E\in E(H)\). The hypergraph \(H\) is balanced if every restriction \(H|_U\) is essentially \(2\)-colorable. Among graphs, the balanced graphs are precisely the bipartite graphs. A circuit is an alternating sequence \((x_1,E_1,\ldots,x_k,E_k)\) of distinct points and distinct lines with \(x_i,x_{i+1}\in E_i\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_1\); it is unbalanced if \(E_i\cap\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}=\{x_i,x_{i+1}\}\) for every \(i\). Essential \(2\)-colorability alone does not imply the König property: the four-point hypergraph whose lines are all triples is a counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced hypergraph is one whose every vertex restriction becomes 2-colorable after singleton edges are removed. For graphs, balancedness is exactly bipartiteness. An unbalanced circuit has no incidences beyond its consecutive circuit incidences. Essential 2-colorability alone does not imply the König property, as shown by the hypergraph of all triples on four points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is balanced}\iff \forall U\subseteq V(H),\ H|_U\text{ is essentially }2\text{-colorable}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hereditary integrality characterizations of balanced hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes balancedness through fractional integrality and hereditary ideal, Mengerian, blocker-Mengerian, and perfect properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every hypergraph $H=(V,\mathcal E)$, the following are equivalent: (i) $H$ is balanced; (ii) $\tau^*(H')\in\mathbb Z$ for every partial subhypergraph $H'$ of $H$; (iii) every partial hypergraph of $H$ is ideal; (iv) every partial hypergraph of $H$ is Mengerian; (v) the blocker of every partial hypergraph of $H$ is Mengerian; (vi) $\alpha^*(H')\in\mathbb Z$ for every partial subhypergraph $H'$ of $H$; and (vii) every partial hypergraph of $H$ is perfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balancedness is equivalent to the stated integrality conditions on every partial subhypergraph and to the stated ideal, Mengerian, blocker-Mengerian, and perfect conditions on every partial hypergraph.
assumptions_latex: H'\text{ ranges over all partial subhypergraphs of }H
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ balanced}\iff[\forall H':\tau^*(H')\in\mathbb Z]\iff[\text{every partial hypergraph of }H\text{ is ideal}]\iff[\text{every partial hypergraph of }H\text{ is Mengerian}]\iff[\text{the blocker of every partial hypergraph of }H\text{ is Mengerian}]\iff[\forall H':\alpha^*(H')\in\mathbb Z]\iff[\text{every partial hypergraph of }H\text{ is perfect}]

children.title: Balanced Incidence Matrices
children.top_down_role: Incidence matrices exhibiting balanced combinatorial structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forbidden-submatrix definition for finite binary matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is balanced if it contains no square submatrix \(B\) of odd order such that every row and every column of \(B\) has exactly two entries equal to \(1\). Equivalently, no odd-order cycle matrix occurs as a submatrix of \(A\), where rows and columns may be selected without requiring them to be consecutive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix is balanced when none of its odd square submatrices has exactly two ones in every row and every column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is balanced}\iff A\text{ contains no odd-order cycle submatrix}.\)

notation.meaning: A square submatrix selected from A.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forbidden odd cycle-submatrix definition is precise and fits the Balanced Incidence Matrices leaf, but the record has no source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: Hypergraph–Matrix Balance Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The representation relationship between balanced hypergraphs and their incidence matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraph–Matrix Balance Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence under the standard vertex-edge incidence convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a finite hypergraph and let \(A_H\in\{0,1\}^{V\times\mathcal E}\) satisfy \((A_H)_{v,e}=1\) exactly when \(v\in e\). Then \(H\) contains a strong odd cycle if and only if \(A_H\) contains an odd-order square submatrix having exactly two ones in every row and every column. Consequently, \(H\) is balanced if and only if its incidence matrix \(A_H\) is balanced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite hypergraph is balanced exactly when its vertex-edge incidence matrix is balanced; strong odd cycles correspond to forbidden odd cycle submatrices.
assumptions_latex: \(A_H\) uses rows for vertices and columns for hyperedges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is balanced}\iff A_H\text{ is balanced}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem correctly states the standard balance correspondence under the declared incidence convention and fits the correspondence leaf. An authoritative locator is required to support both the strong-cycle/submatrix equivalence and its consequence.

children.title: Balance-Preserving Transformations
children.top_down_role: Structural operations under which balance is retained or lost.

knowledge_statements.title: Balance-Preserving Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary matrix operations that preserve balance in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite binary matrix. Every matrix obtained from \(A\) by permuting rows, permuting columns, deleting rows or columns, or transposing is balanced whenever \(A\) is balanced. Row and column permutations and transposition preserve balance equivalently in both directions. For deletion, the converse need not hold: deleting entries may remove every forbidden odd cycle submatrix from a nonbalanced matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balance survives row or column permutations, deletion of rows or columns, and transposition; deletion can remove an obstruction, so its converse fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ balanced}\Longrightarrow PAQ,\ A[R,C],\ A^{\mathsf T}\text{ balanced}\) for permutation matrices \(P,Q\) and index sets \(R,C\).

notation.meaning: Submatrix on row set R and column set C.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure property is correctly scoped: permutations and transposition are reversible, while submatrix deletion preserves balance only forward. Its property kind fits the leaf, but no citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Totally Balanced Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forbidden cycle-submatrix definition, stronger than ordinary balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is totally balanced if it contains no square submatrix \(B\) of order \(k\ge 3\) having exactly two ones in every row and exactly two ones in every column. Thus cycle submatrices of both odd and even order are forbidden. In particular, every totally balanced matrix is balanced, because the latter condition forbids only such submatrices of odd order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix is totally balanced when it contains no cycle submatrix of any order at least three; therefore it is balanced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is totally balanced}\iff A\text{ has no cycle submatrix of order }k\ge 3.\)

notation.meaning: A square cycle submatrix of A.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly excludes cycle submatrices of every order at least three and appropriately records total balance as stronger than balance. It requires an authoritative source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Unimodular Hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-matrix definition using total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a finite hypergraph with vertex-edge incidence matrix \(A_H\in\{0,1\}^{V\times\mathcal E}\). The hypergraph \(H\) is unimodular if \(A_H\) is totally unimodular; that is, every square submatrix of \(A_H\) has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). This property is independent of the ordering chosen for the vertices and hyperedges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite hypergraph is unimodular when every square subdeterminant of its vertex-edge incidence matrix is minus one, zero, or one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is unimodular}\iff \det(B)\in\{-1,0,1\}\text{ for every square submatrix }B\text{ of }A_H.\)

notation.meaning: An arbitrary square submatrix of the incidence matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of unimodular hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent determinantal, polyhedral-integrality, TDI, discrepancy, parity, and excluded-subdeterminant conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) have incidence matrix \(M\). The following are equivalent: (i) every square submatrix of \(M\) has determinant in \(\{0,\pm1\}\); (ii) for every \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal E}\), \(\{x\ge0:Mx\le b\}\) is integral; (iii) for every \(b\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal E}\), \(x\ge0,\ Mx\le b\) is TDI; (iv) for every \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal E}\), \(\{x\ge0:Mx\ge b\}\) is integral; (v) for every \(b\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal E}\), \(x\ge0,\ Mx\ge b\) is TDI; (vi) for all \(a,b\in\mathbb Z^{\mathcal E}\) and \(c,d\in\mathbb Z^V\), \(\{x:c\le x\le d,\ a\le Mx\le b\}\) is integral; (vii) for all \(a,b\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal E}\) and \(c,d\in\mathbb R^V\), \(c\le x\le d,\ a\le Mx\le b\) is TDI; (viii) every \(U\subseteq V\) can be partitioned as \(U=U_1\dot\cup U_2\) so that \(\bigl||E\cap U_1|-|E\cap U_2|\bigr|\le1\) for every \(E\in\mathcal E\); (ix) the entry sum of every square submatrix of \(M\) having even row and column sums is divisible by \(4\); and (x) no square submatrix of \(M\) has determinant \(\pm2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unimodular hypergraphs are equivalently characterized by the ten stated determinant, integral-polyhedron, TDI, discrepancy, parity, and forbidden-subdeterminant conditions.
assumptions_latex: H=(V,\mathcal E)\text{ is a hypergraph with incidence matrix }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{(i)}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{(ii)}\Longleftrightarrow\cdots\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{(x)}.

children.title: Integral Hypergraphs
children.top_down_role: Hypergraph classes characterized through integral incidence-system polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Packing-polyhedron convention for hypergraph integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a finite hypergraph with incidence matrix \(A_H\). Under the packing convention, \(H\) is integral if its fractional matching polytope \[P(H)=\{x\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal E}_{\ge 0}:A_Hx\le \mathbf 1\}\] is integral, meaning every extreme point of \(P(H)\) belongs to \(\mathbb Z^{\mathcal E}\). Equivalently, for every weight vector for which an optimum exists, linear optimization over \(P(H)\) has an integral optimal extreme point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the packing convention, a hypergraph is integral when every vertex of its fractional matching polytope is an integer vector.
assumptions_latex: Integrality uses the fractional-matching, or packing, convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is integral}\iff \operatorname{ext}(P(H))\subseteq\mathbb Z^{\mathcal E}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record explicitly chooses a packing-polytope convention and is coherent under that convention, but 'integral hypergraph' has convention-sensitive usage. A source specifically supporting this terminology and polyhedral definition is required.

children.title: Integrality-Class Implications
children.top_down_role: Containment, implication, and separation relationships among the named structural classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Class Implications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way implications under incidence-matrix and packing conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a finite hypergraph with incidence matrix \(A_H\). If \(A_H\) is totally balanced, then it is balanced. If \(A_H\) is totally unimodular, then it is balanced and the packing polytope \(\{x\ge 0:A_Hx\le\mathbf 1\}\) is integral. Moreover, balancedness of \(A_H\) implies integrality of this packing polytope. Hence totally balanced and unimodular hypergraphs are integral under the packing convention. These implications are not asserted as converses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total balance implies balance, while total unimodularity and balance each imply integrality of the hypergraph packing polytope; the converses are not included.
assumptions_latex: Integrality refers to the packing polytope \(\{x\ge0:A_Hx\le\mathbf1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_H\text{ totally balanced}\Rightarrow A_H\text{ balanced}\Rightarrow H\text{ integral},\qquad A_H\text{ totally unimodular}\Rightarrow A_H\text{ balanced and }H\text{ integral}.\)

source_refs.locator: Section 5.4. Totally Unimodular Matrices p. 115

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5.4. Totally Unimodular Matrices p. 115

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication statement has the correct theorem role and the asserted directions are standard under the packing convention. The cited section on totally unimodular matrices does not by itself document the crucial balanced-matrix packing-integrality implication or the full implication chain.

children.title: Interval Ranges
children.top_down_role: One-dimensional ranges induced by intervals.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Ranges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional geometric range space induced by closed intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R\). The interval range family on \(X\) is \[\mathcal R_{\mathrm{int}}(X)=\{X\cap[a,b]:a,b\in\mathbb R,\ a\le b\}.\] The associated range space is \((X,\mathcal R_{\mathrm{int}}(X))\). Allowing open, closed, or half-open endpoints produces the same traces whenever endpoints may be moved without crossing points of a finite ground set, but the displayed definition fixes the closed-interval convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval ranges are the subsets of a real ground set obtained by intersecting it with closed intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm{int}}(X)\iff R=X\cap[a,b]\text{ for some }a\le b.\)

notation.meaning: Ground set on the real line.
Family of interval-induced ranges on X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed-interval trace definition is precise and fits the Interval Ranges leaf. The finite-ground-set qualification on endpoint conventions is appropriately limited, but the record has no source locator.

children.title: Disk Ranges
children.top_down_role: Planar range systems induced by disks.

knowledge_statements.title: Disk Ranges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Planar range space induced by closed Euclidean disks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), equipped with the Euclidean norm. The disk range family on \(X\) is \[\mathcal R_{\mathrm{disk}}(X)=\{X\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x-c\|_2\le r\}:c\in\mathbb R^2,\ r\ge0\}.\] Thus each range is the trace on \(X\) of a closed Euclidean disk with arbitrary center and nonnegative radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disk ranges are subsets of a planar ground set cut out by closed Euclidean disks of arbitrary center and nonnegative radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm{disk}}(X)\iff R=X\cap\{x:\|x-c\|_2\le r\}\text{ for some }c\in\mathbb R^2,r\ge0.\)

notation.meaning: Family of disk-induced ranges on X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The planar closed-disk trace definition is precise, fully quantified, and appropriate for the Disk Ranges leaf, but no inspectable source is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Four-point transversal theorem for pairwise-intersecting disks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite pairwise-intersecting families of disks in the plane; the universal bound four is best possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D=\{D_1,\ldots,D_n\}\) be a finite family of disks in the plane such that \(D_i\cap D_j\neq\varnothing\) for all \(i,j\). Then there is a set \(T\) of at most four points such that \(T\cap D_i\neq\varnothing\) for every \(i\). Moreover, the universal bound \(4\) is best possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite pairwise-intersecting family of planar disks can be pierced by at most four points, and no smaller universal bound is possible.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D=\{D_1,\ldots,D_n\}\text{ is a finite family of disks in the plane}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists T:\ |T|\le 4\ \land\ \forall i,\ T\cap D_i\neq\varnothing;\quad 4\text{ is the best possible universal bound}

children.title: Ball Ranges
children.top_down_role: Metric or higher-dimensional range systems induced by balls.

knowledge_statements.title: Ball Ranges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean ball ranges in arbitrary positive dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(d\ge1\) and let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). The Euclidean ball range family on \(X\) is \[\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ball}}^{d}(X)=\{X\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\|x-c\|_2\le r\}:c\in\mathbb R^d,\ r\ge0\}.\] For \(d=1\) these are closed interval ranges, and for \(d=2\) they are closed disk ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ball ranges are traces on a ground set in Euclidean space of closed balls with arbitrary centers and nonnegative radii.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ball}}^{d}(X)\iff R=X\cap\{x:\|x-c\|_2\le r\}\text{ for some }c\in\mathbb R^d,r\ge0.\)

notation.meaning: Family of Euclidean-ball ranges on X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The arbitrary-dimensional Euclidean-ball definition is precise and correctly specializes to intervals and planar disks. It fits the Ball Ranges leaf but lacks a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Dimension-Sensitive Range Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural changes arising from ambient dimension or metric choice.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Sensitive Range Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: VC-dimension dependence for Euclidean ball range spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(d\ge1\), the range space of all closed Euclidean balls on \(\mathbb R^d\) has VC dimension \(d+1\). Consequently, for every \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), the trace system \((X,\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ball}}^{d}(X))\) has VC dimension at most \(d+1\), and equality is attained by suitable finite sets \(X\). In particular, interval ranges have VC dimension \(2\), while planar disk ranges have VC dimension \(3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean ball ranges have VC dimension d plus one; intervals therefore have dimension two and planar disks dimension three.
assumptions_latex: Ranges are induced by all closed Euclidean balls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ball}}^{d})=d+1\) and \(\operatorname{VCdim}(X,\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ball}}^{d}(X))\le d+1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The VC-dimension claim is a theorem rather than a generic property, although its subject matches the dimension-sensitive leaf. The exact value, trace bound, and attainment assertion require an authoritative theorem or section locator before a corrected theorem record can be reviewed.

children.title: Rectangular Range Systems
children.top_down_role: Range spaces induced by rectangular regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rect}}(P)=\{P\cap([a,b]\times[c,d]):a\le b,\ c\le d\}\).

notation.meaning: Finite ground set of planar points
Family of subsets induced by closed axis-aligned rectangles

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite planar point ranges induced by closed axis-aligned rectangles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite set \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^2\), the rectangular range system on \(P\) is the range space \((P,\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rect}}(P))\), where
\[
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rect}}(P)=\bigl\{P\cap([a,b]\times[c,d]):a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R},\ a\le b,\ c\le d\bigr\}.
\]
Thus every range consists exactly of the points of \(P\) contained in one closed rectangle whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rectangular range system consists of the subsets of a finite planar point set cut out by closed axis-aligned rectangles.
knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Range Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise and fits the rectangular-range-system leaf, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied. Source support is required before the endpoint and boundedness convention can be reviewed as candidate knowledge.

children.title: Orthogonal Range Systems
children.top_down_role: Axis-aligned range spaces governed by coordinate order.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{R}_{\perp}(X)=\{X\cap\prod_{i=1}^d I_i:I_i\text{ is an interval in }\mathbb{R}\}\).

notation.meaning: Ground set in a fixed coordinate system
Orthogonal range family on the ground set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Products of bounded or unbounded coordinate intervals in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). An orthogonal range is a set
\[
X\cap\prod_{i=1}^d I_i,
\]
where each \(I_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is an interval, possibly bounded, unbounded, open, closed, or half-open. The orthogonal range system is \((X,\mathcal{R}_{\perp}(X))\), with
\[
\mathcal{R}_{\perp}(X)=\left\{X\cap\prod_{i=1}^d I_i:I_i\text{ is an interval for every }i\right\}.
\]
The coordinate axes and endpoint convention are part of the specified system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonal range system is induced by Cartesian products of coordinate intervals, which may be bounded or unbounded and may use specified endpoint conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal Range Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the orthogonal-range-system leaf, but its formula ranges over all intervals while the final sentence says the endpoint convention is specified as part of the system. A source is needed to determine whether the intended family permits all interval types or fixes one endpoint convention.

children.title: Axis-Aligned Box Ranges
children.top_down_role: Higher-dimensional orthogonal ranges induced by boxes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{box}}(X)=\{X\cap\prod_{i=1}^d[a_i,b_i]:a_i\le b_i\}\).

notation.meaning: Ranges induced by closed bounded axis-aligned boxes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed bounded boxes in a fixed coordinate frame.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), an axis-aligned box range is \(X\cap B\), where
\[
B=\prod_{i=1}^d[a_i,b_i],\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb{R},\quad a_i\le b_i.
\]
The associated range family is
\[
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{box}}(X)=\left\{X\cap\prod_{i=1}^d[a_i,b_i]:a_i\le b_i\text{ for every }i\right\}.
\]
Degenerate boxes with \(a_i=b_i\) are included; unbounded coordinate intervals are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Axis-aligned box ranges are intersections of the ground set with closed bounded Cartesian products of coordinate intervals.
knowledge_statements.title: Axis-Aligned Box Ranges

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed, bounded axis-aligned-box definition is precise and appropriate for this leaf, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Orientation-Sensitive Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between axis-aligned ranges and freely oriented rectangles.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U(B)\) is axis-aligned in the original frame if and only if \(U\) is a signed permutation matrix.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of orthogonal-box boundaries on the chosen coordinate orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^d[a_i,b_i]\) with \(a_i<b_i\), and let \(U\) be orthogonal. The facets of \(B\) have outward normals among \(\{\pm e_i:1\le i\le d\}\), while those of \(U(B)\) have normals among \(\{\pm Ue_i:1\le i\le d\}\). Consequently, \(U(B)\) is axis-aligned in the original coordinate frame if and only if \(U\) maps coordinate axes onto coordinate axes, equivalently, if and only if \(U\) is a signed permutation matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rotating a full-dimensional axis-aligned box preserves axis alignment exactly when the rotation only permutes coordinate axes and reverses their signs.
knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Sensitive Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically plausible and fits the orientation-sensitive-boundaries leaf, but no source is supplied. The plain statement also calls every orthogonal transformation a rotation even though signed permutation matrices may include reflections; the intended orientation convention should be source-checked.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VCdim}(X,\mathcal{R})\le k\) exactly when no \((k+1)\)-point subset of \(X\) is shattered.

notation.meaning: Trace family on a finite subset

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interprets dimension as VC dimension of the incidence range space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A subset \(Y\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(\mathcal{R}\) when
\[
\{R\cap Y:R\in\mathcal{R}\}=2^Y.
\]
The range space \((X,\mathcal{R})\) has dimension bounded by \(k\) when \(\operatorname{VCdim}(X,\mathcal{R})\le k\), meaning that no subset of \(X\) having \(k+1\) elements is shattered. Equivalently, every finite \(Y\subseteq X\) with \(|Y|=k+1\) satisfies
\[
\bigl|\{R\cap Y:R\in\mathcal{R}\}\bigr|<2^{k+1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A range space has VC dimension at most k precisely when it cannot realize every subset of any (k+1)-point ground subset.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Dimension Range Spaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The VC-dimension condition is standard and internally correct, but the title alone does not establish that bounded dimension means bounded VC dimension rather than bounded ambient geometric dimension. An authoritative range-space source with a specific locator is needed to resolve the local sense.

children.title: Set-System Polyhedral Certificate Calculus
children.top_down_role: Incidence-system relaxations, blocker relations, integrality classes, and bound-producing certificates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(A)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n:Ax\ge\mathbf{1}\}\).

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix with elements as rows and selectable sets as columns

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard nonnegative covering polyhedron of a finite incidence matrix.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), its covering polyhedron is
\[
Q(A)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n:Ax\ge\mathbf{1}\}.
\]
Each coordinate \(x_j\) assigns nonnegative multiplicity to column \(j\), and each row inequality requires total incident multiplicity at least one. Thus the integral points of \(Q(A)\) encode integral multiset covers; binary covers are the integral points additionally satisfying \(x\le\mathbf{1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The covering polyhedron contains nonnegative column weights that give every incidence-matrix row total weight at least one.
knowledge_statements.title: Covering Polyhedra

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(A)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n:Ax\le\mathbf{1}\}\).

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix with resources as rows and selectable objects as columns

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard unit-capacity packing polyhedron of a finite incidence matrix.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), its unit-capacity packing polyhedron is
\[
P(A)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n:Ax\le\mathbf{1}\}.
\]
Each coordinate \(x_j\) assigns nonnegative weight to column \(j\), while every row has total incident weight at most one. The binary points of \(P(A)\) encode collections of columns in which no row is incident with more than one selected column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The packing polyhedron contains nonnegative column weights whose total on every incidence-matrix row is at most one.
knowledge_statements.title: Packing Polyhedra

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(A)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n:Ax=\mathbf{1}\}\).

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix with elements as rows and selectable sets as columns

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact unit-incidence partitioning polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), its partitioning polyhedron is
\[
E(A)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n:Ax=\mathbf{1}\}.
\]
Every row must receive total incident weight exactly one. Consequently, a binary point \(x\in E(A)\cap\{0,1\}^n\) selects columns whose incident row sets form an exact cover: each row is incident with exactly one selected column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The partitioning polyhedron requires nonnegative column weights that give each incidence-matrix row total weight exactly one.
knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning Polyhedra

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fractional stable sets and fractional edge covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the hypergraph fractional packing and covering objects and their optimal-value parameters; it does not yet assert equality of the two values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a hypergraph. A fractional stable set is a function \(x:V\to\mathbb R_+\) such that \(\sum_{v\in F}x_v\le 1\) for every \(F\in\mathcal E\). A fractional edge cover is a function \(y:\mathcal E\to\mathbb R_+\) such that \(\sum_{F\ni v}y_F\ge 1\) for every \(v\in V\). Their respective maximum and minimum sizes are denoted by \(\alpha^*(H)\) and \(\rho^*(H)\), where size is the sum of the vector components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional stable set gives nonnegative weights to vertices with total weight at most one on every edge. A fractional edge cover gives nonnegative weights to edges with total incident weight at least one at every vertex. Alpha-star and rho-star denote their maximum and minimum total weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha^*(H)=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}x_v:x\in\mathbb R_+^V,\ \sum_{v\in F}x_v\le1\ \forall F\in\mathcal E\right\},\quad \rho^*(H)=\min\left\{\sum_{F\in\mathcal E}y_F:y\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal E},\ \sum_{F\ni v}y_F\ge1\ \forall v\in V\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) and nonnegative column costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n\), the weighted fractional cover parameter is
\[
\tau^*(A,c)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n,\ Ax\ge\mathbf{1}\}.

For unit costs \(c=\mathbf{1}\), write \(\tau^*(A)\). If the covering polyhedron is empty, the extended-value convention assigns \(\tau^*(A,c)=+\infty\); otherwise the displayed minimum is attained.

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix with rows as covered elements and columns as selectable sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality lower certificate for weighted fractional covering.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\), \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{n}\), and suppose \(Q(A)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{n}:Ax\ge\mathbf{1}\}\) is nonempty. Define \(\tau^*(A,c)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in Q(A)\}\). Any vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{m}\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\) is a fractional packing certificate and gives the valid lower bound \(\tau^*(A,c)\ge\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite incidence matrix and nonnegative column costs, any nonnegative row weighting whose load on each column does not exceed that column's cost certifies a lower bound on the minimum fractional-cover cost.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible pair \((x,y)\) is primal-dual optimal if and only if \(x_j(c_j-(A^{\mathsf T}y)_j)=0\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(y_i((Ax)_i-1)=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\), \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{n}\). Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{n}\) be feasible for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge\mathbf{1}\}\), and let \(y\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{m}\) be feasible for \(\max\{\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\). The pair \((x,y)\) certifies mutual optimality if and only if \(x_j\bigl(c_j-(A^{\mathsf T}y)_j\bigr)=0\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(y_i\bigl((Ax)_i-1\bigr)=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Under these conditions, \(c^{\mathsf T}x=\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated finite weighted cover-packing linear-program pair, feasible cover and packing vectors are both optimal exactly when every positive variable has a tight opposing constraint; their objective values then agree.

children.title: Ideal Hypergraphs
children.top_down_role: Hypergraph instances belonging to the ideal structural class.

assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,\mathcal{E})\) is a finite hypergraph with incidence matrix \(A_H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is ideal exactly when every extreme point of \(Q(H)=\{x\ge0:A_Hx\ge\mathbf{1}\}\) is integral.

notation.meaning: Vertex-edge incidence matrix of the hypergraph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideality defined through integrality of the hypergraph edge-covering polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=(V,\mathcal{E})\) be a finite hypergraph and let \(A_H\in\{0,1\}^{V\times\mathcal{E}}\) satisfy \((A_H)_{vE}=1\) exactly when \(v\in E\). Define
\[
Q(H)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{\mathcal{E}}:A_Hx\ge\mathbf{1}\}.
\]
The hypergraph \(H\) is ideal when \(Q(H)\) is an integral polyhedron, equivalently, when every extreme point of \(Q(H)\) has integral coordinates. Under this convention, hypergraph ideality is precisely ideality of its specified incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite hypergraph is ideal when every vertex of its nonnegative edge-covering polyhedron is integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Ideal Hypergraphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines integrality of an edge-covering polyhedron built from a vertex-by-edge incidence matrix. Standard ideal-hypergraph or ideal-clutter terminology commonly applies ideality to a covering polyhedron whose variables index vertices and whose constraints index hyperedges, so the transpose convention may instead describe ideality of a dual incidence system. Because no source is supplied, the intended convention and correspondence cannot be validated reliably.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restriction-wise transversal equality and integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes restriction-wise equality of integral and fractional transversal numbers by integrality of the fractional optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every hypergraph \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\), the following are equivalent: \((i)\ \tau(H')=\tau^*(H')\) for every restriction \(H'\) of \(H\); \((ii)\ \tau^*(H')\in\mathbb Z\) for every restriction \(H'\) of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any hypergraph, equality of the integral and fractional transversal numbers on every restriction is equivalent to integrality of the fractional transversal number on every restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall H'\text{ restriction of }H,\ \tau(H')=\tau^*(H')\bigr]\iff\bigl[\forall H'\text{ restriction of }H,\ \tau^*(H')\in\mathbb Z\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of ideal hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes ideality through weighted covers, minor conditions, integrality of fractional transversal values, and a restricted weight test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any hypergraph \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\), the following are equivalent: (i) \(\tau(H^w)=\tau^*(H^w)\) for every \(w:V\to\mathbb Z_+\); (ii) for every minor \(H'\) of \(H\), one has \(H'\neq J_n\) for every \(n\ge 3\) and \(\tau(H')r_{\min}(H')\le |V(H')|\); (iii) \(\tau^*(H')\in\mathbb Z\) for every minor \(H'\) of \(H\); (iv) \(\tau(H')=\tau^*(H')\) for every minor \(H'\) of \(H\); (v) \(\tau(H^w)=\tau^*(H^w)\) for every \(w:V\to\{0,1,|V|\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hypergraph is ideal exactly when every minor avoids all J_n for n at least three and satisfies the stated transversal-number and minimum-edge-size inequality. Equivalently, every minor has an integral fractional transversal value, every minor has equal integral and fractional transversal values, or weighted equality holds for all weights valued in 0, 1, and |V|.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i)--(v) are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fractional vertex-cover polyhedron and ideal hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ideality through integrality of the fractional vertex-cover polyhedron and records invariance under minimal-edge reduction and upward closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a hypergraph \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\), define \(P_H:=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x_v\geq0\ (v\in V),\ x(F)\geq1\ (F\in\mathcal E)\}\). The hypergraph \(H\) is ideal if \(P_H\) is integral. Moreover, \(H\) is ideal if and only if \(H^{\min}\) is ideal, if and only if \(H^{\uparrow}\) is ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fractional vertex-cover polyhedron consists of nonnegative vertex weights whose sum on every edge is at least one. A hypergraph is ideal when this polyhedron is integral, and ideality is unchanged by taking minimal edges or upward closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is ideal}\iff P_H\text{ is integral},\qquad H\text{ is ideal}\iff H^{\min}\text{ is ideal}\iff H^{\uparrow}\text{ is ideal}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ideality under hypergraph composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation and reflection of ideality under substitution-style composition of two vertex-disjoint hypergraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H'=(V',\mathcal E')\) and \(H''=(V'',\mathcal E'')\) be hypergraphs with \(V'\cap V''=\varnothing\), and choose \(v\in V'\). Define \(V=(V'\setminus\{v\})\cup V''\) and \(\mathcal E=\{E'\in\mathcal E':v\notin E'\}\cup\{(E'\setminus\{v\})\cup E'':E'\in\mathcal E',\ v\in E',\ E''\in\mathcal E''\}\), and let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\). Then \(H\) is ideal if and only if \(H'\) and \(H''\) are both ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a selected vertex of one hypergraph by a disjoint second hypergraph as specified. The resulting composition is ideal exactly when both component hypergraphs are ideal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of perfect hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equates clique representation, contraction conditions, polyhedral integrality, total dual integrality, antiblocker perfection, and numerical conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) satisfy \(\bigcup\mathcal E=V\), and let \(M\) be its \(\mathcal E\times V\) incidence matrix. The following are equivalent: (i) \(H^{\max}\) consists of the maximal cliques of some perfect graph; (ii) \(\alpha(H')=\rho(H')\) for every contraction \(H'\) of \(H\); (iii) \(H\) is perfect, that is, \(\{x\geq\mathbf0\mid Mx\leq\mathbf1\}\) is an integer polytope; (iv) the system \(x\geq\mathbf0,\ Mx\leq\mathbf1\) is totally dual integral; (v) \(a(H)\) is perfect; (vi) \(\alpha^*(H')\) is an integer for every contraction \(H'\) of \(H\); (vii) \(\rho_2(H')=2\rho(H')\) for every contraction \(H'\) of \(H\); and (viii) \(\alpha(H')r_{\max}(H')\geq|V(H')|\) for every contraction \(H'\) of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a hypergraph whose edges cover its vertex set, eight conditions are equivalent: maximal-clique representation by a perfect graph; alpha–rho equality for every contraction; perfection of the hypergraph; total dual integrality of its defining system; perfection of its antiblocker; integrality of alpha-star for every contraction; rho-sub-2 equality for every contraction; and the stated alpha–maximum-rank inequality for every contraction.
assumptions_latex: M\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal E\times V}\text{ is the incidence matrix of }H
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i)--(viii) are equivalent.}
