assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(F\) are finite nonempty sets, with service costs \(c_{ij}\ge 0\).
The symbols \(p\) and \(k\) impose the same exact facility-cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{p\text{-center}}(C,F,c,p)=\operatorname{OPT}_{k\text{-center}}(C,F,c,k)\) whenever \(p=k\) and the remaining data coincide.

notation.meaning: Nearest selected-facility cost of client i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: p-center and k-center are notationally identical when the data and cardinality parameters coincide
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Notational correspondence for finite discrete uncapacitated center models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For identical client set \(C\), candidate set \(F\), and costs \((c_{ij})\), the discrete \(p\)-center and discrete \(k\)-center formulations correspond under \(p=k\):
\[
\min_{S\subseteq F,\ |S|=p}\max_{i\in C}\min_{j\in S}c_{ij}
=
\min_{S\subseteq F,\ |S|=k}\max_{i\in C}\min_{j\in S}c_{ij}.
\]
They consequently have identical feasible sets, objective values, optimizers, and optimal radii. The term metric \(k\)-center additionally asserts that \(c_{ij}\) is induced by a metric; cardinality notation alone does not impose metric structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When p equals k and all other data agree, discrete p-center and k-center coincide; metric k-center adds a metric-cost assumption.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Parameterized Center Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The p=k center correspondence is mathematically precise and representation is appropriate, but the terminology claim requires a cited source.

children.title: Weighted Center Models
children.top_down_role: Center models with demand-specific weights.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(F\) are finite nonempty sets with costs \(c_{ij}\ge 0\).
Each client has weight \(w_i\ge 0\), and \(1\le p\le |F|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq F,\ |S|=p}\max_{i\in C}w_i c(i,S)\).

notation.meaning: Nearest open-facility cost for client i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a weighted center applies client weights multiplicatively before taking the bottleneck objective
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicatively weighted finite discrete \(p\)-center model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each facility set \(S\subseteq F\), define the weighted covering radius
\[
R_w(S):=\max_{i\in C}\left(w_i\min_{j\in S}c_{ij}\right).
\]
The multiplicatively weighted \(p\)-center problem is
\[
\min\left\{R_w(S):S\subseteq F,\ |S|=p\right\}.
\]
An optimizer minimizes the worst weighted service cost. Unit weights recover the ordinary \(p\)-center. A client with \(w_i=0\) imposes no restriction on the objective, whereas larger weights make a given physical service cost more consequential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose p facilities to minimize the largest client service cost after multiplying each client's cost by its nonnegative importance weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Center Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplicatively weighted p-center model is coherent, but its identification as the intended weighted-center model and its distinction from priority center require authoritative support.

children.title: Priority Center Models
children.top_down_role: Center models with explicit service priorities.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(F\) are finite nonempty sets with costs \(c_{ij}\ge 0\).
Each client has a positive service standard \(r_i>0\), and \(1\le p\le |F|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq F,\ |S|=p}\max_{i\in C}c(i,S)/r_i\).

notation.meaning: Positive target radius or service standard for client i.
Nearest open-facility cost for client i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: priority-center formulations commonly normalize client distances by client-specific service standards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Service-standard normalization version of priority \(p\)-center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assign each client \(i\in C\) a positive service standard \(r_i\). For \(S\subseteq F\), define
\[
\rho(S):=\max_{i\in C}\frac{c(i,S)}{r_i},
\qquad c(i,S):=\min_{j\in S}c_{ij}.
\]
The priority \(p\)-center model is
\[
\min\left\{\rho(S):S\subseteq F,\ |S|=p\right\}.
\]
The value \(\rho(S)\) is the smallest common dilation factor making every inequality \(c(i,S)\le \rho(S)r_i\) valid. Smaller \(r_i\) gives client \(i\) stricter priority. Equivalently, this is a weighted center with weights \(w_i=1/r_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the worst ratio of client service cost to its positive service standard; stricter standards give clients greater priority.
knowledge_statements.title: Priority Center Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized service-standard formulation is mathematically coherent, but priority-center conventions vary and no source establishes that this is the intended local sense.

children.title: Lexicographic Center Priorities
children.top_down_role: Center-location regimes using ordered priority classes.

assumptions_latex: Each client has weight \(w_i\ge 0\), and \(1\le p\le |F|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}^{\mathrm{lex}}_{S\subseteq F,\ |S|=p}\mathbf{z}^{\downarrow}(S)\).

notation.meaning: Weighted nearest-facility cost of client i.
Vector of weighted service costs sorted nonincreasingly.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: lexicographic center refines minimax by lexicographically minimizing the descending vector of client service costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descending-cost lexicographic refinement of weighted discrete \(p\)-center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each feasible \(S\subseteq F\), set
\[
z_i(S):=w_i\min_{j\in S}c_{ij},
\]
and let \(\mathbf{z}^{\downarrow}(S)=(z_{(1)}(S),\ldots,z_{(n)}(S))\) be these values sorted so that \(z_{(1)}(S)\ge\cdots\ge z_{(n)}(S)\). A lexicographic center is any feasible set \(S^*\) with \(|S^*|=p\) such that
\[
\mathbf{z}^{\downarrow}(S^*)\le_{\mathrm{lex}}\mathbf{z}^{\downarrow}(S)
\]
for every feasible \(S\). It first minimizes the worst weighted service cost, then the second worst among minimax-optimal sets, and continues through all ranks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lexicographically minimize the descending vector of weighted client service costs, refining minimax successively through the second-worst and later costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Lexicographic Center Priorities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The descending-vector lexicographic refinement is internally consistent, but its weighted convention and identification with lexicographic center priorities require a specific source.

knowledge_statements.title: Center Location with Outliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete metric p-center allowing at most z clients to remain unserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a finite facility set, \(D\) a nonempty finite client set, and \(d:F\times D\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) a distance function. For integers \(1\le p\le |F|\) and \(0\le z<|D|\), center location with outliers is
\[\min_{\substack{S\subseteq F,\ |S|\le p\\ O\subseteq D,\ |O|\le z}}\ \max_{j\in D\setminus O}\ \min_{i\in S} d(i,j).\]
The selected set \(S\) contains the centers, while \(O\) contains clients exempted from the radius requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose at most p centers and discard at most z clients so that the greatest distance from any remaining client to its nearest center is minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r^*=\min_{|S|\le p,\ |O|\le z}\max_{j\in D\setminus O}\min_{i\in S}d(i,j)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied. The feasible family permits S=empty, for which the inner minimum is undefined, and the scope calls the model metric although only nonnegativity of d is assumed. A source-supported revision should require a nonempty center set (commonly |S|=p) and clarify the distance assumptions.

children.title: Facility-System Extensions
children.top_down_role: Classical extensions retained by authoritative location-science structures.

children.title: Multi-Level Facility Location
children.top_down_role: Facility systems containing multiple operational levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Level Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated sequential-path formulation with finitely many facility levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let levels \(1,\ldots,L\) have finite candidate sets \(F_1,\ldots,F_L\), and let \(D\) be a finite client set. A feasible solution selects \(S_\ell\subseteq F_\ell\) and assigns each client \(j\) a path \((i_1,\ldots,i_L)\in S_1\times\cdots\times S_L\). With opening costs \(f_i^\ell\), client costs \(c^0_{ji_1}\), and consecutive-level costs \(c^\ell_{i_\ell i_{\ell+1}}\), multi-level facility location minimizes
\[\sum_{\ell=1}^L\sum_{i\in S_\ell}f_i^\ell+\sum_{j\in D}\left(c^0_{ji_1(j)}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L-1}c^\ell_{i_\ell(j)i_{\ell+1}(j)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Open facilities at several levels and assign every client through one open facility per level, minimizing opening and interlevel connection costs.
assumptions_latex: All opening and connection costs are nonnegative.
Each client must receive one complete level-by-level path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_1,\ldots,S_L\) and the client paths jointly minimize total opening and path cost.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is internally coherent as an uncapacitated sequential-path variant, and definition is an appropriate content kind, but multi-level facility location has several distinct formulations. A specific source and locator must support this exact path-cost model.

children.title: Hierarchical Facility Location
children.top_down_role: Facility systems organized by nested service hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ancestor-closed facility selection on a rooted hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=(V,A)\) be a rooted forest of candidate facilities, with parent map \(p(v)\) for every nonroot vertex. Binary variables \(y_v\) indicate opened facilities, and \(x_{jv}\) assign each client \(j\in D\) to an admissible facility \(v\in A_j\). Hierarchical facility location minimizes
\[\sum_{v\in V}f_vy_v+\sum_{j\in D}\sum_{v\in A_j}c_{jv}x_{jv}\]
subject to \(\sum_{v\in A_j}x_{jv}=1\), \(x_{jv}\le y_v\), and \(y_v\le y_{p(v)}\) for every nonroot \(v\). Thus every opened facility has all its ancestors open.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select an ancestor-closed collection of facilities in a rooted hierarchy and assign each client to one admissible open facility at minimum total cost.
assumptions_latex: Each admissible set \(A_j\subseteq V\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_v=1\) implies \(y_u=1\) for every ancestor \(u\) of \(v\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No evidence supports identifying hierarchical facility location specifically with ancestor-closed opening decisions. The symbol A is also used both for the forest arc set and within admissible sets A_j. The exact modeling sense and notation require a sourced revision.

children.title: Cross-Level Service Coupling
children.top_down_role: Dependencies linking decisions or service flows across facility levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Level Service Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency conditions linking service decisions at consecutive facility levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For consecutive levels \(\ell\) and \(\ell+1\), let \(y_i^\ell\) indicate that facility \(i\in F_\ell\) is open, and let \(q_{iu}^\ell\) indicate that open facility \(i\in F_\ell\) receives upstream service from \(u\in F_{\ell+1}\). Cross-level service coupling requires
\[\sum_{u\in F_{\ell+1}}q_{iu}^\ell=y_i^\ell,\qquad q_{iu}^\ell\le y_u^{\ell+1}\]
for every \(i\in F_\ell\), together with \(q_{iu}^\ell\in\{0,1\}\). Hence each open lower-level facility is linked to exactly one open facility at the next level, while closed lower-level facilities receive no such link.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every open facility at one level must be linked to exactly one open facility at the next level; closed facilities induce no link.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_u q_{iu}^\ell=y_i^\ell\) and \(q_{iu}^\ell\le y_u^{\ell+1}\) enforce consecutive-level service consistency.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the appropriate content kind, but no source supports this particular exactly-one upstream-link convention. The admissible range of level index ell and the encompassing number of levels are not explicitly introduced.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Period Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon dynamic location with opening, closing, and assignment decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For periods \(t=1,\ldots,T\), let \(y_{it}\) indicate whether facility \(i\in F\) operates, \(x_{ijt}\) whether client \(j\in D_t\) is assigned to it, and \(u_{it},v_{it}\) whether it opens or closes. Multi-period facility location minimizes
\[\sum_{t=1}^T\left(\sum_i(f_{it}y_{it}+a_{it}u_{it}+b_{it}v_{it})+\sum_{i,j}c_{ijt}x_{ijt}\right)\]
subject to \(\sum_i x_{ijt}=1\), \(x_{ijt}\le y_{it}\), and \(y_{it}-y_{i,t-1}=u_{it}-v_{it}\), with a specified initial state \(y_{i0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Plan facility operation and client assignment over time while charging operating, opening, closing, and service costs and enforcing interperiod state transitions.
assumptions_latex: \(F\), every \(D_t\), and the horizon \(\{1,\ldots,T\}\) are finite.
The initial operating state \(y_{i0}\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y,u,v)\) minimizes total horizon cost while satisfying assignment and facility-state transitions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports this particular dynamic formulation. The domains of the objective sums should be explicit, and a source should confirm the opening/closing transition convention and whether simultaneous opening and closing must be excluded.

knowledge_statements.title: Competitive Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure-strategy Stackelberg location under nearest-facility customer choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be weighted clients in a metric space, and let \(F_L,F_R\) be finite leader and rival candidate sets. The leader chooses \(S\subseteq F_L\) with \(|S|\le p\); after observing \(S\), the rival chooses \(T\subseteq F_R\) with \(|T|\le q\). Under a fixed tie rule, client \(j\) is captured by the leader when \(d(j,S)<d(j,T)\). The Stackelberg competitive location value is
\[\max_{|S|\le p}\ \min_{T\in\operatorname{BR}(S)}\sum_{j\in D}w_j\mathbf{1}\{d(j,S)<d(j,T)\},\]
where \(\operatorname{BR}(S)\) is the rival's specified best-response set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A leader locates facilities first, a rival responds, and the leader optimizes captured client weight under nearest-facility choice and an explicit tie rule.
assumptions_latex: The rival objective and customer tie rule are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*\in\arg\max_{|S|\le p}\min_{T\in\operatorname{BR}(S)}\sum_jw_j\mathbf{1}\{d(j,S)<d(j,T)\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rival objective defining BR(S) is not given, so the displayed value is not mathematically determined. Moreover, strict inequality implements a specific rival-favoring tie rule rather than an arbitrary fixed tie rule. Competitive location has multiple game models, so an exact source-supported formulation is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario version with one facility set shared by all demand scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a finite facility set and \(\Omega\) a finite family of demand scenarios, where scenario \(\omega\) has clients \(D_\omega\) and service costs \(c_{ij}^\omega\). A universal facility solution selects one set \(S\subseteq F\) before the scenario is known; after \(\omega\) is revealed, each client is assigned to its cheapest facility in \(S\). In the worst-case finite-scenario formulation, the objective is
\[\min_{S\subseteq F}\left\{\sum_{i\in S}f_i+\max_{\omega\in\Omega}\sum_{j\in D_\omega}\min_{i\in S}c_{ij}^\omega\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one facility set before demand is revealed, then adapt assignments to each scenario while minimizing opening cost plus worst-case service cost.
assumptions_latex: Every scenario has a finite client set.
Opening and service costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*\) minimizes fixed opening cost plus the greatest scenario-dependent assignment cost.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The title can refer to universal, robust, or simultaneous-approximation formulations, and no source establishes that this worst-case finite-scenario model is the intended sense. The feasible family also permits S=empty although the service-cost minimum over S is undefined unless an extended-value convention is stated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facility-cost bound under approximate star-and-comet local optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal facility-location cost-component inequality under the stated approximate local-optimality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,x^*\) be feasible solutions to a given instance. If \(c^x(A,\delta)\ge -\frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal F|}c(x)\) for every star or comet \(A\) and every \(\delta\in\Delta_A^x\), then \(c_F(x)\le 4c_F(x^*)+2c_S(x^*)+2c_S(x)+\epsilon c(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let x and x* be feasible solutions. If every admissible star or comet modification satisfies the stated approximate local-optimality inequality, then the facility-cost component of x is at most four times that of x*, plus twice the service-cost component of x*, twice that of x, and epsilon times the total cost of x.
assumptions_latex: x,x^*\text{ are feasible solutions to the given instance}
\forall A\text{ that is a star or comet},\ \forall\delta\in\Delta_A^x:\ c^x(A,\delta)\ge -\frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal F|}c(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_F(x)\le 4c_F(x^*)+2c_S(x^*)+2c_S(x)+\epsilon c(x)

children.title: Location–Routing Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Coupling between facility-location decisions and route design.

knowledge_statements.title: Location–Routing Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated location-routing model with routes based at selected depots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be candidate depots, \(D\) clients with demands \(q_j\), and let \(\mathcal R_i\) be feasible vehicle routes beginning and ending at depot \(i\), each serving total demand at most \(Q\). With route cost \(c_r\), opening cost \(f_i\), depot variables \(y_i\), and route variables \(z_r\), the location-routing problem is
\[\min\sum_{i\in F}f_iy_i+\sum_i\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_i}c_rz_r\]
subject to \(\sum_i\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_i:j\in r}z_r=1\) for every client and \(z_r\le y_i\) for every \(r\in\mathcal R_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Open depots and choose capacity-feasible depot-based routes so that every client is visited once at minimum opening and routing cost.
assumptions_latex: \(F\), \(D\), and every route family \(\mathcal R_i\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y,z)\) jointly minimizes depot-opening and vehicle-routing cost while serving each client exactly once.

notation.meaning: feasible routes based at depot i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The route-based capacitated location-routing definition is mathematically coherent and fits the interface leaf, but no facility-location or location-routing citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Location–Logistics Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Coupling between facility location and broader logistics systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Location–Logistics Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facility selection coupled to capacitated commodity movement through a logistics network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a directed logistics network, let \(F\subseteq V\) be candidate facilities, and let \(K\) index commodities. Binary \(y_i\) opens facility \(i\), while \(x_e^k\ge 0\) is commodity flow. A location-logistics model minimizes
\[\sum_{i\in F}f_iy_i+\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{e\in E}c_e^kx_e^k\]
subject to commodity flow conservation at every node, arc capacities \(\sum_kx_e^k\le u_e\), and facility throughput bounds \(\sum_k h_i^k(x^k)\le U_iy_i\). Thus no commodity may enter, leave, or be processed by a closed facility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose facilities and commodity flows together, enforcing network conservation, arc capacities, and zero throughput at closed facilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y,x)\) minimizes facility and logistics costs subject to conservation and capacity coupling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this generic location-logistics formulation. The throughput functional h_i^k is undefined, and the displayed aggregate bound does not by itself justify the stronger claim that no commodity may enter, leave, or be processed at a closed facility.

children.title: Integrated Service-Network Design
children.top_down_role: Joint organization of facilities, movements, and service networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrated Service-Network Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint selection of service facilities, network edges, and client connections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph, \(F\subseteq V\) candidate facilities, and \(D\subseteq V\) clients. Binary variables \(y_i\), \(z_e\), and \(x_{ij}\) select facilities, network edges, and client assignments. Integrated service-network design minimizes
\[\sum_{i\in F}f_iy_i+\sum_{e\in E}c_ez_e+\sum_{j\in D}\sum_{i\in F}a_{ij}x_{ij}\]
subject to \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\), \(x_{ij}\le y_i\), and, whenever \(x_{ij}=1\), vertices \(i\) and \(j\) lie in the same connected component of the selected subgraph \((V,\{e:z_e=1\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select facilities and network edges jointly, assigning every client to an open facility connected to it by the designed network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every assigned client is connected through selected edges to its assigned open facility, and total design and service cost is minimized.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint facility, edge, and assignment model fits the leaf and definition role, but integrated service-network design admits multiple connectivity and service formulations. No cited source supports this exact connected-assignment version.

children.top_down_role: Location models driven by service thresholds, coverage benefit, redundancy, uncertainty, or avoidance.

knowledge_statements.title: Location Set Covering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical binary covering model at a fixed service radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be demand points, \(F\) candidate facilities, and \(R\ge 0\) a service radius. Define \(a_{ij}=1\) exactly when facility \(i\) covers demand point \(j\), for example when \(d(i,j)\le R\). With opening costs \(f_i\ge 0\), the location set covering problem is
\[\min_{y\in\{0,1\}^{F}}\sum_{i\in F}f_iy_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{i\in F}a_{ij}y_i\ge 1\quad(j\in D).\]
For unit opening costs, the objective minimizes the number of selected facilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a minimum-cost collection of facilities so that every demand point lies within the prescribed coverage relation of at least one selected facility.
assumptions_latex: Every demand point is coverable by at least one candidate facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^*\) has minimum opening cost among all facility sets covering every \(j\in D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is a precise standard location set-covering definition and the content kind is appropriate, but no authoritative coverage-location source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Covering Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical budgeted model maximizing covered demand weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be demand points with weights \(w_j\ge 0\), let \(F\) be candidate facilities, and let \(a_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether facility \(i\) covers point \(j\). Given a facility budget \(p\), the maximal covering location problem is
\[\max\sum_{j\in D}w_jz_j\]
subject to \(z_j\le\sum_{i\in F}a_{ij}y_i\) for every \(j\), \(\sum_{i\in F}y_i\le p\), and \(y_i,z_j\in\{0,1\}\). A point contributes its weight only when at least one selected facility covers it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose at most p facilities to maximize the total weight of demand points covered by at least one chosen facility.
assumptions_latex: Coverage by multiple facilities is counted once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_jw_jz_j\) is maximized over all selections of at most \(p\) facilities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is a precise standard maximal covering location definition and the content kind is appropriate, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate facility set \(J\) are finite.
Coverage coefficients satisfy \(a_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), demand weights satisfy \(w_i\ge 0\), and the required covered weight is \(Q\in[0,\sum_{i\in I}w_i]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min \left\{\sum_{j\in J}c_jx_j:\ y_i\le \sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_j\ \forall i\in I,\ \sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\ge Q,\ x_j,y_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Binary decision that candidate site j is opened.
Binary indicator that demand point i is counted as covered.
Minimum total demand weight required to be covered.

review_flags: Exact partial-covering convention and authoritative location-model source are required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost partial covering with an aggregate covered-demand requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given finite demand and facility sets \(I\) and \(J\), opening costs \(c_j\ge 0\), demand weights \(w_i\ge 0\), and incidence coefficients \(a_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), partial covering location selects open sites while requiring only a prescribed aggregate amount of demand to be covered. Its binary formulation is
\[\min \left\{\sum_{j\in J}c_jx_j:\ y_i\le \sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_j\ \forall i\in I,\ \sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\ge Q,\ x_j,y_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]
Demand not represented by \(y_i=1\) may remain uncovered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Open minimum-cost facilities so that the total weight of covered demand reaches a prescribed target, while permitting some demand to remain uncovered.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Covering Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-cost aggregate-quota formulation is mathematically coherent and fits partial covering location, but no source is cited. An authoritative location-model source is required to establish that this exact quota convention is intended.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate facility set \(J\) are finite.
Each demand point has a required multiplicity \(r_i\in\mathbb Z_+\), and \(a_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) records coverage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min \left\{\sum_{j\in J}c_jx_j:\ \sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_j\ge r_i\ \forall i\in I,\ x_j\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Binary decision that facility j is opened.
Number of distinct open facilities required to cover demand i.
Coverage incidence between demand i and site j.

review_flags: Authoritative source for the selected heterogeneous multiplicity formulation is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic multiple coverage by distinct open facilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite demand points \(I\) and candidate sites \(J\), let \(a_{ij}=1\) exactly when a facility at \(j\) covers demand \(i\). Given opening costs \(c_j\ge 0\) and integer coverage requirements \(r_i\ge 1\), multiple-coverage location is
\[\min \left\{\sum_{j\in J}c_jx_j:\ \sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_j\ge r_i\ \forall i\in I,\ x_j\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]
Thus every demand point is covered by at least \(r_i\) distinct selected sites; the uniform case uses \(r_i=r\) for all \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost sites so every demand point lies within the coverage sets of a prescribed number of distinct open facilities.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Coverage Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The heterogeneous multiplicity formulation is coherent and fits multiple-coverage location, but it has no supporting citation. A source must establish the intended distinct-facility and demand-specific multiplicity convention.

assumptions_latex: Demand and candidate-site sets \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.
Primary assignments are fixed or jointly selected, and a backup must use a distinct open facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[z_{ij}\le a_{ij}x_j,\qquad \sum_{j\in J}z_{ij}=1,\qquad z_{i,p(i)}=0\quad (i\in I).\]

notation.meaning: Binary assignment of facility j as the backup for demand i.
Coverage incidence between demand i and facility j.

review_flags: Backup-coverage objectives differ across the literature; a source is needed to fix the intended variant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit primary-and-backup assignment model with distinct facilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p(i)\in J\) denote the primary facility assigned to each demand point \(i\in I\). A backup-coverage location solution opens sites using \(x_j\in\{0,1\}\) and selects binary backup assignments \(z_{ij}\) satisfying
\[z_{ij}\le a_{ij}x_j,\qquad \sum_{j\in J}z_{ij}=1,\qquad z_{i,p(i)}=0\quad (i\in I).\]
Hence each demand has a covering open backup distinct from its primary facility. A model may minimize opening and assignment costs or maximize the weight receiving such backup coverage, but the displayed constraints define backup feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign every demand point a covering open backup facility distinct from its primary facility; objectives may price or maximize this backup protection.
knowledge_statements.title: Backup-Coverage Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed constraints describe a distinct covering backup, but the record does not state constraints ensuring that the primary facility p(i) is open and covers i. More importantly, no source fixes this assignment-based variant among the differing backup-coverage models.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate-site set \(J\) are finite.
At most \(f\in\mathbb Z_+\) opened facilities may fail simultaneously, and failures are arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_j\ge f+1\quad\text{for every }i\in I.\]

notation.meaning: Maximum number of simultaneous facility failures.
Binary decision that facility j is opened.
Coverage incidence between demand i and facility j.

review_flags: Authoritative source for the cardinality-failure interpretation is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust coverage against arbitrary cardinality-bounded facility failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an opened set represented by \(x_j\in\{0,1\}\), complete coverage after every failure set \(F\subseteq J\) with \(|F|\le f\) means
\[\sum_{j\in J\setminus F}a_{ij}x_j\ge 1\quad\text{for every }i\in I\text{ and every }F\subseteq J\text{ with }|F|\le f.\]
Under independent site failures and binary coverage, this robust condition is equivalent to
\[\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_j\ge f+1\quad\text{for every }i\in I.\]
Thus loss of any \(f\) selected facilities leaves at least one covering facility for each demand point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A location plan is fault tolerant to any f facility failures exactly when each demand point is initially covered by at least f+1 open facilities.
knowledge_statements.title: Fault-Tolerant Coverage Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The f+1 multiplicity condition is correct for protection against arbitrary failure of up to f selected facilities and the content kind condition fits the record. No authoritative source is supplied, and the phrase "independent site failures" is inapposite to the stated adversarial cardinality-bounded model.

assumptions_latex: Demand points \(I\) and candidate sites \(J\) are finite.
Each response function \(g_i:[0,\infty]\to[0,1]\) is nonincreasing, with \(g_i(\infty)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max \left\{\sum_{i\in I}w_i g_i\!\left(\min_{j:x_j=1}d_{ij}\right):\ x\in X\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Distance or generalized service disutility from demand i to site j.
Coverage response of demand i as a function of nearest-service distance.
Feasible set of binary facility-opening vectors.

review_flags: A source is needed to select among gradual-cover formulations using nearest, additive, or probabilistic response.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearest-facility coverage benefit that decays continuously or stepwise with distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\) encode feasible facility selections, and define the nearest-open-facility distance by \(D_i(x)=\min_{j:x_j=1}d_{ij}\), with \(D_i(x)=\infty\) if no site opens. Given nonincreasing response functions \(g_i:[0,\infty]\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(g_i(\infty)=0\), gradual coverage maximizes
\[\sum_{i\in I}w_i g_i(D_i(x))\quad\text{over }x\in X.\]
Unlike binary coverage, the contribution of demand \(i\) may take intermediate values and weakly decreases as its nearest selected facility becomes farther away.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize demand benefit when coverage decreases gradually, rather than discontinuously, with distance to the nearest open facility.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradual Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nearest-facility response formulation is internally coherent and fits one standard sense of gradual coverage, but no citation establishes this aggregation convention rather than additive or probabilistic gradual coverage.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\), candidate sites \(J\), and allowable radii \(R_j\) are finite.
Selecting radius \(r\in R_j\) at site \(j\) incurs cost \(c_{jr}\), and at most one radius is selected per site.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max \left\{\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i:\ y_i\le\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{r\in R_j:\ d_{ij}\le r}u_{jr},\ \sum_{r\in R_j}u_{jr}\le1,\ \sum_{j,r}c_{jr}u_{jr}\le B,\ u_{jr},y_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Binary choice of opening site j with service radius r.
Finite allowable radius set for site j.
Binary indicator that demand i is covered.

review_flags: A source is required to fix whether radii are discrete, continuous, or capacity induced.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete endogenous service radii with radius-dependent opening costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each candidate site \(j\), let \(R_j\) be a finite set of allowable radii and let \(u_{jr}=1\) select site \(j\) at radius \(r\). Variable-radius coverage requires \(\sum_{r\in R_j}u_{jr}\le1\) and permits demand indicator \(y_i=1\) only if
\[y_i\le\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{r\in R_j:\ d_{ij}\le r}u_{jr}.\]
With radius-dependent costs \(c_{jr}\) and budget \(B\), a canonical objective is to maximize \(\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\) subject to \(\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{r\in R_j}c_{jr}u_{jr}\le B\) and binary decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jointly choose facility sites and their service radii, paying radius-dependent costs and maximizing the demand lying within at least one chosen radius.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Radius Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The discrete radius-choice model fits variable-radius coverage, but no source establishes the discrete, radius-costed variant. The record also does not explicitly state domains for distances, budget, and demand weights.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate-site set \(J\) are finite.
Benefits satisfy \(b_{ij}\ge0\), with \(b_{ij}=0\) when site \(j\) gives no useful coverage to demand \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max\left\{\sum_{i\in I}w_i z_i:\ z_i\le b_{ij}+M_i(1-x_j)\ \forall i,j,\ 0\le z_i\le M_i,\ x\in X\right\},\qquad M_i=\max_{j\in J}b_{ij}.\]

notation.meaning: Benefit delivered to demand i by facility j.
Realized coverage benefit for demand i.
Feasible set of binary facility selections.

review_flags: Weighted-benefit coverage may instead mean additive benefit; a source is needed to resolve the aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-open-facility benefit aggregation with demand weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b_{ij}\ge0\) be the coverage benefit that site \(j\) can provide to demand \(i\), and let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\) describe feasible openings. Under best-facility aggregation, the realized benefit is
\[z_i(x)=\max\bigl(\{b_{ij}:x_j=1\}\cup\{0\}\bigr),\]
and weighted-benefit coverage solves
\[\max_{x\in X}\sum_{i\in I}w_i z_i(x).\]
This formulation distinguishes demand importance \(w_i\) from service benefit \(b_{ij}\); ordinary binary maximal coverage is recovered when \(b_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose facilities to maximize demand-weighted service benefit, where each demand point receives the greatest benefit offered by any open facility.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Benefit Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement defines coherent best-open-facility benefit aggregation, but no source establishes that interpretation of weighted-benefit coverage. Moreover, conclusion_latex is not a valid formulation of the stated maximum: its inequalities over every open j bound z_i by the minimum benefit among open facilities, not the maximum.

children.title: Capture Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage regimes based on demand capture or competitive attraction.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate sites \(J\) are finite.
For each demand point, facility attractiveness is nonnegative and total incumbent attractiveness is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{x\in X}\sum_{i\in I}w_i\frac{\sum_{j\in J}v_{ij}x_j}{h_i+\sum_{j\in J}v_{ij}x_j}.\]

notation.meaning: Attractiveness of candidate site j to demand i.
Aggregate attractiveness of incumbent alternatives to demand i.
Feasible set of binary facility selections.

review_flags: Capture coverage has several competitive-choice definitions; a source is required for the proportional-attraction version.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Competitive capture under a proportional-attraction response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_{ij}\ge0\) be the attractiveness of candidate facility \(j\) to demand \(i\), let \(h_i>0\) be the total attractiveness of incumbent alternatives, and let \(x\in X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\). Under proportional attraction, the fraction of demand \(i\) captured by the selected facilities is
\[q_i(x)=\frac{\sum_{j\in J}v_{ij}x_j}{h_i+\sum_{j\in J}v_{ij}x_j}.\]
Capture coverage selects \(x\in X\) to maximize \(\sum_{i\in I}w_iq_i(x)\). The response is endogenous because adding or removing selected sites changes the captured fraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select facilities to maximize competitively captured demand, with each demand fraction determined by candidate attractiveness relative to incumbents and selected candidates.
knowledge_statements.title: Capture Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proportional-attraction objective is mathematically coherent, but "capture coverage" admits multiple competitive-choice models and no source supports this exact one. The domain and nonnegativity of demand weights w_i are also not introduced.

children.title: Threshold Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage regimes activated by service or benefit thresholds.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate-site set \(J\) are finite.
Each demand point has a threshold \(\tau_i\ge0\), and contributions satisfy \(s_{ij}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y_i=\mathbf 1\!\left\{\sum_{j\in J}s_{ij}x_j\ge\tau_i\right\},\qquad \max_{x\in X}\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i.\]

notation.meaning: Contribution of open site j toward covering demand i.
Binary threshold-coverage indicator for demand i.

review_flags: A source is needed to determine whether the intended threshold acts on distance, count, capacity, or aggregate attraction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary coverage triggered by an aggregate service threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible facility selection \(x\in X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\), define the aggregate service received by demand point \(i\) as \(S_i(x)=\sum_{j\in J}s_{ij}x_j\), where \(s_{ij}\ge0\). Given threshold \(\tau_i\ge0\), demand \(i\) is threshold-covered precisely when
\[y_i=\mathbf 1\!\left\{S_i(x)\ge\tau_i\right\}.\]
A canonical threshold-coverage problem maximizes \(\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\) over \(x\in X\). Thus subthreshold service contributes no covered-demand credit, while attaining the threshold yields the full weight \(w_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A demand point counts as covered only when the aggregate service contributed by selected facilities reaches its prescribed threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aggregate-service threshold definition is coherent, but no source establishes that the leaf refers to this convention rather than a distance, count, capacity, or attraction threshold. The demand weights w_i are used without an explicit domain.

children.title: Threshold-Triggered Capture
children.top_down_role: Capture regimes whose outcomes change at specified thresholds.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate-site set \(J\) are finite.
Capture responses \(q_i(x)\in[0,1]\) and activation thresholds \(\theta_i\in(0,1]\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y_i=\mathbf 1\!\left\{q_i(x)\ge\theta_i\right\},\qquad \max_{x\in X}\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i.\]

notation.meaning: Captured fraction or capture score of demand i under selection x.
Minimum capture response required to activate demand i.
Binary indicator that capture is triggered for demand i.

review_flags: A source is required to establish the intended capture response and whether activation is binary or discontinuous payoff.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary capture payoff activated when endogenous capture reaches a threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q_i(x)\in[0,1]\) denote the capture response of demand point \(i\) generated by a feasible facility selection \(x\in X\), and let \(\theta_i\in(0,1]\). Threshold-triggered capture defines
\[y_i=\mathbf 1\!\left\{q_i(x)\ge\theta_i\right\}.\]
The associated location problem maximizes \(\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\) over \(x\in X\). Consequently, a positive captured fraction below \(\theta_i\) receives no activation credit, whereas reaching or exceeding \(\theta_i\) captures the full modeled weight \(w_i\). This couples an endogenous capture response to a discontinuous threshold payoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Demand yields capture credit only when its endogenous captured fraction reaches a specified threshold; below that threshold, it yields none.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Triggered Capture

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The thresholded capture response is internally coherent and matches the coupling suggested by the path, but it is unsupported by a citation. The feasible set X and the domain of demand weights w_i are not explicitly specified, and a source must fix the intended capture response and payoff convention.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate-site set \(J\) are finite.
Demand quantities satisfy \(w_i\ge0\), facility capacities satisfy \(u_j\ge0\), and assignments use only covering incidences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min\left\{\sum_{j\in J}c_jx_j:\ \sum_{j\in J}z_{ij}=1,\ z_{ij}\le a_{ij}x_j,\ \sum_{i\in I}w_i z_{ij}\le u_jx_j,\ x_j\in\{0,1\},\ z_{ij}\ge0\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Fraction of demand i assigned to facility j.
Coverage incidence between demand i and facility j.

review_flags: A source is required to fix whether assignments are splittable and whether capacity is hard or workload based.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost capacitated set covering with splittable demand assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given opening costs \(c_j\), capacities \(u_j\), demand quantities \(w_i\), and coverage incidences \(a_{ij}\), capacitated location set covering opens facilities and assigns all demand by solving
\[\min\left\{\sum_{j\in J}c_jx_j:\ \sum_{j\in J}z_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\ z_{ij}\le a_{ij}x_j\ \forall i,j,\ \sum_{i\in I}w_i z_{ij}\le u_jx_j\ \forall j,\ x_j\in\{0,1\},\ z_{ij}\ge0\right\}.\]
Here assignments are splittable; imposing \(z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) gives the single-source variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Open minimum-cost capacitated facilities and assign all demand only to covering open sites without exceeding any facility capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Location Set Covering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation coherently models minimum-cost capacitated covering with splittable assignments, but no source establishes that splittable demand is the intended capacitated location set covering convention rather than the common single-source variant.

assumptions_latex: Demand and candidate-site sets \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.
At most \(p\) facilities open; demand quantities and facility capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max\left\{\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i:\ \sum_j z_{ij}=y_i,\ z_{ij}\le a_{ij}x_j,\ \sum_i w_i z_{ij}\le u_jx_j,\ \sum_jx_j\le p,\ x_j,y_i\in\{0,1\},\ z_{ij}\ge0\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Fraction of covered demand i assigned to facility j.
Binary indicator that demand i is counted as covered.

review_flags: A source is required to fix splittable versus single-source assignment and the facility-limit convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum covered demand under facility-count and capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given demand weights \(w_i\), capacities \(u_j\), coverage incidences \(a_{ij}\), and facility limit \(p\), capacitated maximal covering is
\[\max\left\{\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i:\ \sum_{j\in J}z_{ij}=y_i\ \forall i,\ z_{ij}\le a_{ij}x_j\ \forall i,j,\ \sum_{i\in I}w_i z_{ij}\le u_jx_j\ \forall j,\ \sum_{j\in J}x_j\le p\right\},\]
where \(x_j,y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and \(z_{ij}\ge0\). Thus counted demand must be assigned to covering open facilities, and assigned load cannot exceed capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Open at most p capacitated facilities and maximize covered demand that can actually be assigned to covering sites without exceeding capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Maximal Covering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation coherently maximizes assigned covered demand under capacities and a facility limit, but no source supports the chosen splittable-assignment and at-most-p conventions. These choices materially distinguish variants of capacitated maximal covering.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate-facility set \(J\) are finite.
Each demand \(i\) has load \(d_i\ge 0\), and each facility \(j\) has capacity \(u_j\ge 0\).
The incidence coefficient \(a_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicates whether facility \(j\) can cover demand \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1,\qquad x_{ij}\le a_{ij}y_j,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}d_i x_{ij}\le u_jy_j.\]

notation.meaning: Binary opening decision for candidate facility \(j\).
Binary assignment of all demand at \(i\) to facility \(j\).
Facility capacity and demand load, respectively.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite capacitated coverage with indivisible demand and exactly one serving facility per demand point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-source coverage assignment is a pair of binary vectors \(y\in\{0,1\}^{J}\) and \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\) such that every demand is assigned to exactly one open facility capable of covering it. Its feasible set is defined by \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in I\), \(x_{ij}\le a_{ij}y_j\) for every \((i,j)\in I\times J\), and \(\sum_{i\in I}d_i x_{ij}\le u_jy_j\) for every \(j\in J\). Thus demand cannot be split among facilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every demand point is assigned wholly to one open, eligible facility, while the total assigned load at each facility remains within its capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Source Coverage Assignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is mathematically plausible for finite, indivisible single-source capacitated assignment, but no citation supports this exact coverage-location interpretation. The local inventory concerns network optimization generally and does not establish the stated model.

assumptions_latex: Demand and candidate sets \(I,J\) are finite.
Facility availabilities are independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities \(p_j\in[0,1]\).
A selected facility covers \(i\) only when \(a_{ij}=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{y\in Y}\sum_{i\in I}w_i\left(1-\prod_{j:a_{ij}=1}(1-p_jy_j)\right).\]

notation.meaning: Binary incidence indicating deterministic coverage eligibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-facility reliability model for expected covered demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a selection \(y\in Y\), probabilistic coverage assigns demand \(i\) the coverage probability \(P_i(y)=1-\prod_{j:a_{ij}=1}(1-p_jy_j)\). This is the probability that at least one selected facility eligible to cover \(i\) is available. With nonnegative demand weights \(w_i\), the probabilistic maximal-coverage problem is \(\max_{y\in Y}\sum_{i\in I}w_iP_i(y)\). The product formula specifically uses mutual independence; correlated availability requires a joint probability model instead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select facilities to maximize expected covered demand, where a point is covered if at least one selected eligible facility is available.
knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product formula is correct under independent Bernoulli facility availability, but no source is cited for selecting this particular reliability model as probabilistic coverage. Correlated and demand-specific coverage models are materially different.

children.title: Scenario-Based Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage evaluated across an explicit collection of scenarios.

assumptions_latex: The scenario set \(S\), demand set \(I\), and candidate set \(J\) are finite.
Each scenario has probability \(q_s\ge 0\), with \(\sum_{s\in S}q_s=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{y\in Y,\,z}\sum_{s\in S}q_s\sum_{i\in I}w_i z_{is}\quad\text{subject to}\quad z_{is}\le\sum_{j\in J}a_{ijs}y_j.\]

notation.meaning: Binary coverage indicator for demand \(i\) in scenario \(s\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario expected-coverage formulation with common first-stage facility decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Scenario-based coverage is represented by a common facility selection \(y\in Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\) and scenario-specific indicators \(z_{is}\in\{0,1\}\). Feasibility requires \(z_{is}\le\sum_{j\in J}a_{ijs}y_j\) for all \((i,s)\in I\times S\), so coverage is evaluated using the incidence system realized in scenario \(s\). For nonnegative weights \(w_i\), expected covered demand is maximized by \(\max_{y,z}\sum_{s\in S}q_s\sum_{i\in I}w_i z_{is}\), subject to these constraints and \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One facility plan is evaluated across finitely many scenarios, and scenario probabilities weight the covered demand obtained in each realization.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Based Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-scenario expected-coverage representation is coherent, with binary scenario indicators and common first-stage decisions, but no cited source supports this exact formulation or its role in the terminal container.

children.title: Robust Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage protected against adverse realizations from an uncertainty set.

assumptions_latex: The uncertainty set \(U\) is nonempty and specifies admissible coverage-incidence matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{y\in Y}\min_{A\in U}\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min\left\{1,\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}y_j\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Uncertainty set of admissible incidence matrices.
Coverage value of selection \(y\) under incidence matrix \(A\).
Feasible family of binary facility selections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static maximin coverage under incidence uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A=(a_{ij})\in U\) and \(y\in Y\), define realized covered demand by \(F(y,A)=\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min\{1,\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}y_j\}\). Robust coverage selects facilities before the incidence matrix is known and solves \(\max_{y\in Y}\min_{A\in U}F(y,A)\). A selection is robustly feasible for a required level \(L\) precisely when \(F(y,A)\ge L\) for every \(A\in U\). This definition imposes no probability distribution on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose facilities to maximize the covered demand guaranteed under every admissible realization of uncertain coverage incidences.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The static maximin interpretation is plausible, but no source establishes it as the intended robust-coverage model. The assumptions also do not explicitly state that every matrix in U has binary incidence entries, which the coverage formula implicitly presumes.

children.title: Scenario-to-Robustness Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between finite scenarios and robust uncertainty representations.

assumptions_latex: The uncertainty set consists exactly of finitely many scenarios \(U=\{A^s:s\in S\}\).
The scenario coverage values \(F(y,A^s)\) are finite for every feasible \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min_{s\in S}F(y,A^s)=\min_{q\in\Delta_S}\sum_{s\in S}q_sF(y,A^s).\]

notation.meaning: Probability simplex on the scenario set.
Covered-demand value of selection \(y\) in scenario \(A\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario equivalence between worst-case coverage and adversarial scenario weighting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed feasible facility selection \(y\), the finite-scenario worst-case value satisfies \(\min_{s\in S}F(y,A^s)=\min_{q\in\Delta_S}\sum_{s\in S}q_sF(y,A^s)\). Consequently, \(\max_{y\in Y}\min_{s\in S}F(y,A^s)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{q\in\Delta_S}\sum_{s\in S}q_sF(y,A^s)\). Thus finite robust coverage equals scenario-based expected coverage when scenario probabilities are chosen adversarially after \(y\); it does not generally equal a model with fixed exogenous probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case finite-scenario coverage equals expected coverage under an adversary allowed to choose any probability distribution over the scenarios.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-to-Robustness Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed finite-set identity is mathematically correct, including the warning that adversarial probabilities differ from fixed exogenous probabilities. Nevertheless, it has no citation, and its role is more naturally a property or representation correspondence than a duality unless a supporting source explicitly presents it as such.

children.title: Disruption-Aware Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage behavior under facility, link, or service disruptions.

assumptions_latex: Facility and demand sets \(J,I\) and disruption scenarios \(S\) are finite.
The first-stage selection \(y\) must belong to \(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{y\in Y}\mathcal R_{s\in S}\left[\max_{x^s\in X(y,s)}\sum_{i\in I}w_i z_i^s\right].\]

notation.meaning: Availability of facility \(j\) after disruption scenario \(s\).
Scenario recourse set compatible with the initial plan.
Specified expectation, minimum, or coherent risk functional over scenarios.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage coverage model separating predisruption selection from disruption-contingent service decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Disruption-aware coverage chooses a predisruption facility vector \(y\in Y\) and, after scenario \(s\) reveals facility availabilities \(r_{js}\), chooses recourse decisions \(x^s\in X(y,s)\). The set \(X(y,s)\) permits service only from facilities satisfying \(y_jr_{js}=1\) and defines coverage indicators \(z_i^s\). With weights \(w_i\), the model optimizes \(\max_{y\in Y}\mathcal R_{s\in S}[\max_{x^s\in X(y,s)}\sum_{i\in I}w_i z_i^s]\), where the selected functional \(\mathcal R\) explicitly determines expected, worst-case, or risk-averse coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A predisruption facility plan is evaluated with scenario-specific service recourse after facility failures are observed.
knowledge_statements.title: Disruption-Aware Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-stage description is plausible but is not a single well-defined model until the reward-oriented functional R and recourse set X(y,s) are specified. No authoritative source identifies this umbrella formulation as the intended meaning of disruption-aware coverage.

children.title: Protective Coverage
children.top_down_role: Pre-disruption protection of coverage capacity or infrastructure.

assumptions_latex: Candidate facilities \(J\) and disruption scenarios \(S\) are finite.
Opening and protection decisions are binary and satisfy a budgeted feasible set \(H\).
Protection changes scenario availability through specified values \(r_{js}(h_j)\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{(y,h)\in H}\mathcal R_{s\in S}\left[\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min\left\{1,\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}y_jr_{js}(h_j)\right\}\right].\]

notation.meaning: Binary decision to protect or harden facility \(j\).
Availability of facility \(j\) in scenario \(s\) under protection decision \(h_j\).
Jointly feasible opening and protection decisions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predisruption hardening formulation for preserving coverage after failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Protective coverage jointly selects facility openings \(y_j\) and predisruption protection decisions \(h_j\). In scenario \(s\), facility \(j\) can cover demand \(i\) only when \(a_{ij}y_jr_{js}(h_j)=1\). For a budgeted feasible set \(H\), its objective is \(\max_{(y,h)\in H}\mathcal R_{s\in S}[\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min\{1,\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}y_jr_{js}(h_j)\}]\). Protection is therefore chosen before disruption and changes survival or operability, rather than reallocating service afterward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opening and hardening decisions are made before disruption to preserve as much weighted coverage as possible across failure scenarios.
knowledge_statements.title: Protective Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The predisruption hardening interpretation fits the lifecycle position, but the functional R is left unspecified and different survival, interdiction, and risk models produce nonequivalent formulations. No citation supports this selected version.

children.title: Recovery Coverage
children.top_down_role: Post-disruption restoration or reconfiguration of coverage.

assumptions_latex: An initial facility plan \(y\in Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\) and a disruption scenario \(s\) are given.
Recovery decisions have nonnegative costs \(c_j^s\) and budget \(B_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{v^s}\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min\left\{1,\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}v_j^s\right\}\quad\text{subject to}\quad v_j^s\le y_j,\quad v_j^s\le r_{js}+u_j^s,\quad \sum_jc_j^su_j^s\le B_s.\]

notation.meaning: Binary decision to restore failed facility \(j\) after scenario \(s\).
Binary postrecovery operability of initially selected facility \(j\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Postdisruption restoration of selected facilities under a recovery budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an initial plan \(y\) and realized scenario \(s\), recovery coverage chooses restoration variables \(u_j^s\in\{0,1\}\) and postrecovery operability variables \(v_j^s\in\{0,1\}\). They satisfy \(v_j^s\le y_j\), \(v_j^s\le r_{js}+u_j^s\), and \(\sum_{j\in J}c_j^su_j^s\le B_s\). The recovered covered demand is \(\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min\{1,\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}v_j^s\}\), which is maximized over feasible restoration decisions after the disruption is observed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a disruption, failed facilities from the initial plan may be restored within budget to maximize recovered weighted coverage.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restoration-only interpretation is plausible but unsupported. In addition, conclusion_latex maximizes only over v^s even though u^s is also a decision appearing in feasibility constraints; the authoritative formulation is needed before correcting the optimization domain and any restoration restrictions.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate set \(J\) are finite.
Exactly \(p\) facilities must be selected, where \(1\le p\le |J|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max\sum_{i\in I}w_i z_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad z_i\le 1-y_j\ \text{for all }j\text{ with }a_{ij}=1,\quad \sum_{j\in J}y_j=p.\]

notation.meaning: Binary indicator that demand point \(i\) avoids every selected forbidden neighborhood.
Forbidden-proximity incidence between demand \(i\) and site \(j\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete maximum-weight nonexposure model using forbidden coverage neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In discrete anti-covering location, \(a_{ij}=1\) means that selecting site \(j\) undesirably covers demand point \(i\). With \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\), \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\), and \(\sum_{j\in J}y_j=p\), nonexposure is enforced by \(z_i\le1-y_j\) for every pair satisfying \(a_{ij}=1\). Maximizing \(\sum_{i\in I}w_i z_i\) therefore selects \(p\) sites so that the greatest total demand weight lies outside every forbidden neighborhood of a selected site.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a fixed number of sites to maximize the weight of demand points lying outside all forbidden proximity neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.title: Anti-Covering Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonexposure model is internally coherent, but anti-covering terminology is not uniform and may denote different separation or forbidden-service models. No location-theory source supports this exact maximum-weight formulation.

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate set \(J\) are finite.
Distances satisfy \(d_{ij}\ge 0\), and demand weights satisfy \(w_i\ge 0\).
Exactly \(p\) facilities are selected, with \(1\le p\le |J|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{S\subseteq J,\ |S|=p}\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min_{j\in S}d_{ij}.\]

notation.meaning: Distance or separation between demand point \(i\) and candidate site \(j\).
Nonnegative importance or population weight at demand point \(i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete obnoxious-location model maximizing weighted distance to the nearest selected facility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The weighted nearest-distance obnoxious facility problem chooses a set \(S\subseteq J\) with \(|S|=p\) to maximize \(\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min_{j\in S}d_{ij}\). Each demand point is evaluated against its nearest selected undesirable facility, so the objective rewards selections that keep heavily weighted demand far from all such facilities. This formulation is distinct from maximin dispersion, which measures distances between selected facilities rather than distances from demand points to selected facilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Place a fixed number of undesirable facilities to maximize the weighted demand-to-nearest-facility distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Obnoxious Facility Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula defines a coherent weighted maxisum nearest-distance obnoxious-location model and correctly distinguishes demand separation from facility dispersion. The generic terminal title covers several objectives, however, and no source establishes this particular variant as its defining statement.

assumptions_latex: The finite candidate set \(J\) has symmetric pairwise distances \(d_{jk}\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{S\subseteq J,\ |S|=p}\min_{\substack{j,k\in S\\j\ne k}}d_{jk}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete cardinality-constrained max-min pairwise dispersion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each set \(S\subseteq J\) with \(|S|\ge2\), define its separation by \(\delta(S)=\min\{d_{jk}:j,k\in S,\ j\ne k\}\). The maximin dispersion location problem selects exactly \(p\) sites and solves \(\max_{S\subseteq J,\ |S|=p}\delta(S)\). Equivalently, it finds the largest \(\lambda\) for which some \(p\)-site selection contains no pair \(j,k\) with \(d_{jk}<\lambda\). No demand-to-facility assignment is part of this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose exactly p candidate sites so that the smallest distance between any two selected sites is as large as possible.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximin Dispersion Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cardinality-constrained maximin pairwise-dispersion definition is mathematically precise and matches the terminal title, but it has no cited authoritative source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Location Geometry-Service Regime Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Spatial, metric, assignment, and demand structures that alter formulations and algorithmic behavior.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Facility Location: Concepts, Models, Algorithms and Case Studies
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Distance Functions, Single Facility, Multifacility, and Location Allocation
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Facility Location: Concepts, Models, Algorithms and Case Studies

assumptions_latex: Demand set \(I\) and candidate-location set \(J\) are finite.
Facility decisions are restricted to the binary vector \(y\in Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\).
The service value \(V(y)\) is well-defined for every \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max\{V(y):y\in Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\}.\]

notation.meaning: Finite set of admissible facility sites.
Binary vector indicating selected candidate sites.
Service value after any prescribed assignment or recourse optimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate-space regime in which every facility must occupy one of finitely many enumerated sites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A discrete candidate location model has a finite site set \(J\) and represents a facility configuration by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{J}\), where \(y_j=1\) exactly when site \(j\) is selected. Side constraints define a feasible family \(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\). If \(V(y)\) denotes the resulting coverage or service value, including any prescribed assignment optimization, the location problem has the form \(\max\{V(y):y\in Y\}\). Hence the spatial decision is combinatorial rather than a choice from a continuum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facilities may be placed only at finitely many enumerated candidate sites, so each location plan is represented by a binary selection vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Candidate Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite candidate-space characterization is mathematically coherent and fits the geometry-service regime taxonomy. No facility-location source is cited, and the supplied network-optimization inventory does not specifically substantiate this definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate and demand points lie on a weighted network, with service measured along network paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected graph with positive edge lengths \(\ell:E\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}\), and let \(|G|\) denote its geometric realization. A network-location instance has nonempty demand and candidate sets \(D,C\subseteq |G|\), a demand-weight function \(w:D\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\), and a nonempty chosen facility set \(S\subseteq C\). For each \(i\in D\), its service distance is \(d_G(i,S)=\min_{s\in S}d_G(i,s)\), where \(d_G\) is weighted shortest-path distance in \(|G|\). Thus service is measured along paths within \(G\), rather than by an ambient straight-line distance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facilities range over a continuum rather than a prescribed finite candidate list.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(C\subseteq X\) a feasible candidate region. knowledge_statements.title: Metric Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Service costs are generated by a genuine metric on the location space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set. A metric-location model uses a function \(d:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) satisfying, for all \(x,y,z\in X\), \(d(x,y)=0\iff x=y\), \(d(x,y)=d(y,x)\), and \(d(x,z)\leq d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). If \(S\subseteq X\) is a nonempty facility set, the service distance of \(x\) is \(d(x,S)=\inf_{s\in S}d(x,s)\). A metric-location objective or constraint is formed from these point-to-set distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric location measures service with a nonnegative, separating, symmetric distance satisfying the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(d(x,S)=\inf_{s\in S}d(x,s)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Travel or service cost depends on direction between demand and facility points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\) and let \(c:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\) denote directed service cost. An asymmetric-location instance is one for which there exist \(x,y\in X\) with \(c(x,y)\neq c(y,x)\). The ordered arguments must therefore be fixed by convention: if the first argument is a demand and the second a facility, then a facility set \(S\subseteq X\) serves \(x\) at cost \(c(x,S)=\inf_{s\in S}c(x,s)\), which need not equal \(\inf_{s\in S}c(s,x)\).

children.title: Triangle-Inequality Failure Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Triangle-Inequality Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The metric triangle inequality fails for at least one intermediate location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\) be a service dissimilarity. The triangle-inequality failure regime is characterized by points \(x,y,z\in X\) such that \(c(x,z)>c(x,y)+c(y,z)\). Consequently, replacing direct service from \(x\) to \(z\) by two legs through \(y\) strictly reduces the displayed cost, so metric arguments that shortcut a route by deleting intermediate points are invalid. For example, on \(X=\{a,b,c\}\), the symmetric costs \(c(a,b)=c(b,c)=1\) and \(c(a,c)=3\) exhibit this failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Triangle-inequality failure occurs when serving or traveling through an intermediate point is cheaper than the stated direct dissimilarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x,y,z\in X:\ c(x,z)>c(x,y)+c(y,z)\).

children.title: Euclidean Location

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facilities and demands lie in finite-dimensional Euclidean space with ordinary straight-line distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(d\geq1\), let the location space be a subset \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). A Euclidean-location model measures service between \(x,y\in X\) by \(d_2(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d(x_j-y_j)^2)^{1/2}\). For a nonempty facility set \(S\subseteq X\), the service distance is \(d_2(x,S)=\inf_{s\in S}\lVert x-s\rVert_2\). Candidate regions may be discrete or continuous, but the governing geometry is the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean location places points in finite-dimensional real space and uses ordinary straight-line distance for service.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_2(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert_2\) governs service.

knowledge_statements.title: Normed-Space Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Service distance is induced by a norm on a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a real vector space equipped with a norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\), and let \(X\subseteq E\) be nonempty. A normed-space location model assigns service distance \(d(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert\) to \(x,y\in X\). For every nonempty facility set \(S\subseteq X\), the point-to-set service distance is \(d(x,S)=\inf_{s\in S}\lVert x-s\rVert\). Translation invariance and positive homogeneity follow from the norm, while the shape of equal-distance sets is determined by its unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normed-space location uses the distance between two points given by the norm of their difference.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a real normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert\) defines the service metric on \(X\).

children.title: Norm-Specific Facility Geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Specific Facility Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-dimensional norm and its facility-service geometry are represented by the same origin-symmetric convex unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\geq1\) be an integer and let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be compact and convex, satisfy \(K=-K\), and contain \(0\) in its interior. Its Minkowski functional \(\lVert u\rVert_K=\inf\{t>0:u\in tK\}\) is a norm with unit ball \(K\). Conversely, the unit ball of every norm on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has these properties. For a facility \(s\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and radius \(r\geq0\), the corresponding service ball is \(B_K(s,r)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\lVert x-s\rVert_K\leq r\}=s+rK\). Thus the selected norm fixes the geometry of all facility service balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional real space, an origin-symmetric convex unit ball determines a norm, and every facility service ball is obtained from it by scaling and translation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert u\rVert_K=\inf\{t>0:u\in tK\}\) is a norm and \(B_K(s,r)=s+rK\).

notation.meaning: origin-symmetric convex unit ball determining the norm geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Metric Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Service distance is the weighted length of the unique path in a tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(V,E)\) be a connected acyclic graph with positive edge lengths \(\ell:E\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}\). For vertices \(u,v\in V\), let \(P_T(u,v)\) be their unique simple path and define \(d_T(u,v)=\sum_{e\in P_T(u,v)}\ell(e)\). A tree-metric location model takes demands and candidate facilities in \(V\), or in the geometric realization \(|T|\) with the analogous path-length extension, and evaluates service using \(d_T\). The uniqueness of \(P_T(u,v)\) is the defining structural feature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree-metric location measures service by summing edge lengths along the unique tree path between two points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_T(u,v)=\sum_{e\in P_T(u,v)}\ell(e)\) is the service metric.

notation.meaning: unique simple u-v path in T

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Metric Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The underlying tree is a weighted finite path graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the path graph with ordered vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) and positive edge lengths \(\ell_i\) on \(v_iv_{i+1}\). A path-metric location model measures service by \(d_P(v_i,v_j)=\sum_{k=\min\{i,j\}}^{\max\{i,j\}-1}\ell_k\) for \(i\neq j\), with \(d_P(v_i,v_i)=0\). Demands and facilities may also lie on the geometric realization \(|P|\), where distance is arc length along its unique subpath. Hence the model is a tree-metric location instance whose tree has maximum degree at most two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Path-metric location uses weighted distance along a finite ordered path, optionally including points inside its edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_P(v_i,v_j)=\sum_{k=\min\{i,j\}}^{\max\{i,j\}-1}\ell_k\) for \(i\neq j\).

notation.meaning: length of edge joining consecutive vertices

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Metric Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locations are real coordinates and service distance is absolute coordinate difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be a nonempty set of admissible locations. A line-metric location model measures service between \(x,y\in X\) by \(d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y)=|x-y|\), and from \(x\) to a nonempty facility set \(S\subseteq X\) by \(d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,S)=\inf_{s\in S}|x-s|\). The set \(X\) may be discrete, an interval, or a union of intervals; its ordering is inherited from \(\mathbb{R}\). Every finite weighted path metric embeds isometrically into this regime by cumulative edge-length coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Line-metric location represents every location by a real coordinate and uses absolute coordinate difference as service distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y)=|x-y|\) and \(d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,S)=\inf_{s\in S}|x-s|\).
