knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Static Demand

source_witnesses.locator: Section 1.3. Linear Optimization Problems p. 8

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and fits the demand-regime leaf, but a generic linear-optimization section does not specifically support the deterministic, static, single-period demand distinction.

assumptions_latex: Demand is a random vector \(D\) on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\).
First-stage location decisions are chosen before \(D\) is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Performance is evaluated using the specified probability law and scenario-dependent recourse.

notation.meaning: optimal recourse value after demand realization \(d\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage risk-neutral demand formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Demand is stochastic when it is modeled by a random vector \(D:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}_+^{I}\) with specified law \(P\). In a two-stage risk-neutral formulation, a location decision \(x\in X\) is selected before observing \(D\), recourse is selected afterward, and the problem is \(\min_{x\in X}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\mathbb{E}_{P}[Q(x,D)]\}\), provided the expectation is well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic demand is a random demand vector with a specified law; locations precede observation, while assignments or other recourse may adapt afterward.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Demand

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly describes a two-stage risk-neutral stochastic-demand model, but no source supports the formulation or its required expectation conditions.

children.title: Robust Demand
children.top_down_role: Demand represented through deterministic uncertainty sets.

assumptions_latex: Demand belongs to a nonempty uncertainty set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^{I}\).
The location decision \(x\) is chosen before the realized demand is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chosen location must remain feasible, or have feasible recourse, for every demand vector in \(U\).

notation.meaning: uncertainty set of admissible demand vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static uncertainty-set robustness with optional adjustable recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A demand model is robust when uncertainty is represented by a set \(U\), without assigning probabilities to its elements, and decisions are judged against every \(d\in U\). With recourse value \(Q(x,d)\), the robust objective is \(\min_{x\in X}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\sup_{d\in U}Q(x,d)\}\), subject to the existence of feasible recourse for every \(d\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust demand uses a set of possible demand vectors and protects the location decision against every member, typically through worst-case cost and feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Demand

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uncertainty-set and worst-case formulation fits robust demand, but no source supports the distinction or the asserted universal recourse requirement.

children.title: Distributionally Robust Demand
children.top_down_role: Demand represented through ambiguity over probability distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributionally Robust Demand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage risk-neutral distributional robustness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Demand is distributionally robust when its law is allowed to range over an ambiguity set \(\mathcal{P}\) of probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}_+^{I}\). A two-stage risk-neutral formulation is \(\min_{x\in X}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}_{P}[Q(x,D)]\}\), provided \(Q(x,D)\) is measurable and integrable for every \(P\in\mathcal{P}\). Thus ambiguity concerns probability laws rather than individual demand realizations alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributionally robust demand optimizes against the worst probability law in an ambiguity set, while retaining expectation-based evaluation under each candidate law.
assumptions_latex: The probability law of demand is unknown but belongs to a nonempty ambiguity set \(\mathcal{P}\).
The location decision \(x\) is selected before demand is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decision minimizes cost under the worst admissible demand distribution.

notation.meaning: ambiguity set of probability measures for demand
random demand vector under a measure \(P\)
recourse value for decision \(x\) and realization \(d\)

children.title: Demand-Ambiguity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing distributional ambiguity in demand.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite demand and facility sets.
\(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\) is a nonempty feasible location set.
Every ambiguity set under consideration is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak P=\{P\}\) gives a known-distribution regime, \(\mathfrak P\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal D)\) gives distributional ambiguity, and \(U\subseteq\mathcal D\) gives robust demand without probabilities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes deterministic, robust, stochastic, and distributionally robust demand information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A demand-ambiguity regime specifies the information available about a demand vector \(d\in\mathcal D\). Deterministic demand fixes \(d=\bar d\); robust demand specifies a set \(U\subseteq\mathcal D\) and evaluates \(\sup_{d\in U}Q(y,d)\); stochastic demand specifies one distribution \(P\in\Delta(\mathcal D)\) and evaluates \(\mathbb E_P[Q(y,d)]\); distributionally robust demand specifies an ambiguity set \(\mathfrak P\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal D)\) and evaluates \(\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P}\mathbb E_P[Q(y,d)]\). Thus ambiguity concerns uncertainty about the probability law, whereas robust demand may omit a probability model entirely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A demand regime is determined by whether demand is fixed, belongs to an uncertainty set, follows a known distribution, or follows an unknown distribution from an ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Ambiguity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the ambiguity-regime leaf, but no inspectable source supports the four-way classification or its objective functionals. The unused assumptions involving I, J, and Y should also be removed when sourced.

children.title: Dynamic Demand
children.top_down_role: Demand that changes across planning or operating periods.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite set of demand locations and \(T=\{1,\ldots,H\}\) is a finite planning horizon.
Demand is represented by nonnegative quantities \(d_{it}\).
Decisions at time \(t\) may use only information revealed through time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dynamic demand requires a time-indexed demand process and a nonanticipative sequence of location or service decisions.

notation.meaning: Demand at location i during period t
Location or service decision in period t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon dynamic demand with information-respecting decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Demand is dynamic when it is indexed by decision time and may change between periods: \(d=(d_{it})_{i\in I,t\in T}\). If demand is uncertain, it is adapted to an information filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\in T}\). A feasible policy \(\pi=(a_t)_{t\in T}\) must satisfy \(a_t\in\mathcal A_t\) and require \(a_t\) to be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. Facility openings may be permanent, relocatable, or period-specific, but the defining feature is that service feasibility or cost in period \(t\) depends on \(d_{ullet t}\), rather than on one time-invariant demand vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic demand varies over decision periods, and each location or service decision must depend only on demand information available when that decision is made.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Demand

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes the intended local meaning of dynamic demand. The record additionally makes sequential nonanticipative decisions mandatory although deterministic multiperiod demand can also be dynamic, and the undefined expression d_{ullet t} is evidently malformed. The plain statement is narrower than the filtration-based formulation.

children.title: Mobile Demand
children.top_down_role: Demand whose spatial position changes over time.

assumptions_latex: \((X,\rho)\) is a metric service space and \(T=\{1,\ldots,H\}\).
Each demand entity has a trajectory \(s_i:T\to X\) and nonnegative weight \(w_{it}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Demand is mobile precisely when service incidence or cost depends on the time-varying positions \(s_i(t)\).

notation.meaning: Position of demand entity i at time t
Position of facility j at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trajectory-based demand mobility, distinct from changing demand magnitude at fixed sites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Demand is mobile when demand entities change spatial position over time. Entity \(i\) has trajectory \(s_i(t)\in X\) and weight \(w_{it}\ge 0\). Under radius-based service, facility \(j\) can serve entity \(i\) in period \(t\) only if \(\rho(s_i(t),z_{jt})\le R\); under distance cost, its contribution is \(w_{it}\rho(s_i(t),z_{jt})\). Mobility therefore changes the incidence relation between facilities and demand over time, even when every weight \(w_{it}\) is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mobile demand consists of entities whose positions follow trajectories, so facility-demand distances and feasible service incidences change over time.
knowledge_statements.title: Mobile Demand

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The trajectory-based definition and definition content kind fit Mobile Demand, but the incidence and distance-cost characterization has no inspectable supporting source.

children.title: Spatiotemporal Demand Regimes
children.top_down_role: Demand structures coupling temporal variation with spatial mobility.

assumptions_latex: \((X,\mathcal B)\) is a measurable spatial domain.
\(T\) is a finite or measurable time domain.
Demand has finite nonnegative mass on the relevant planning horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A spatiotemporal regime is represented by a nonnegative measure \(\mu\) on \(X\times T\), with discrete arrays and trajectories as special cases.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified measure representation for discrete, continuous, dynamic, and mobile demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spatiotemporal demand regime is represented by a finite nonnegative measure \(\mu\) on the product space \(X\times T\). For finite sites and periods, \(\mu=\sum_{i,t}d_{it}\delta_{(s_i,t)}\). For mobile entities, \(\mu=\sum_i\int_T w_i(t)\delta_{(s_i(t),t)}\,dt\). A facility policy induces a measurable service cost \(c_	heta(x,t)\), and total demand-weighted cost is \(\int_{X\times T}c_	heta(x,t)\,d\mu(x,t)\). Uncertainty may act on masses, arrival times, locations, trajectories, or the entire measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spatiotemporal demand is a measure over space and time; fixed-site dynamic arrays and weighted moving trajectories are special cases of this representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Spatiotemporal Demand Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate content kind, but no source supports this proposed unification. For a general measurable time domain, the trajectory formula requires a specified base measure rather than an unexplained dt, together with measurability and integrability conditions for trajectories, weights, and costs.

children.title: Location Formulation-Certificate Algorithm Synthesis
children.top_down_role: Location-specific representations, relaxations, certificates, and major exact or approximation method families.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite demand and candidate-facility sets.
Each demand \(i\) must be assigned to one opened facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed mixed-integer model is a compact formulation with \(O(|I||J|)\) assignment variables and constraints.

notation.meaning: Indicator that facility j is opened
Fraction or indicator assigning demand i to facility j
Demand, capacity, and assignment cost data

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical capacitated compact assignment-opening formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A compact assignment-location formulation is
\[\min\ \sum_{j\in J}f_jy_j+\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}\]
subject to \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in I\), \(x_{ij}\le y_j\) for every \((i,j)\in I\times J\), and \(\sum_{i\in I}d_ix_{ij}\le U_jy_j\) for every \(j\in J\), with \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\) and \(x_{ij}\ge0\). Requiring \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) gives unsplittable assignment; allowing continuous \(x_{ij}\) gives splittable service.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact location model uses opening variables and explicit customer-facility assignment variables, linked by opening and capacity constraints in polynomial model size.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Assignment–Location Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the compact-formulation leaf and is mathematically recognizable, but it lacks a cited facility-location source. The opening cost f_j is used without introduction, and the claimed model-size bound should be tied to a specific formulation reference.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite demand and candidate-facility sets.
\(N_i\subseteq J\) contains exactly the facilities capable of covering demand \(i\).
Every demand has at least one potential covering facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible openings are exactly the binary vectors satisfying \(\sum_{j\in N_i}y_j\ge1\) for all \(i\in I\).

notation.meaning: Facilities capable of covering demand i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical set-covering location formulation with exogenous service incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The covering incidence matrix is \(A\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\), where \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when facility \(j\) can serve demand \(i\), and \(N_i=\{j\in J:A_{ij}=1\}\). The minimum-cost covering location formulation is
\[\min\ \sum_{j\in J}f_jy_j\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j\in N_i}y_j\ge1\ \ (i\in I),\qquad y_j\in\{0,1\}\ \ (j\in J).\]
Coverage multiplicities replace the right-hand side by prescribed integers, while a budgeted maximum-covering variant introduces demand-coverage variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering-based location model opens facilities so every demand row of a binary service-incidence matrix is covered at least once.
knowledge_statements.title: Covering-Based Location Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covering representation and selected content kind fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the canonical model or the stated multiplicity and maximum-covering variants.

children.title: Flow-Based Location Formulations
children.top_down_role: Location formulations structured around network flows.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed network with source \(s\), facility nodes \(J\), and demand nodes \(I\).
Facility \(j\) has capacity \(U_j\), and demand node \(i\) consumes \(d_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Location and routing are coupled by \(0\le f_{sj}\le U_jy_j\), so flow can enter the service network through facility \(j\) only when it is opened.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-commodity network formulation with opening-controlled source arcs.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Flow and Divergence p. 6
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flow-based location formulation augments a service network by an arc \((s,j)\) from a super-source to each candidate facility. It imposes \(0\le f_{sj}\le U_jy_j\), ordinary arc bounds \(0\le f_a\le u_a\), and flow balance \(Bf=b\), where each demand node \(i\) has balance \(b_i=-d_i\) and the source supplies \(\sum_i d_i\). With linear arc costs and opening costs, the objective is \(\sum_{a\in A}c_af_a+\sum_{j\in J}F_jy_j\), with \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow-based location model sends service through a network and uses opening-controlled capacity arcs to prevent closed facilities from supplying flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Based Location Formulations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.2 Flow and Divergence p. 6
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited sections support ordinary flow balance and minimum-cost flow, but they do not directly support the defining facility-location construction with binary openings and opening-controlled source arcs. A facility-location or network-design source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Path-Based Location Formulations
children.top_down_role: Location formulations whose principal objects are network paths.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed service network.
For each demand \(i\), \(\mathcal P_i\) is a finite set of feasible facility-to-demand paths.
Every path \(p\in\mathcal P_i\) has an origin facility \(o(p)\in J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The path formulation is the flow formulation expressed through nonnegative path-flow variables and opening-controlled facility capacities.

notation.meaning: Fraction of demand i routed on path p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-flow representation for splittable capacitated facility service.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Path Flows and Conformal Decomposition p. 7
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Network Flow Models - Examples p. 8
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A path-based location formulation assigns a variable \(\lambda_{ip}\ge0\) to every \(p\in\mathcal P_i\). Complete service requires \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_i}\lambda_{ip}=1\) for each \(i\in I\). Facility capacity and opening are enforced by
\[\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_i:o(p)=j}d_i\lambda_{ip}\le U_jy_j\qquad(j\in J),\]
with \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\). Arc capacities, when present, impose \(\sum_{i,p:a\in p}d_i\lambda_{ip}\le u_a\). Path costs are summed linearly over \(d_i\lambda_{ip}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path-based model routes each demand over explicit feasible paths and couples all paths originating at a facility to that facility's opening and capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Path-Based Location Formulations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Path Flows and Conformal Decomposition p. 7
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Network Flow Models - Examples p. 8
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The citations support path-flow decomposition generally, not this facility-location formulation or its opening-capacity coupling. The claimed equivalence with the flow formulation needs appropriate conditions, and d_i, U_j, y_j, u_a, and the relevant index sets are not all explicitly introduced.

children.title: Pattern-Based Location Formulations
children.top_down_role: Location formulations using feasible service or assignment patterns.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite demand and facility sets.
\(\mathcal S_j\) is a family of feasible demand subsets for facility \(j\).
Each pattern cost \(c_{jS}\) includes the service cost for its selected subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pattern column \(z_{jS}\\) simultaneously selects facility \(j\) and the feasible service configuration \(S\).

notation.meaning: Feasible service patterns for facility j
Indicator or weight for pattern S at facility j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-partitioning pattern formulation for facility-level feasible service configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each facility \(j\), a pattern \(S\in\mathcal S_j\) is a demand subset that facility \(j\) can serve while satisfying all local restrictions, such as \(\sum_{i\in S}d_i\le U_j\). The pattern formulation is
\[\min\ \sum_{j\in J}f_jy_j+\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_j}c_{jS}z_{jS}\]
subject to \(\sum_{j,S:i\in S}z_{jS}=1\) for every \(i\in I\), \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_j}z_{jS}\le y_j\) for every \(j\in J\), \(z_{jS}\ge0\), and \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pattern-based formulation chooses feasible facility-level customer subsets as columns, covers each demand exactly once, and activates patterns only at opened facilities.
knowledge_statements.title: Pattern-Based Location Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind fits the pattern-formulation leaf, but the set-partitioning model lacks an authoritative source. The conclusion contains the malformed fragment z_{jS}\\ and must be repaired in a sourced replacement.

children.title: Facility-Opening Relaxation Structure
children.top_down_role: Opening-variable structure within location LP relaxations.

assumptions_latex: Facility-opening variables are relaxed from binary to continuous bounds.
The uncoupled opening restriction is \(\sum_{j\in J}y_j=p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every vertex of \(Y_p=\{y\in[0,1]^J:\sum_jy_j=p\}\) is binary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform cardinality opening polytope before assignment coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The isolated facility-opening relaxation with a fixed facility count is
\[Y_p=\left\{y\in\mathbb R^J:0\le y_j\le1\ \text{for all }j\in J,\ \sum_{j\in J}y_j=p\right\}.\]
Every extreme point of \(Y_p\) belongs to \(\{0,1\}^J\) and has exactly \(p\) unit components. Hence optimizing a linear opening cost over \(Y_p\) alone has a binary optimum. Fractional opening values can nevertheless occur after assignment, capacity, fairness, or other side constraints are coupled to \(y\), because those constraints alter the feasible polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-cardinality opening relaxation alone has only binary vertices, although coupling it to assignments or side constraints can create fractional vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Facility-Opening Relaxation Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits the relaxation-structure leaf, and the fixed-cardinality polytope claim is precise, but no inspectable polyhedral source is supplied.

children.title: Assignment Relaxation Structure
children.top_down_role: Client-assignment structure within location LP relaxations.

assumptions_latex: Assignments are splittable and have no opening, capacity, or side constraints.
Each demand must receive one unit of total assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every vertex of \(X=\prod_{i\in I}\{x_i\in\mathbb R_+^J:\sum_jx_{ij}=1\}\) assigns each demand integrally to one facility.

notation.meaning: Unit vector associated with facility j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-of-simplices assignment relaxation before opening and capacity coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The uncoupled assignment relaxation is
\[X=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_+^{I\times J}:\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\ \text{for every }i\in I\right\}.\]
It is the Cartesian product of one simplex for each demand. Its vertices satisfy \(x_i=e^j\) for some \(j\in J\) independently for every \(i\in I\); consequently all vertices are binary. Fractional assignments arise at nonvertex feasible points or at vertices of a larger relaxation after assignment rows are coupled to fractional openings, shared capacities, routing restrictions, or additional side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without coupling constraints, assignment rows form independent simplices whose vertices assign every demand wholly to one facility.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Relaxation Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-of-simplices property fits the assignment-relaxation leaf and is stated consistently, but it has no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Opening–Assignment Coupling Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraint families linking facility activation to admissible assignments.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite demand and facility sets.
\(x_{ij}\ge0\) denotes assigned demand fraction and \(0\le y_j\le1\) denotes relaxed opening.
Each facility \(j\) has capacity \(U_j\ge0\), and each demand has size \(d_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(x_{ij}\le y_j\) and \(\sum_i d_ix_{ij}\le U_jy_j\) are valid opening-assignment coupling conditions.

notation.meaning: Fraction of demand i assigned to facility j
Relaxed opening level of facility j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical disaggregated activation and aggregate capacity coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Opening-assignment coupling requires
\[x_{ij}\le y_j\qquad(i\in I,\ j\in J)\]
and, for capacitated service,
\[\sum_{i\in I}d_ix_{ij}\le U_jy_j\qquad(j\in J).\]
The first family forbids any positive assignment to facility \(j\) when \(y_j=0\) and bounds each assignment by its opening level in the relaxation. The second family similarly forces zero aggregate load at a closed facility and scales available capacity by \(y_j\). With \(\sum_jx_{ij}=1\), these inequalities couple otherwise independent opening and assignment polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Activation inequalities and opening-scaled capacity inequalities prevent service by closed facilities and link fractional assignment levels to fractional opening levels.
knowledge_statements.title: Opening–Assignment Coupling Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct content kind for this leaf, and the two coupling families are stated consistently for fractional assignments. An authoritative facility-location formulation source with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: Opening–Assignment Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Weaknesses arising from fractional opening or assignment behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Opening–Assignment Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality gap for a minimization facility-location formulation with coupled opening and assignment variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_{\mathrm{IP}}\) be a facility-location integer formulation with opening variables \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), assignment variables \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), and coupling constraints \(x_{ij}\le y_i\). Let \(P_{\mathrm{LP}}\) replace integrality by \(0\le x_{ij},y_i\le1\). For a nonnegative cost vector \(c\), write \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)\) and \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\) for their optimal minimization values. The instance gap is \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)/z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\) when \(0<z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)<\infty\); the formulation gap is the supremum of this ratio over admissible instances and costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The opening–assignment gap is the worst-case ratio between the integer optimum and the coupled LP-relaxation optimum over admissible location instances and nonnegative costs having a positive finite LP optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{IP}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{LP}}\) have identical linear constraints except for integrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gap}(P_{\mathrm{IP}},P_{\mathrm{LP}})=\sup_{\text{admissible instances and }c}\frac{z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)}{z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)}\).

notation.meaning: assignment of client j to facility i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard minimization integrality-gap definition specialized to opening–assignment coupling

children.title: Configuration-Based Location Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Location relaxations organized around local or facility configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Based Location Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-configuration extended relaxation for capacitated facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each facility \(i\), let \(\mathcal C_i\) be a family of client subsets feasible for one open copy of \(i\). A configuration relaxation introduces \(z_{iS}\ge0\) for \(S\in\mathcal C_i\), interpreted as selecting configuration \(S\) at \(i\), and imposes \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal C_i}z_{iS}=y_i\) and \(x_{ij}=\sum_{S\in\mathcal C_i:j\in S}z_{iS}\). Together with \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\) for every client \(j\), these equations form a configuration-based location relaxation; additional global opening constraints may be appended.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each facility fraction is decomposed into feasible local client subsets, whose marginals recover the ordinary opening and assignment variables.
assumptions_latex: Every \(S\in\mathcal C_i\) satisfies the local feasibility restrictions at facility \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_i=\sum_{S\in\mathcal C_i}z_{iS}\) and \(x_{ij}=\sum_{S\ni j}z_{iS}\), with \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\).

notation.meaning: weight assigned to configuration S at facility i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard configuration-LP construction by local feasible subsets and marginalization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The configuration-variable definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports this capacitated facility-location specialization.

children.title: Extended Location Formulations
children.top_down_role: Higher-dimensional location formulations using auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended Location Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended formulations whose projection yields a relaxation in the original location variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^{I\times J}\times\mathbb R^I\) be a location polytope or relaxation in variables \((x,y)\). An extended location formulation is a polyhedron \(Q=\{(x,y,z):A x+B y+C z\le b\}\) in the original variables and auxiliary variables \(z\) such that \(P=\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(Q)=\{(x,y):\exists z,\ (x,y,z)\in Q\}\). Its size is conventionally the number of inequalities in a chosen description of \(Q\), with equations either counted separately or represented by pairs of inequalities under a stated convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended location formulation adds auxiliary variables but projects exactly onto the intended opening–assignment polytope or relaxation.

children.title: Projection Links for Location Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relationships induced by projecting extended representations into base spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Links for Location Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection and lifting equivalence between an extended relaxation and its opening–assignment image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{I\times J}\times\mathbb R^I\times\mathbb R^k\) be an extended location relaxation and define \(P=\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(Q)\). Then \((x,y)\in P\) if and only if there exists \(z\in\mathbb R^k\) with \((x,y,z)\in Q\). Consequently, for every objective depending only on original variables, \[\inf_{(x,y)\in P}\{c^\top x+f^\top y\}=\inf_{(x,y,z)\in Q}\{c^\top x+f^\top y\},\] whenever either side has a well-defined finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection membership is equivalent to existence of an extended-space lift, and objectives using only original variables have identical optimal values.
assumptions_latex: The displayed minimization problem has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y)\in P\iff\exists z\,((x,y,z)\in Q)\), and the two displayed optimal values coincide.

children.title: Size–Strength Tradeoffs

knowledge_statements.title: Size–Strength Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic relation between relaxation containment, lower-bound strength, and integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_{\mathrm{IP}}\subseteq P_2\subseteq P_1\) be feasible regions for the same minimization location problem, and let \(c\ge0\) have positive finite relaxation optima. Then \(z_{P_1}(c)\le z_{P_2}(c)\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)\), so \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)/z_{P_2}(c)\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)/z_{P_1}(c)\). Thus adding valid inequalities or using an extension whose projection is contained in the previous relaxation cannot weaken its lower bound, although the formulation may require more inequalities, variables, or separation effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smaller valid relaxation gives at least as strong a lower bound and no larger minimization gap, potentially at greater representational or computational cost.
assumptions_latex: All formulations use the same minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{P_1}(c)\le z_{P_2}(c)\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}(c)\) and \(\operatorname{gap}_{P_2}(c)\le\operatorname{gap}_{P_1}(c)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Assignment Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual lower-bound certificate for capacitated assignment with fixed fractional openings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(y_i\ge0\). Consider \(\min\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) subject to \(\sum_i x_{ij}=d_j\), \(\sum_jx_{ij}\le u_i y_i\), and \(x_{ij}\ge0\). Any \(\alpha_j\in\mathbb R\) and \(\beta_i\ge0\) satisfying \(\alpha_j-\beta_i\le c_{ij}\) certify the lower bound \[\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\ge\sum_jd_j\alpha_j-\sum_i u_i y_i\beta_i\] for every primal-feasible assignment \(x\). Equality, together with primal and dual feasibility, certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible client prices and nonnegative facility-capacity prices provide a verifiable lower bound; matching primal cost certifies optimal assignment.
assumptions_latex: The capacitated assignment primal is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_jd_j\alpha_j-\sum_i u_i y_i\beta_i\le\min_x\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\).

children.title: Radius Feasibility Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Radius Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct certificate for assignment feasibility under a prescribed service radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given facilities \(F\), clients \(C\), open facilities \(Y\subseteq F\), metric \(d\), and radius \(R\ge0\), a map \(\phi:C\to Y\) is a radius-feasibility certificate when \(d(j,\phi(j))\le R\) for every \(j\in C\). The certificate is verified by checking membership \(\phi(j)\in Y\) and the distance inequality for each client. Its existence is equivalent to feasibility of the uncapacitated radius-restricted assignment problem for the fixed open set \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A client-to-open-facility map whose every assigned distance is at most the radius certifies uncapacitated radius feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\) certifies feasibility exactly when \(\phi(j)\in Y\) and \(d(j,\phi(j))\le R\) for all \(j\in C\).

children.title: Capacity Feasibility Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut characterization of splittable capacitated assignment feasibility on an admissibility graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(C\cup F,E)\) be bipartite, with client demands \(d_j\ge0\) and facility capacities \(u_i\ge0\). A splittable assignment \(x_{ij}\ge0\) supported on \(E\), satisfying \(\sum_{i:(j,i)\in E}x_{ij}=d_j\) and \(\sum_{j:(j,i)\in E}x_{ij}\le u_i\), exists if and only if every \(S\subseteq C\) satisfies \[\sum_{j\in S}d_j\le\sum_{i\in N(S)}u_i.\] A feasible flow certifies feasibility; a violating set \(S\) certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splittable capacitated assignment is feasible exactly when every client subset has no more demand than the capacity of its neighboring facilities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite bipartite admissibility graph.
Client demand may be split among adjacent facilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) exists if and only if \(d(S)\le u(N(S))\) for every \(S\subseteq C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Radius–Capacity Interaction Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood-cut certificate for simultaneous radius and splittable-capacity feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix radius \(R\), open facilities \(Y\), client demands \(d_j\ge0\), and capacities \(u_i\ge0\). Define \(N_R(S)=\{i\in Y:\exists j\in S,\ d(i,j)\le R\}\). There exists a splittable assignment supported only on pairs of distance at most \(R\), meeting every demand and respecting every capacity, if and only if \[\sum_{j\in S}d_j\le\sum_{i\in N_R(S)}u_i\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq C.\] A feasible assignment flow certifies feasibility, while any violating \(S\) certifies joint radius–capacity infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint feasibility holds exactly when every client subset has enough total capacity among facilities reachable within the prescribed radius.
assumptions_latex: The client and facility sets are finite.
Only open facilities within distance \(R\) are admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\)-bounded capacitated assignment is feasible if and only if \(d(S)\le u(N_R(S))\) for all \(S\subseteq C\).

children.title: Feasibility Certificate Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where isolated certificate families fail to capture joint infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Certificate Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate radius and aggregate-capacity checks do not certify their joint feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{a,b\}\), \(F=Y=\{p,q\}\), \(d_a=d_b=1\), and \(u_p=u_q=1\). For some \(R\ge0\), suppose the radius-admissible edges are exactly \((a,p)\) and \((b,p)\). Every client has an open facility within radius \(R\), and total capacity equals total demand: \(u_p+u_q=d_a+d_b=2\). Nevertheless no radius-respecting capacitated assignment exists, because \(S=\{a,b\}\) has \(N_R(S)=\{p\}\) and \(d(S)=2>u_p=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Individual radius reachability plus sufficient aggregate capacity can fail: both clients may reach only the same unit-capacity facility.
assumptions_latex: Each client has unit demand and each facility unit capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall j\,N_R(\{j\})\ne\varnothing\) and \(u(F)\ge d(C)\) do not imply joint radius–capacity feasibility.

notation.meaning: facilities reachable within radius R from clients in S

children.title: Location Branching Schemes
children.top_down_role: Branching choices tailored to facility, assignment, or service decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Location Branching Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-and-cut disjunctions for binary facility-opening and assignment decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a mixed-integer location formulation with binary opening variables \(y_i\), binary assignment variables \(x_{ij}\), and a valid LP relaxation at each search node. Repeatedly select a live node, solve its LP relaxation, and prune the node if the relaxation is infeasible or its lower bound is no better than the incumbent value. Violated valid location cuts may be separated and added before branching. If the resulting LP solution is integer feasible, update the incumbent when its objective value is better and then fathom the node. Otherwise, if some opening variable satisfies \(0<y_i<1\), create children with \(y_i=0\) and \(y_i=1\); if no opening variable is fractional but some assignment variable satisfies \(0<x_{ij}<1\), create children with \(x_{ij}=0\) and \(x_{ij}=1\). When no live nodes remain, return the incumbent, or report infeasibility if no incumbent was found.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve valid node relaxations, add valid cuts, update the incumbent at integer solutions, branch first on fractional openings and then on fractional assignments, and prune by infeasibility or incumbent bounds.
assumptions_latex: The formulation has finitely many binary variables \(y_i\) and \(x_{ij}\), and these include every variable required to be integral.
Every added cut is valid for all integer-feasible descendants of the node where it is used.
Each branching disjunction covers every integer-feasible solution at its parent node.
Node relaxations are solved exactly and provide valid lower bounds for the minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When the live-node set is exhausted, the incumbent is an optimal integer-feasible solution; if no incumbent exists, the formulation is infeasible.

children.title: Location Cut Families

knowledge_statements.title: Location Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius-neighborhood capacity inequalities valid for capacitated location formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let clients have demands \(d_j\ge0\), facilities have capacities \(u_i\ge0\), and \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate opening. Under a service radius \(R\), define \(N_R(S)=\{i:\exists j\in S,\ d(i,j)\le R\}\). Every feasible radius-restricted capacitated location solution satisfies the cut family \[\sum_{i\in N_R(S)}u_i y_i\ge\sum_{j\in S}d_j\qquad(S\subseteq C).\] Any inequality violated by a relaxation point separates that point from the convex hull of feasible integer location solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every client subset requires enough opened capacity among facilities reachable within the radius; violations yield valid location cuts.
assumptions_latex: Assignments use only pairs at distance at most \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in N_R(S)}u_i y_i\ge d(S)\) is valid for every \(S\subseteq C\).

children.title: Location Cut Separation

knowledge_statements.title: Location Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation oracle for valid inequalities used in location branch-and-cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rational relaxation point \(\bar z\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and a family \(\mathcal C=\{(a,b):a^Tz\le b\text{ is valid for }P\}\), a separation algorithm either returns \((a,b)\in\mathcal C\) satisfying \(a^T\bar z>b\), or certifies that \(a^T\bar z\le b\) for every \((a,b)\in\mathcal C\). The returned inequality is added to the current location relaxation and the relaxation is reoptimized. Exact separation requires the certificate to cover the entire declared family \(\mathcal C\); failure merely to find a cut is not such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separation oracle finds a valid location inequality violated by the current fractional solution or certifies that none exists in the specified family.
assumptions_latex: The inequality family \(\mathcal C\) is explicitly specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns a violated valid inequality or a valid nonviolation certificate for \(\mathcal C\).

children.title: Location Search-Tree Control
children.top_down_role: Node management and bounding roles within exact location search.

knowledge_statements.title: Location Search-Tree Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact node processing and fathoming rules for a finite location branch-and-cut tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain active nodes \(\mathcal N\), incumbent value \(U\), and for each node \(N\) a relaxation lower bound \(L_N\). Select an active node, separate valid cuts, and solve its relaxation. Fathom \(N\) if the relaxation is infeasible, if \(L_N\ge U\), or if its solution is integral after updating \(U\). Otherwise branch into children whose feasible sets cover the integer-feasible set of \(N\). Stop when \(\mathcal N=\varnothing\); then the incumbent is globally optimal, or infeasibility is certified if no incumbent exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process nodes by relaxation bounds, prune infeasible or dominated nodes, branch on unresolved fractional nodes, and terminate when no active nodes remain.
assumptions_latex: Every branching disjunction covers all integer-feasible solutions at its parent.
The generated search tree is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustion of \(\mathcal N\) certifies global optimality of the incumbent or integer infeasibility.

notation.meaning: Valid lower bound at node N.
Objective value of the best incumbent.

children.title: Benders Master Location Problems
children.top_down_role: Master formulations governing strategic location decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Benders Master Location Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Benders master representation with location variables and a recourse epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Ty+q^Tx:y\in Y,\;Wx\ge h-Ty,\;x\ge0\}\). Let \(D=\{\pi\ge0:W^T\pi\le q\}\), with vertex set \(P\), and let \(R\) contain the extreme rays of \(\{r\ge0:W^Tr\le0\}\). Its Benders master is \[\min_{y,\theta}\ c^Ty+\theta\quad\text{subject to}\quad y\in Y,\quad \theta\ge\pi^T(h-Ty)\ (\pi\in P),\quad r^T(h-Ty)\le0\ (r\in R).\] Under linear-programming duality and complete inclusion of these cuts, the master has the original problem's optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Benders master retains location variables and represents assignment cost and feasibility through dual-point and dual-ray cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) contains the admissible, typically integral, location vectors.
For feasible \(y\), the assignment subproblem has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The complete master is an exact projection-and-epigraph representation of the original problem in \((y,\theta)\)-space.

notation.meaning: Dual vertices and recession rays generating Benders cuts.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation has the standard Benders master structure, but its exactness depends on polyhedral and dual-attainment conditions governing the asserted vertex and ray descriptions. With no cited source, those conditions and the complete-master conclusion cannot be validated reliably.

children.title: Assignment Subproblem Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Subproblem structures governing assignment recourse.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Subproblem Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clientwise decomposition of an uncapacitated assignment subproblem for fixed facility openings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be facilities, \(J\) clients, and fix \(y\in[0,1]^I\). The assignment value \[Q(y)=\min\left\{\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{i\in I}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\ (j\in J),\ 0\le x_{ij}\le y_i\right\}\] decomposes as \(Q(y)=\sum_{j\in J}Q_j(y)\), where \[Q_j(y)=\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1,\ 0\le x_{ij}\le y_i\right\}.\] Thus each client subproblem can be solved and dualized independently once \(y\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing facility openings separates the uncapacitated assignment problem into one independent linear program per client.
assumptions_latex: Assignment constraints contain no capacity or coupling constraint shared by distinct clients.
\(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\) is finite for every permitted assignment arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-location recourse value equals \(\sum_{j\in J}Q_j(y)\).

notation.meaning: Availability or opening value of facility i.
Fraction of client j assigned to facility i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clientwise decomposition is correct for the displayed uncapacitated formulation when values are interpreted in the extended-real sense if recourse is infeasible, and representation fits the leaf. children.title: Benders Feasibility Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cut families communicating assignment infeasibility to the master problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Benders Feasibility Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas-ray certificate excluding a location vector with infeasible assignment recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed candidate \(\bar y\), consider \(Wx\ge h-T\bar y\) with \(x\ge0\). If there exists \(r\ge0\) satisfying \(W^Tr\le0\) and \(r^T(h-T\bar y)>0\), then the subproblem is infeasible. The inequality \[r^T(h-Ty)\le0\] is valid for every location vector admitting feasible recourse and is violated by \(\bar y\). Consequently, \(r\) is a directly checkable certificate supporting a Benders feasibility cut that removes \(\bar y\) without excluding any recourse-feasible location vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual recession ray certifies assignment infeasibility and yields a valid inequality excluding the offending location vector.
assumptions_latex: The recourse system is linear and has the form \(Wx\ge h-Ty\), \(x\ge0\).
The vector \(r\) satisfies the displayed ray conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cut \(r^T(h-Ty)\le0\) is valid for recourse-feasible \(y\) and violated by \(\bar y\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ray conditions have the correct sign for the displayed recourse system and yield the claimed feasibility cut. Certificate is appropriate for this leaf, but no inspectable source supports the Farkas certificate and its Benders specialization.

children.title: Benders Optimality Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cut families communicating assignment cost information to the master problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Benders Optimality Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-feasible certificate lower-bounding assignment recourse in a Benders master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(Q(y)=\min\{q^Tx:Wx\ge h-Ty,\ x\ge0\}\). For any \(\pi\ge0\) with \(W^T\pi\le q\), weak duality gives \(Q(y)\ge\pi^T(h-Ty)\) whenever the subproblem is feasible. Hence \[\theta\ge\pi^T(h-Ty)\] is a valid Benders optimality cut. If \(\bar y\) has finite recourse and \(\bar\pi\) is dual-optimal at \(\bar y\), then the cut is tight there: \(Q(\bar y)=\bar\pi^T(h-T\bar y)\). Dual feasibility and this equality are checkable certificates of the generated cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any dual-feasible assignment solution gives a recourse lower bound; a dual optimum gives a cut tight at the current location vector.
assumptions_latex: The assignment subproblem is feasible and bounded at the point where tightness is claimed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality is globally valid, and a dual-optimal cut is tight at \(\bar y\).

notation.meaning: Master epigraph variable for recourse cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Location Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian relaxation of complicating constraints in a minimization location model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v_P=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_k(x)\le0\ (k=1,\ldots,m)\}\), define \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_kg_k(x)\) for \(\lambda\ge0\), and \(\theta(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)\). The Lagrangian dual is \[v_D=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\theta(\lambda).\] Every multiplier vector gives the valid lower bound \(\theta(\lambda)\le v_P\). Location methods choose constraints whose relaxation makes evaluation of \(\theta\) tractable, then optimize the concave function \(\theta\); equality \(v_D=v_P\) is not guaranteed for discrete \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relax complicating location constraints with nonnegative multipliers, optimize the resulting lower bound, and retain any duality gap for discrete models.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem is a minimization problem.
The relaxed constraints are written as \(g_k(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\lambda\ge0\), \(\theta(\lambda)\le v_D\le v_P\).

notation.meaning: Residual feasible set after selected constraints are relaxed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplier signs, lower-bound direction, concavity claim, and warning about a discrete duality gap are mathematically consistent, and duality is a suitable knowledge kind. No source or locator is supplied for either Lagrangian relaxation or its use in location models.

knowledge_statements.title: Column Generation for Location Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pricing loop for a finite pattern-based location linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the full master be \(\min\{\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}c_r\lambda_r:\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}a_r\lambda_r\ge b,\ \lambda\ge0\}\). Start with a feasible subset \(\mathcal R_0\). At iteration \(t\), solve the restricted master on \(\mathcal R_t\), obtain a dual optimum \(\pi^t\ge0\), and solve the pricing problem \(\min_{r\in\mathcal R}(c_r-(a_r)^T\pi^t)\). Add a column of negative reduced cost and repeat. If the minimum reduced cost is nonnegative, stop and return the restricted-master solution; it is optimal for the full linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve a restricted location master and add a minimum-reduced-cost pattern until exact pricing finds no improving column.
assumptions_latex: The initial restricted master is feasible, possibly through artificial columns.
The column set \(\mathcal R\) is finite and pricing is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonnegative minimum reduced cost certifies optimality for the full master linear program.

notation.meaning: Set of all admissible location patterns or columns.
Master weight assigned to column r.

knowledge_statements.title: LP Rounding for Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation framework rounding the standard uncapacitated facility-location relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solve \[L^*=\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}f_iy_i+\sum_{i\in I,j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1,\ 0\le x_{ij}\le y_i,\ 0\le y_i\le1\right\}.\] Apply a rounding map \(R\) to an optimal fractional pair \((x,y)\), producing opened facilities \(S\subseteq I\) and an assignment \(\sigma:J\to S\). An \(\alpha\)-LP-rounding algorithm must satisfy \[\mathbb E\left[\sum_{i\in S}f_i+\sum_{j\in J}c_{\sigma(j)j}\right]\le\alpha L^*.\] For deterministic rounding, omit the expectation. The returned pair \((S,\sigma)\) is integral and feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the facility-location LP, round openings and assignments jointly, and bound the integral expected cost by a factor of the LP optimum.
assumptions_latex: Facility and connection costs are nonnegative.
The rounding map always assigns every client to an opened facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is feasible and has expected cost at most \(\alpha L^*\).

notation.meaning: Integral opened set and client assignment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Randomized LP Rounding for Uncapacitated Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A clustering-and-rounding procedure using complete optimal primal and optimal dual LP solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute an optimal complete primal solution $(x^*,y^*)$ and an optimal dual solution $(v^*,w^*)$. Initialize $C\leftarrow D$, $T\leftarrow F$, and $k\leftarrow0$. While $C\ne\varnothing$, increment $k$, choose $j_k\in C$ minimizing $v_j^*$, and open exactly one $i_k\in N(j_k)$, choosing each $i\in N(j_k)$ with probability $x^*_{ij_k}=y_i^*$. Then set $C\leftarrow C\setminus(\{j_k\}\cup N^2(j_k))$ and $T\leftarrow T\setminus N(j_k)$. Independently open each $i\in T$ with probability $y_i^*$, and assign each client to its nearest open facility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from complete optimal primal and optimal dual solutions, repeatedly cluster around the remaining client with smallest dual value and randomly open one of its fractional neighbors according to the LP weights. Open each unclustered facility with its LP opening probability, then assign every client to its nearest open facility.
assumptions_latex: (x^*,y^*)\text{ is an optimal complete primal LP solution}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure produces a randomized integral set of open facilities and assigns every client to a nearest open facility.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic LP rounding for uncapacitated facility location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rounds optimal primal and dual facility-location LP solutions by repeatedly clustering unassigned clients around a minimum-dual-value client.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solve the facility-location LP and its dual to obtain optimal $(x^*,y^*)$ and $(v^*,w^*)$. Initialize $C\leftarrow D$ and $k\leftarrow0$. While $C\ne\varnothing$, increment $k$; choose $j_k\in C$ minimizing $v_j^*$; choose a facility $i_k\in N(j_k)$ of minimum opening cost; open $i_k$ and assign to it $j_k$ and every currently unassigned client in $N^2(j_k)$; then set $C\leftarrow C\setminus(\{j_k\}\cup N^2(j_k))$. The process terminates with every client assigned, and the selected neighborhoods $N(j_k)$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from optimal primal and dual LP solutions, repeatedly select the unassigned client with smallest dual value, open its cheapest positive-support facility, and assign that client and all still-unassigned clients in its two-hop neighborhood to the opened facility. Remove those clients and continue until all are assigned. The selected facility neighborhoods are pairwise disjoint.
assumptions_latex: (x^*,y^*)\text{ is an optimal primal facility-location LP solution}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure opens facilities and assigns every client, with }N(j_k)\cap N(j_\ell)=\varnothing\text{ whenever }k\ne\ell.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shmoys–Tardos–Aardal LP-Rounding Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-based construction for uncapacitated facility location; the metric assumption belongs to its approximation guarantee, not to the algorithm specification itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an uncapacitated facility-location instance \((\mathcal D,\mathcal F,(f_i)_{i\in\mathcal F},(c_{ij})_{i\in\mathcal F,j\in\mathcal D})\), compute optimal solutions \((x^*,y^*)\) and \((v^*,w^*)\) to formulations (22.2) and (22.3). Initialize \(k:=1\), \(X:=\varnothing\), and \(U:=\mathcal D\). While \(U\neq\varnothing\), choose \(j_k\in U\) minimizing \(v_{j_k}^*\); choose \(i_k\in\mathcal F\) with \(x_{i_kj_k}^*>0\) and minimum \(f_{i_k}\); set \(X:=X\cup\{i_k\}\); define \(N_k:=\{j\in U:\exists i\in\mathcal F,\ x_{ij_k}^*>0\text{ and }x_{ij}^*>0\}\); set \(\sigma(j):=i_k\) for all \(j\in N_k\); replace \(U\) by \(U\setminus N_k\); and increment \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute optimal solutions to the two specified formulations. Repeatedly choose an unassigned client of minimum optimal v-value, open a minimum-opening-cost facility fractionally supporting that client, and assign every remaining client whose fractional support overlaps the selected client's support. Remove those clients and continue until all clients are assigned.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and dual linear programs underlying uncapacitated facility-location primal–dual algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard relaxation is \[\min\ \sum_{i\in I}f_iy_i+\sum_{i\in I,j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}\] subject to \(\sum_i x_{ij}\ge1\) for \(j\in J\), \(x_{ij}\le y_i\), and \(x,y\ge0\). Its dual is \[\max\ \sum_{j\in J}\alpha_j\] subject to \(\alpha_j-\beta_{ij}\le c_{ij}\), \(\sum_{j\in J}\beta_{ij}\le f_i\), and \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\). Primal–dual location methods grow client variables \(\alpha_j\), interpret \(\beta_{ij}\) as contributions toward facility \(i\), and construct an integral solution while maintaining dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facility-location primal–dual methods raise feasible client duals, fund tight facilities, and build an integral solution against the dual lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Opening costs \(f_i\) and connection costs \(c_{ij}\) are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak duality gives \(\sum_j\alpha_j\le\sum_i f_iy_i+\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) for every feasible primal-dual pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Facility-Location Algorithm: Dual-Growth Phase
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-growth phase producing temporarily open facilities, connecting witnesses, and dual variables for the subsequent facility-selection phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initially every city is unconnected. Increase \(\alpha_j\) uniformly at unit rate for each unconnected city \(j\). When \(\alpha_j=c_{ij}\), declare \((i,j)\) tight; thereafter raise \(\beta_{ij}\) as \(\alpha_j\) grows so that the corresponding dual constraint remains feasible, and call \((i,j)\) special when \(\beta_{ij}>0\). When \(\sum_j\beta_{ij}=f_i\), declare facility \(i\) temporarily open, connect every unconnected city having a tight edge to \(i\), and record \(i\) as its connecting witness. Subsequently, connect any unconnected city as soon as it acquires a tight edge to a temporarily open facility, using that facility as its witness. Terminate when all cities are connected; simultaneous events may be processed in arbitrary order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raise the dual value of every unconnected city uniformly. An edge becomes tight when the city's dual value reaches its connection cost, after which its contribution toward the facility cost is raised while dual feasibility is maintained. A facility becomes temporarily open when its accumulated contributions equal its opening cost, and unconnected cities with tight edges to it become connected with that facility as witness. The phase ends when every city is connected; simultaneous events may be handled in any order.
assumptions_latex: j\text{ ranges over cities and }i\text{ over facilities}
c_{ij}\text{ is the connection cost and }f_i\text{ is the facility-opening cost}
\alpha_j\text{ and }\beta_{ij}\text{ are the dual variables of the facility-location LP pair}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At termination every city has a temporarily open connecting witness, while the prescribed updates maintain dual feasibility.}

knowledge_statements.title: Facility-Location Scaling Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric framework combining scaled opening costs with augmentation and evaluation under original costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each scale \(\lambda\) in a finite set \(\Lambda\subset(0,\infty)\), replace opening costs by \(f_i^{\lambda}=\lambda f_i\), run a base facility-location algorithm to obtain \(S_\lambda\), and apply an augmentation operator \(A\) to produce \(\widehat S_\lambda=A(S_\lambda)\supseteq S_\lambda\). Assign each client to its least-cost facility in \(\widehat S_\lambda\). Evaluate every candidate using the original objective \[F(S)=\sum_{i\in S}f_i+\sum_{j\in J}\min_{i\in S}c_{ij},\] and return a candidate minimizing \(F\). Any approximation guarantee requires a separate bound coupling scaled opening cost, connection cost, and augmentation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run a location method at several opening-cost scales, augment each solution, and select the best candidate under the original objective.
assumptions_latex: The base algorithm and augmentation operator return nonempty facility sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The framework returns \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda\in\Lambda}F(\widehat S_\lambda)\).

children.title: Greedy Facility Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Greedy enlargement of provisional facility solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Facility Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-facility-at-a-time augmentation for an uncapacitated location objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonempty initial facility set \(S_0\subseteq I\), define \(F(S)=\sum_{i\in S}f_i+\sum_{j\in J}\min_{i\in S}c_{ij}\). At iteration \(t\), compute \(\Delta_i=F(S_t\cup\{i\})-F(S_t)\) for every \(i\in I\setminus S_t\). If \(\min_i\Delta_i<0\), choose a minimizer \(i_t\) and set \(S_{t+1}=S_t\cup\{i_t\}\); otherwise stop and output \(S_t\), assigning each client to a nearest open facility. The algorithm terminates after at most \(|I|-|S_0|\) additions and returns a set admitting no improving single-facility addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly add the facility giving the greatest objective decrease, stopping when no single unopened facility improves the solution.
assumptions_latex: The facility and client sets are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(S\) satisfies \(F(S\cup\{i\})\ge F(S)\) for every \(i\in I\setminus S\).

notation.meaning: Opening-plus-nearest-assignment cost of facility set S.
Opened facility set at iteration t.
Objective change caused by adding facility i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal service-cost gain bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facility-location service costs and positive facility-opening costs, with aggregate facility cost given by the sum of opening costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne X,X^*\subseteq\mathcal F\). Then \[\sum_{i\in X^*}\left(c_S(X)-c_S(X\cup\{i\})\right)\ge c_S(X)-c_S(X^*).\] Consequently, there exists \(i\in X^*\) such that \[\frac{c_S(X)-c_S(X\cup\{i\})}{f_i}\ge \frac{c_S(X)-c_S(X^*)}{c_F(X^*)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of the individual service-cost reductions from adding facilities in X* to X is at least the service-cost difference between X and X*. Hence some facility in X* attains at least the aggregate service-cost reduction per unit facility cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in X^*}(c_S(X)-c_S(X\cup\{i\}))\ge c_S(X)-c_S(X^*)\), and \(\exists i\in X^*:\frac{c_S(X)-c_S(X\cup\{i\})}{f_i}\ge\frac{c_S(X)-c_S(X^*)}{c_F(X^*)}\).

children.title: Scaling–Augmentation Interaction
children.top_down_role: How scaling choices influence subsequent augmentation behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling–Augmentation Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact objective identity for opening-cost scaling followed by facility augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a finite facility set, let \(f_i\ge 0\), and let \(C(S)\) be the assignment cost induced by a nonempty set \(S\subseteq F\). Define \(f(S)=\sum_{i\in S}f_i\) and \(\Phi_\delta(S)=C(S)+\delta f(S)\) for \(\delta>0\). For every augmentation set \(A\subseteq F\),
\[
\Phi_\delta(S)-\Phi_\delta(S\cup A)=C(S)-C(S\cup A)-\delta f(A\setminus S).
\]
Thus augmentation improves the scaled objective exactly when its assignment-cost reduction exceeds \(\delta f(A\setminus S)\); it improves the original objective exactly when that reduction exceeds \(f(A\setminus S)\). Consequently, scaling with \(0<\delta<1\) can accept augmentations that do not improve the original objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling opening costs changes an augmentation’s acceptance threshold but not its assignment-cost gain; down-scaling can admit moves that worsen the original objective.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite and \(f_i\ge 0\) for every \(i\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_\delta(S)-\Phi_\delta(S\cup A)=C(S)-C(S\cup A)-\delta f(A\setminus S)\).

notation.meaning: assignment cost when facilities S are open

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The objective identity and its threshold interpretation are mathematically correct, and property is appropriate for this interaction leaf. However, the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator, so its interpretation of the taxonomy-specific scaling framework cannot be evidence-reviewed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaling and greedy-augmentation approximation conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a weighted facility/service-cost guarantee into an approximation guarantee through facility-cost scaling followed by greedy augmentation in the original instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\beta,\gamma_S,\gamma_F>0\) and an algorithm \(A\) computes, for every instance, a solution \(X\) satisfying \[\beta c_F(X)+c_S(X)\le \gamma_Fc_F(X^*)+\gamma_Sc_S(X^*)\] for every \(\varnothing\ne X^*\subseteq\mathcal F\). If \(\delta\ge 1/\beta\), then scaling the facility costs by \(\delta\), applying \(A\) to the modified instance, and greedily augmenting the result with respect to the original instance produces a solution of cost at most \[\max\left\{\frac{\gamma_F}{\beta}+\ln(\beta\delta),\;1+\frac{\gamma_S-1}{\beta\delta}\right\}\] times the optimum cost of the original instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm satisfying the stated weighted facility-and-service-cost inequality can be converted into an approximation algorithm by scaling facility costs, running the algorithm, and greedily augmenting its output under the original costs.
assumptions_latex: For every instance and every \(\varnothing\ne X^*\subseteq\mathcal F\), algorithm \(A\) returns \(X\) with \(\beta c_F(X)+c_S(X)\le\gamma_Fc_F(X^*)+\gamma_Sc_S(X^*)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cost}(Y)\le\max\left\{\frac{\gamma_F}{\beta}+\ln(\beta\delta),\;1+\frac{\gamma_S-1}{\beta\delta}\right\}\operatorname{OPT}\) for the original instance.

opening cost of the redundant facility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded failure of facility-addition search when deletion is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(M>1\), let the facility set be \(F=\{a,b\}\), let there be one client located at \(b\), let \(d(a,b)=1\), and let \(f_a=M\) and \(f_b=1\). For every nonempty \(S\subseteq F\), define the uncapacitated facility-location objective by \(\Phi(S)=\sum_{i\in S}f_i+\min_{i\in S}d(i,b)\). Start an add-only augmentation method from \(S_0=\{a,b\}\). No addition is available, so the method returns \(S_0\), for which \(\Phi(S_0)=M+1\). The optimal set is \(S^*=\{b\}\), for which \(\Phi(S^*)=1\). Consequently, \[\frac{\Phi(S_0)}{\Phi(S^*)}=M+1\to\infty\quad\text{as }M\to\infty.\] Thus add-only augmentation has no approximation guarantee when its initial set may contain costly redundant facilities that cannot be deleted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For metric uncapacitated facility location, add-only augmentation can have an unbounded approximation ratio when its initial solution contains costly redundant facilities that cannot be deleted.

Local Search for Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-move local search for metric uncapacitated facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given finite facilities \(F\), clients \(D\), opening costs \(f_i\ge0\), client weights \(w_j\ge0\), and metric distances \(d\), initialize a nonempty set \(S\subseteq F\). Its objective is
\[
\Phi(S)=\sum_{i\in S}f_i+\sum_{j\in D}w_j\min_{i\in S}d(i,j).
\]
While there exists an addition \(S\cup\{i\}\), a nonempty deletion \(S\setminus\{i\}\), or a swap \((S\setminus\{i\})\cup\{h\}\) having strictly smaller objective, perform such a move. Output \(S\) when none exists. Because \(F\) is finite and every move strictly decreases \(\Phi\), the procedure terminates at a one-move local optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly add, delete, or swap one facility whenever the metric facility-location objective strictly decreases; return a one-move local optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(S)\le \Phi(S')\) for every feasible one-addition, one-deletion, or one-swap neighbor \(S'\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite strict-descent procedure correctly terminates at a one-add, one-delete, one-swap local optimum, and algorithm fits the topic container. It states no approximation factor, so the unspecified approximation variant is not itself an error. No source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Lagrangian Median Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Lagrangian relaxation regimes for median-location objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Median Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform-penalty relaxation of the at-most-k metric median constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a finite facility set and let \(C(S)\) denote the assignment cost of a nonempty set \(S\subseteq F\). For the at-most-\(k\) median value
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_k=\min\{C(S):1\le |S|\le k\},
\]
the Lagrangian relaxation with multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\) is
\[
L(\lambda)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq F}\bigl(C(S)+\lambda(|S|-k)\bigr)
=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq F}\bigl(C(S)+\lambda|S|\bigr)-\lambda k.
\]
The inner minimization is an uncapacitated facility-location problem with uniform opening cost \(\lambda\), and \(L(\lambda)\le\operatorname{OPT}_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalizing every opened facility by a multiplier converts at-most-k median into uniform-cost facility location and yields a lower bound on the median optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(C(S)\ge0\) is defined for every nonempty \(S\subseteq F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\lambda)=\min_{S\ne\varnothing}(C(S)+\lambda|S|)-\lambda k\le\operatorname{OPT}_k\).

notation.meaning: assignment cost of facility set S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign of the multiplier, the uniform-opening-cost reformulation, and the lower-bound direction are correct for the at-most-k constraint. Duality is suitable for this relaxation leaf, but the record has no source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Multiplier-Preserving Median Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Approximation guarantees preserving selected multiplier relationships.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Preserving Median Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian-multiplier-preserving guarantee for uniform-opening-cost facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(\rho\ge1\). An algorithm for the uniform-penalty relaxation is \(\rho\)-Lagrangian-multiplier-preserving if, for every finite instance and every \(\lambda\ge0\), its output \(S_\lambda\ne\varnothing\) satisfies
\[
C(S_\lambda)+\rho\lambda|S_\lambda|
\le
\rho\min_{\varnothing\ne T\subseteq F}\bigl(C(T)+\lambda|T|\bigr).
\]
Unlike an ordinary \(\rho\)-approximation, the opening penalty on the output is multiplied by \(\rho\) before comparison. This stronger placement of the multiplier is the property that permits exact cancellation of the penalty when \(|S_\lambda|=k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplier-preserving algorithm charges its output’s facility penalty at the approximation factor, enabling the penalty to cancel in a cardinality transfer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(S_\lambda)+\rho\lambda|S_\lambda|\le\rho\min_{T\ne\varnothing}(C(T)+\lambda|T|)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is a coherent multiplier-preserving condition, and condition fits a leaf about such guarantees. Its terminology and exact placement of the factor rho require an authoritative citation, but none is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-cardinality transfer from a multiplier-preserving penalized solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be finite, let \(1\le k\le |F|\), let \(C(S)\ge0\) be defined for every nonempty \(S\subseteq F\), and fix \(\rho\ge1\). Let \(S^*\) minimize \(C(S)\) over all \(S\subseteq F\) satisfying \(|S|=k\). Suppose that, for some \(\lambda\ge0\), an algorithm returns a nonempty set \(S_\lambda\subseteq F\) with \(|S_\lambda|=k\) and \[C(S_\lambda)+\rho\lambda|S_\lambda|\le\rho\min_{\varnothing\ne T\subseteq F}\bigl(C(T)+\lambda|T|\bigr).\] Then \[C(S_\lambda)\le\rho C(S^*).\] Thus an exact-k output satisfying the rho-multiplier-preserving inequality is a rho-approximate solution for the corresponding exact-k median instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a multiplier-preserving penalized algorithm returns exactly k facilities, cancellation of the equal cardinality penalties transfers its approximation factor to exact-k median.

children.top_down_role: Regimes where multiplier-preserving behavior weakens or ceases.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite, \(1\le k\le|F|\), and \(C(S)\ge0\) is defined for every nonempty \(S\subseteq F\).
\(\rho\ge1\), \(\lambda\ge0\), \(|S_\lambda|=|S^*|=k\), and \(S^*\) is optimal among exact-k sets.
Only the displayed ordinary approximation inequality is assumed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why an ordinary penalized approximation does not automatically transfer to k-median.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be finite, let \(1\le k\le|F|\), let \(C(S)\ge0\) be defined for every nonempty \(S\subseteq F\), and let \(S^*\) minimize \(C(S)\) over all \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|=k\). Suppose \(\rho\ge1\), \(\lambda\ge0\), and a nonempty set \(S_\lambda\subseteq F\) with \(|S_\lambda|=k\) satisfies only the ordinary penalized guarantee \[C(S_\lambda)+\lambda|S_\lambda|\le\rho\min_{\varnothing\ne T\subseteq F}\bigl(C(T)+\lambda|T|\bigr).\] Comparison with \(S^*\) yields only \[C(S_\lambda)\le\rho C(S^*)+(\rho-1)\lambda k.\] For \(\rho>1\), the assumptions provide no bound on \(\lambda k\) in terms of \(C(S^*)\), so this ordinary guarantee alone does not imply a multiplicative exact-k median guarantee. Such a transfer requires multiplier preservation or an additional bound controlling \(\lambda k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordinary penalized approximation leaves an additive penalty after cardinality matching. For approximation factors greater than one, that penalty prevents a multiplicative k-median transfer unless it is separately controlled.
