children.title: Swap-Based Local Search for Median Location

knowledge_statements.title: Swap-Based Local Search for Median Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite p-swap descent for metric exact-k median.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite facilities \(F\), clients \(D\), metric distances \(d\), weights \(w_j\ge0\), an integer \(k\), and a swap parameter \(p\ge1\), initialize \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|=k\). Define \(C(S)=\sum_{j\in D}w_j\min_{i\in S}d(i,j)\). While there exist sets \(R\subseteq S\) and \(A\subseteq F\setminus S\) with \(1\le|R|=|A|\le p\) and \(C((S\setminus R)\cup A)<C(S)\), replace \(S\) by \((S\setminus R)\cup A\). Output \(S\) when no improving exchange exists. Strict descent over finitely many \(k\)-subsets guarantees termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange up to p open facilities for the same number of closed facilities until no exchange strictly improves the metric k-median cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(S)\le C((S\setminus R)\cup A)\) whenever \(R\subseteq S\), \(A\subseteq F\setminus S\), and \(|R|=|A|\le p\).

notation.meaning: current set of k median facilities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The p-swap descent is well-defined, preserves exact cardinality, and terminates because it strictly descends over finitely many k-subsets. Algorithm is appropriate for the topic. The record does not claim an approximation factor, but it still needs a source and locator for this standard local-search formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Polynomial (5+epsilon)-Approximation by Swap Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm and approximation guarantee for metric k-median, conditional on the specified instance transformation from Lemma 22.15.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\epsilon\le 1\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact discrete radius search using a monotone covering-feasibility oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(D\) be finite nonempty sets, let \(d\) be a metric on \(F\cup D\), and let \(1\le k\le|F|\). For every nonempty \(S\subseteq F\), define \(d(j,S)=\min_{i\in S}d(j,i)\), and form the finite nonempty candidate set \(R=\{d(i,j):i\in F,\ j\in D\}\). For \(r\in R\), let \(\operatorname{Feas}(r)\) hold exactly when some nonempty \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|\le k\) satisfies \(d(j,S)\le r\) for every \(j\in D\). Because \(\operatorname{Feas}(r)\) is monotone in \(r\), binary-search the sorted set \(R\) with an exact feasibility oracle and return a witnessing set at the smallest feasible radius \(r^*\). Then \[r^*=\min_{S\subseteq F,\ 1\le|S|\le k}\max_{j\in D}d(j,S).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty finite client and facility sets, binary-search the client-facility distances using an exact monotone covering oracle; the smallest feasible distance is the exact discrete k-center radius.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farthest-first greedy two-approximation for metric k-center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,d)\) be a finite metric space and let \(1\le k\le|X|\). Choose any \(x_1\in X\) and set \(S_1=\{x_1\}\). For \(t=1,\ldots,k-1\), select
\[
x_{t+1}\in\arg\max_{x\in X}d(x,S_t),\qquad S_{t+1}=S_t\cup\{x_{t+1}\},
\]
where \(d(x,S)=\min_{s\in S}d(x,s)\). Return \(S_k\) with radius \(r(S_k)=\max_{x\in X}d(x,S_k)\). If \(r^*=\min_{|S|\le k}r(S)\), then
\[
r(S_k)\le2r^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly choose the point farthest from existing centers. The resulting k centers have covering radius at most twice optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(S_k)\le2\min_{S\subseteq X,\ |S|\le k}r(S)\).

children.title: Tree Location Structure
children.top_down_role: Structural features specific to location problems on trees.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,E)\) is a finite tree with strictly positive edge lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\arg\min_{x\in V}H(x)\iff w(Q)\le W/2\) for every component \(Q\) of \(T-v\).

notation.meaning: weighted sum of tree distances to v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component-balance characterization of weighted vertex medians on a tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(V,E)\) be a finite tree with strictly positive edge lengths and vertex weights \(w_u\ge0\), and let \(W=\sum_{u\in V}w_u>0\). Define \[H(v)=\sum_{u\in V}w_u d_T(u,v)\qquad(v\in V).\] A vertex \(v\in V\) minimizes \(H\) over \(V\) if and only if every connected component \(Q\) of \(T-v\) has total weight \[w(Q)=\sum_{u\in Q}w_u\le W/2.\] Thus the weighted vertex one-median structure on a positively edge-weighted tree is determined by the balance of the components incident to the candidate vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite tree with strictly positive edge lengths, a vertex is a weighted one-median exactly when every component remaining after its removal contains at most half the total vertex weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree Location Structure

children.title: Tree Location Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization approaches exploiting tree topology.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,E)\) is a finite tree represented by adjacency lists and has nonnegative edge lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\arg\min_{x\in V}\sum_{u\in V}w_u d_T(u,x)\), and \(v\) is computed in \(O(|V|)\) time using \(O(|V|)\) storage.

notation.meaning: vertex reached by the heavy-component search
shortest-path distance induced by the nonnegative edge lengths

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-time heavy-component search for a weighted tree vertex median.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite tree \(T=(V,E)\) with nonnegative edge lengths and vertex weights \(w_u\ge0\), represented by adjacency lists, root it arbitrarily and compute every rooted-subtree weight and \(W=\sum_{u\in V}w_u>0\) in one postorder traversal. Starting at the root, move to a child whenever that child's rooted subtree has weight greater than \(W/2\); stop when no such child exists and output the current vertex \(v\). After every move, the component behind the search has weight less than \(W/2\), and at termination every component of \(T-v\) has weight at most \(W/2\). Consequently, \[v\in\arg\min_{x\in V}\sum_{u\in V}w_u d_T(u,x).\] The preprocessing and search take \(O(|V|)\) time and \(O(|V|)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute subtree weights and follow any child subtree containing more than half the total vertex weight. The terminal vertex is a weighted tree median, found in linear time.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree Location Optimization

children.title: Network Location Structure
children.top_down_role: Structural features of location problems on general networks.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph whose edges have positive lengths.
Each edge is realized as a closed line segment, and points may lie at vertices or in edge interiors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The realization of \(G\) is a compact metric space under shortest-path distance.

notation.meaning: shortest-path metric induced by edge lengths

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric realization used by continuous and vertex-demand network location models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace every edge \(e=uv\in E\) of length \(\ell_e>0\) by an interval of length \(\ell_e\), identifying its endpoints with \(u\) and \(v\). The resulting network realization is \(|G|\). For \(x,y\in |G|\), define \(d_G(x,y)\) as the minimum length of an \(x\)-to-\(y\) path in \(|G|\). Thus \((|G|,d_G)\) is a compact geodesic metric space; unlike a tree network, it may contain several distinct shortest or simple paths between two points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite edge-weighted network becomes a compact metric space by realizing edges as intervals and measuring distance by shortest paths; cycles may create multiple paths between points.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Location Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and compact-geodesic conclusion are mathematically standard and fit Network Location Structure, but the record cites no inspectable source. The supplied network-optimization inventory does not specifically support metric-graph realization and compactness.

children.title: Network Location Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization approaches for location models on general networks.

assumptions_latex: \((|G|,d_G)\) is the compact realization of a finite connected network with positive edge lengths and contains at least \(p\) distinct points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a set \(S^*\subseteq |G|\) with \(|S^*|=p\) minimizing the total weighted demand-to-nearest-facility distance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous network weighted \(p\)-median formulation with discrete demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The continuous network \(p\)-median problem is
\[\min\left\{F(S):S\subseteq |G|,\ |S|=p\right\},\qquad F(S)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i\min_{s\in S}d_G(a_i,s).\]
A feasible solution places exactly \(p\) distinct facilities at arbitrary network points, including edge interiors. Compactness of \(|G|^p\) and continuity of the objective on ordered facility tuples yield a minimizing tuple; if it contains fewer than \(p\) distinct points, it can be padded with distinct network points without increasing the objective. Hence an optimal set \(S^*\) exists. If admissible facilities are restricted to a finite set \(C\subseteq |G|\) with \(|C|\ge p\), the same formula defines the discrete network \(p\)-median problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose exactly p distinct points on a compact network to minimize total weighted demand-to-nearest-facility distance. An optimum exists when the network contains at least p points; restricting facilities to a sufficiently large finite candidate set gives the discrete version.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Location Optimization

children.title: Tree-to-Network Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on extending tree-specific structure to broader network classes.

assumptions_latex: A transfer argument uses the Helly property for connected subgraphs of a tree.
The host network is allowed to contain a cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pairwise-intersection Helly argument for subtrees does not extend to all connected subsets of networks containing cycles.

notation.meaning: three closed connected arcs on the cycle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete obstruction to transferring subtree-intersection arguments from trees to cyclic networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Identify a cycle with \(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}	o\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\) be the quotient map. Define the closed connected arcs
\[A_1=\pi([0,1/2]),\qquad A_2=\pi([1/3,5/6]),\qquad A_3=\pi([2/3,7/6]).\]
Each pair of arcs intersects: \(A_1\cap A_2
e\varnothing\), \(A_2\cap A_3
e\varnothing\), and \(A_3\cap A_1
e\varnothing\). However, \(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3=\varnothing\). Hence pairwise-intersection certificates valid for subtrees cannot be transferred unchanged to connected subsets of networks with cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three explicitly specified connected arcs of a cycle intersect pairwise but have no common point, so Helly-based subtree arguments do not transfer unchanged to cyclic networks.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-to-Network Transfer Boundaries

assumptions_latex: The dimension satisfies \(d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), and demand points \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^d\) have weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_m>0\).
The initial point satisfies \(x^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), and no generated iterate coincides with a demand point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed nonsingular iteration is the classical Weiszfeld method for the weighted Euclidean geometric-median objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsingular Weiszfeld method for the Euclidean single-facility median; singular iterates are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i\lVert x-a_i\rVert_2,\]
initialize \(x^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\). Whenever \(x^{(k)}\notin\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), compute
\[x^{(k+1)}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\dfrac{w_i a_i}{\lVert x^{(k)}-a_i\rVert_2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\dfrac{w_i}{\lVert x^{(k)}-a_i\rVert_2}}.\]
If \(\lVert x^{(k+1)}-x^{(k)}\rVert_2\le\varepsilon\), stop and output \(x^{(k+1)}\); otherwise continue. Coincidence with a demand point requires a modified singularity rule and is outside this record.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonsingular Weiszfeld method repeatedly forms an inverse-distance-weighted average of the demand points and stops when successive iterates are within the specified positive tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Space Location Methods

children.title: Geometric Partition Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Spatial partition structures used in location optimization.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space equipped with its Borel sigma-algebra.
The sites \(s_1,ldots,s_m\in X\) are indexed, with \(m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\).
Ties are assigned to the least-index nearest site when disjoint cells are required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed nearest-site regions cover \(X\), and least-index tie-breaking produces a disjoint Borel partition whose cells retain the nearest-site property.

notation.meaning: closed nearest-site region of site i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric Voronoi regions and their disjoint Borel refinement under deterministic tie-breaking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}\subseteq X\), the closed nearest-site region of \(s_i\) is
\[V_i=\{x\in X:d(x,s_i)\le d(x,s_j)\text{ for every }j\}.\]
These regions satisfy \(X=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}V_i\), although they may overlap at tied points. Assign each point to the least index attaining \(\min_{1\le j\le m}d(x,s_j)\). Because distance functions are continuous and the site set is finite, the resulting disjoint cells are Borel sets. They cover \(X\) and retain the nearest-site property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed Voronoi regions cover a metric space but may overlap at ties; assigning every tied point to its least-index nearest site gives a disjoint Borel nearest-site partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Partition Frameworks

children.title: Geometric Dissection Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Recursive spatial dissection structures used in location optimization.

assumptions_latex: The dimension satisfies \(din\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), and \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is a bounded full-dimensional polytope.
\(\mathcal{T}\) is a finite family of full-dimensional simplices satisfying \(P=\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}}T\).
Distinct simplices have disjoint relative interiors, and every intersection \(T\cap T'\) is empty or a common face of both simplices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family \(\mathcal{T}\) is a face-to-face simplicial dissection of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-to-face simplicial dissections of bounded full-dimensional polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite family \(\mathcal{T}\) of full-dimensional simplices is a face-to-face simplicial dissection of \(P\) when
\[P=\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}}T,\qquad \operatorname{relint}(T)\cap\operatorname{relint}(T')=\varnothing\quad\text{for }T\ne T',\]
and, for all \(T,T'\in\mathcal{T}\), the intersection \(T\cap T'\) is empty or a common face of both simplices. These conditions say that the simplices cover \(P\), have disjoint relative interiors, and meet face-to-face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face-to-face simplicial dissection covers a full-dimensional bounded polytope by full-dimensional simplices with disjoint relative interiors, and any two simplices meet only in a common face or not at all.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Dissection Frameworks

children.title: Partition Boundary Interactions
children.top_down_role: Effects of region boundaries on facilities, clients, or assignments.

assumptions_latex: The dimension satisfies \(d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is measurable.
The measurable cells \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) cover \(D\), and \(\lambda_d(C_i\cap C_j)=0\) whenever \(i\ne j\).
Each cell boundary has \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cellwise integration is additive, and reassignment restricted to the union of cell boundaries does not change the integral objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Null-boundary invariance for additive Lebesgue-integral partition objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[B=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\partial C_i.\]
Because the union is finite and every \(\partial C_i\) is \(\lambda_d\)-null, \(\lambda_d(B)=0\). Since the cells cover \(D\) and have pairwise null intersections,
\[\int_D g(x)\,dx=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{C_i}g(x)\,dx.\]
Any two disjoint tie-breaking refinements that differ only on \(B\) agree almost everywhere and therefore give the same Lebesgue-integral objective. This invariance need not hold for an objective containing a singular measure supported on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite measurable cover whose cells overlap only on null sets and have null boundaries, a nonnegative measurable integral decomposes over the cells and is unchanged by boundary-only tie reassignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Partition Boundary Interactions

children.title: Dimension-Sensitive Decomposition Regimes
children.top_down_role: How geometric decomposition behavior varies with ambient dimension.

assumptions_latex: The dimension \(d\) is fixed when polynomial dependence on \(m\) is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The arrangement has at most \(\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom{m}{i}\) full-dimensional regions, a bound attained in general position.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hyperplane-arrangement cell count illustrating fixed- versus variable-dimension decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximum number of full-dimensional cells formed by \(m\) affine hyperplanes in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is
\[R_d(m)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom{m}{i}.\]
Equality holds when the hyperplanes are in general position. Hence \(R_d(m)=O(m^d)\) for fixed \(d\), while the exponent grows with dimension. Decomposition algorithms that explicitly enumerate arrangement cells are therefore polynomial in \(m\) only under a fixed-dimension convention; this guarantee does not yield polynomial time when \(d\) is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arrangement of m hyperplanes has at most a degree-d number of cells, so explicit cell enumeration is polynomial only in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Sensitive Decomposition Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hyperplane-arrangement formula, general-position equality condition, and fixed-dimension interpretation are mathematically standard, mutually consistent, and well matched to the complexity-bound role of this leaf. No source with a theorem or page locator is cited, however, and none of the supplied inventory items addresses hyperplane arrangements.

children.title: Set-Cover Logarithmic Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Logarithmic approximation performance for general set cover.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite universe with \(|U|=n\ge1\), and \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq2^U\) covers \(U\).
Every set has nonnegative cost, and the optimum cover has positive total cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cost-effectiveness greedy returns a cover of cost at most \(H_n\) times optimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted set cover under the standard polynomial-time greedy algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Starting with \(R=U\), repeatedly choose a set \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) minimizing \(c(S)/|S\cap R|\) among sets covering an uncovered element, and replace \(R\) by \(R\setminus S\). The selected sets form a cover \(C\) satisfying
\[\sum_{S\in C}c(S)\le H_n\,\mathrm{OPT}\le(1+\ln n)\mathrm{OPT}.\]
With explicitly represented incidences and rational costs, the rule is implementable in polynomial time. For unit costs it specializes to choosing a set containing the largest number of uncovered elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cost-effectiveness greedy algorithm for weighted set cover is an H_n-approximation, and therefore a 1+ln n approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Cover Logarithmic Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted greedy rule and its harmonic approximation guarantee are standard, precise, and appropriately classified as a complexity bound for this leaf. The record nevertheless has no citation supporting the approximation theorem or polynomial-time implementation claim.

children.title: Set-Cover Hardness Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Inapproximability boundaries associated with logarithmic set-cover performance.

assumptions_latex: Set cover instances have universe size \(n\).
Complexity is measured under polynomial-time approximation algorithms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A \((1-\varepsilon)\ln n\)-approximation would contradict the stated quasi-polynomial-time complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical near-logarithmic inapproximability threshold with its explicit complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), if a polynomial-time algorithm approximates set cover within factor \((1-\varepsilon)\ln n\) on every instance with \(n\) universe elements, then
\[\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(n^{O(\log\log n)}\right).\]
Consequently, under the assumption \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{DTIME}(n^{O(\log\log n)})\), no such approximation algorithm exists. Together with the harmonic greedy upper bound, this places unrestricted set cover at a logarithmic approximation threshold, up to lower-order terms and the stated assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unless NP has quasi-polynomial-time deterministic algorithms of the stated form, set cover cannot be approximated within (1-epsilon) ln n in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Cover Hardness Thresholds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim resembles the classical near-logarithmic set-cover hardness threshold, but the exact complexity assumption and quantifiers require inspection of the original hardness theorem. The symbol n is also used both for universe cardinality and inside the complexity-class notation, where the variable conventionally denotes encoded input length; a sourced version must distinguish these roles or quote the theorem's convention exactly.

There exists an infinite family of unweighted set cover instances with universe sizes \(n\to\infty\), together with a fixed resolution of greedy ties, such that
\[\frac{\mathrm{GREEDY}}{\mathrm{OPT}}\ge (1-o(1))\ln n.\]

children.title: Restricted Set-Cover Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural restrictions that alter the general logarithmic landmark.

assumptions_latex: \((U,\mathcal{S},c)\) is a weighted set cover instance with nonnegative costs.
Every element belongs to at most \(f\) sets, where \(f\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Threshold rounding of the covering LP gives an \(f\)-approximate integral cover.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-frequency weighted set cover via deterministic LP threshold rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Solve the covering relaxation
\[\min\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}c(S)x_S\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\ge1\ (e\in U),\qquad x_S\ge0.\]
Given an optimum solution \(x^*\), output \(C=\{S:x_S^*\ge1/f\}\). For each \(e\in U\), at most \(f\) variables occur in its covering constraint, so at least one is at least \(1/f\); hence \(C\) covers \(U\). Moreover, \(\sum_{S\in C}c(S)\le f\sum_Sc(S)x_S^*\le f\,\mathrm{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When each element occurs in at most f sets, solving the covering LP and selecting variables at least 1/f yields an f-approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Restricted Set-Cover Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold-rounding algorithm is internally correct: every covering constraint has at most f variables, so one reaches the 1/f threshold, and the cost inequality gives an f-approximation. The algorithm content kind fits the restricted-regime leaf, but the record provides no authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Frequency Covering Landmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP threshold rounding for weighted set cover with bounded element frequency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite, let \(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^U\) have costs \(c_S\ge 0\), and suppose every \(e\in U\) belongs to at most \(f\ge 1\) sets. Solve the relaxation \(\min\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S:\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\ge 1\ (e\in U),\ x_S\ge 0\}\), and output \(\mathcal C=\{S:x_S\ge 1/f\}\). Every element is covered because one of its at most \(f\) incident variables reaches \(1/f\), and \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal C}c_S\le f\sum_Sc_Sx_S\le f\,\mathrm{OPT}\). Thus bounded frequency gives a polynomial-time \(f\)-approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Threshold rounding of the covering LP gives a polynomial-time factor-f approximation when each element occurs in at most f sets.
assumptions_latex: Each element has frequency at most \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(\mathcal C)\le f\,\mathrm{OPT}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Cardinality Packing Landmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal-packing guarantee for unweighted sets of bounded cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite and let \(\mathcal S\) consist of nonempty sets satisfying \(|S|\le k\). Starting with \(P=\varnothing\), repeatedly add any set disjoint from every member of \(P\), stopping when no addition is possible. For an optimal disjoint subfamily \(P^*\), maximality makes every member of \(P^*\) intersect some member of \(P\). Because \(P^*\) is disjoint, a set \(S\in P\) intersects at most \(|S|\le k\) members of \(P^*\). Hence \(|P^*|\le k|P|\), so the maximal packing is a polynomial-time \(k\)-approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any maximal packing of nonempty sets of size at most k contains at least one kth of the optimum number of sets.

children.title: Maximum-Coverage Approximation Guarantees

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Coverage Approximation Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical greedy guarantee for weighted maximum coverage under a cardinality budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite with weights \(w_e\ge 0\), let \(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^U\), and let \(k\ge 1\). Define \(G_0=\varnothing\). For \(i=0,\ldots,k-1\), choose \(S_{i+1}\in\mathcal S\) maximizing the newly covered weight and put \(G_{i+1}=G_i\cup\{S_{i+1}\}\). If \(F(G)=\sum_{e\in\cup_{S\in G}S}w_e\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}=\max_{|G|\le k}F(G)\), then \(F(G_k)\ge \bigl(1-(1-1/k)^k\bigr)\mathrm{OPT}\ge (1-1/e)\mathrm{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedily choosing the set with greatest uncovered weight achieves at least 1−1/e of optimal weighted maximum coverage.
assumptions_latex: At most \(k\) sets may be selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(G_k)\ge \bigl(1-(1-1/k)^k\bigr)\mathrm{OPT}\ge (1-1/e)\mathrm{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: weight covered by selected family G
optimal covered weight using at most k sets

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Coverage Hardness Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tight polynomial-time approximation threshold for unrestricted maximum coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), consider unweighted maximum coverage with a finite universe \(U\), an explicitly listed family \(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^U\), and budget \(k\) included in the input. Unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), no polynomial-time algorithm can always return a family \(G\subseteq\mathcal S\) with \(|G|\le k\) and \(|\bigcup_{S\in G}S|\ge (1-1/e+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\). Together with the greedy guarantee, \(1-1/e\) is therefore the optimal worst-case polynomial-time approximation threshold under this assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unless P equals NP, unrestricted maximum coverage cannot be approximated beyond 1−1/e by any fixed positive constant.
assumptions_latex: The set system is explicitly represented and \(k\) is input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No polynomial-time \((1-1/e+\varepsilon)\)-approximation exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Tight Maximum-Coverage Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case tightness of greedy maximum coverage, including its finite-budget factor.

Consequently, analysis using only the largest-current-marginal rule cannot improve its factor beyond \(1-(1-1/k)^k\); as \(k\to\infty\), these ratios converge to \(1-1/e\).

assumptions_latex: Greedy ties may be resolved adversarially.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Maximum-Coverage Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact maximum coverage for laminar families with nonnegative element weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S\subseteq 2^U\) be laminar: for any \(A,B\in\mathcal S\), either \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), \(A\subseteq B\), or \(B\subseteq A\). Give elements nonnegative weights and impose budget \(k\). Every selected nonmaximal set can be replaced by an inclusion-maximal ancestor without decreasing covered weight. The inclusion-maximal members \(M_1,\ldots,M_r\) are pairwise disjoint; therefore compute \(W_i=\sum_{e\in M_i}w_e\) and select the \(\min\{k,r\}\) members with largest \(W_i\). This produces an optimal solution in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a laminar set family, maximum coverage is solved exactly by choosing the heaviest inclusion-maximal, pairwise-disjoint sets.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) is a finite laminar family.
Every selected set has unit budget cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected maximal members attain \(\max_{|G|\le k}\sum_{e\in\cup_{S\in G}S}w_e\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Cover Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness of exact cover by 3-sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact Cover by 3-Sets has input a finite universe \(U\) with \(|U|=3q\) and a family \(\mathcal S\subseteq\binom{U}{3}\). The question is whether there exists \(C\subseteq\mathcal S\) such that every element of \(U\) lies in exactly one member of \(C\), equivalently the members of \(C\) are pairwise disjoint and \(\bigcup_{S\in C}S=U\). This decision problem is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions, even though every available set has cardinality exactly three.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deciding whether 3-element sets can partition a universe is NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal S\) has cardinality three.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{X3C}\) is NP-complete.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Partitioning Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness of binary set-partitioning feasibility under sparse columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) have exactly three ones in every column. Deciding whether there is \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying \(Ax=\mathbf 1\) is NP-complete. Indeed, columns encode 3-element subsets and each row encodes an element that must occur in exactly one chosen subset. Consequently, binary set-partitioning optimization \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=\mathbf 1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\) is NP-hard even with \(c=\mathbf 0\) and three nonzero coefficients per column, when infeasibility must be detected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary set-partitioning feasibility is NP-complete even when each variable occurs in exactly three covering constraints.
assumptions_latex: Every column of \(A\) has exactly three ones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deciding \(Ax=\mathbf 1\) with binary \(x\) is NP-complete, and set-partitioning optimization is NP-hard.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Exact-Cover Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-time exact-cover feasibility on acyclic incidence graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an exact-cover instance \((U,\mathcal S)\), form the bipartite incidence graph with vertices \(U\cup\mathcal S\) and edge \(eS\) exactly when \(e\in S\). If this graph is a forest, exact-cover feasibility and a feasible selected family can be computed by tree dynamic programming. A set vertex records its selected or unselected state; an element vertex accepts precisely those child states for which exactly one incident set is selected. Processing every directed edge once and retaining a realizing state yields an \(O(|U|+|\mathcal S|+|E|)\)-time algorithm, where \(E\) is the incidence edge set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact cover is solvable by linear-time tree dynamic programming when its bipartite incidence graph is a forest.
assumptions_latex: Its bipartite incidence graph is a forest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility and a witness exact cover are computable in \(O(|U|+|\mathcal S|+|E|)\) time.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric–Nonmetric Location Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-ratio approximability separates metric from unrestricted k-median costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In metric \(k\)-median, facilities and clients lie in a common finite metric space and assignment costs satisfy the triangle inequality; this problem admits polynomial-time constant-factor approximation. Without the metric condition, even costs in \(\{0,1\}\) preclude every finite multiplicative factor unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\): encode a set system by setting \(c_{ij}=0\) when facility-set \(i\) contains client-element \(j\), and \(c_{ij}=1\) otherwise. With at most \(k\) facilities, optimum cost is zero exactly when \(k\) sets cover all elements, so any finite-ratio algorithm would decide an NP-complete covering problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric k-median has constant approximations, whereas unrestricted nonmetric costs admit no finite multiplicative approximation unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The metric model uses nonnegative symmetric distances satisfying the triangle inequality.
The nonmetric model permits arbitrary explicitly represented costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric \(k\)-median is constant-factor approximable, while unrestricted nonmetric \(k\)-median has no finite approximation ratio unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: cost of assigning client j to facility i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the metric versus nonmetric container, but both the metric constant-factor result and the zero-optimum nonmetric hardness reduction need precise citations. The statement also embeds proof-style reduction reasoning.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncapacitated–Capacitated Location Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity semantics must be fixed before stating a location approximation threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For demands \(d_j\), capacitated facility location adds \(\sum_j d_jx_{ij}\le u_i y_i\) to assignment and opening constraints. Hard capacities require \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\); soft capacities permit multiple copies, typically \(y_i\in\mathbb Z_+\). If \(u_i\ge\sum_jd_j\) for every facility, the capacity inequalities are redundant and the uncapacitated model is recovered. Thus uncapacitated instances embed in the capacitated class, but the label “capacitated” alone determines no unique approximation boundary: hard versus soft, uniform versus nonuniform, and permitted capacity violation define mathematically different feasible regions and guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncapacitated location embeds into capacitated location, but approximation claims depend essentially on hard, soft, uniform, and violation conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(u_i\ge\sum_jd_j\) for all \(i\), the capacitated feasible region reduces to the uncapacitated one; otherwise the approximation boundary is model-dependent.

notation.meaning: fraction of client j assigned to facility i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but the claim deliberately spans hard capacities, soft capacities, uniformity, and capacity violation conventions. Specific sources fixing those models are required before the asserted boundary can be reviewed reliably.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Metric–Geometric Location Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PTAS boundary between fixed-dimensional Euclidean and general-metric k-median.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed dimension \(d\ge 1\) and every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), Euclidean \(k\)-median on finite points in \(\mathbb R^d\), with \(k\) included in the input, admits a polynomial-time solution of cost at most \((1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\). In contrast, general finite metric \(k\)-median is APX-hard; consequently it has no polynomial-time approximation scheme unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). The geometric conclusion requires fixed dimension: allowing dimension to grow with the input does not assert the same scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-dimensional Euclidean k-median has a PTAS, while general metric k-median is APX-hard and has no PTAS unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) are fixed constants in the Euclidean regime.
Distances are Euclidean in \(\mathbb R^d\) or are given by a finite metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Euclidean \(k\)-median in fixed dimension has a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation scheme; general metric \(k\)-median has no PTAS unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Center Approximation Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp polynomial-time approximation threshold for discrete metric \(k\)-center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((V,d)\) be a finite metric space and let \(1\le k<|V|\). For \(C\subseteq V\), define \(r(C)=\max_{v\in V}\min_{c\in C}d(v,c)\) and \(r^*=\min_{|C|\le k}r(C)\). The farthest-first traversal, initialized at any vertex and repeatedly adding a vertex farthest from the current centers until \(k\) centers have been chosen, returns \(C\) satisfying \(r(C)\le 2r^*\). Conversely, for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for all finite metric instances would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Thus the metric discrete \(k\)-center approximation threshold is \(2\), subject to \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete metric k-center admits a factor-2 approximation, while any uniformly better polynomial-time factor would imply P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sharp polynomial-time approximation factor is \(2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck Approximation Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation-threshold definition for minimization problems governed by a maximum local cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family \(\mathcal I\) of minimization instances, let each feasible solution \(S\in\mathcal F(I)\) have bottleneck value \(B_I(S)=\max_{e\in E(I)}b_{I,e}(S)\), and write \(B_I^*=\min_{S\in\mathcal F(I)}B_I(S)\). Its polynomial-time bottleneck approximation threshold is \(\rho^*=\inf\{\rho\ge1:\text{a polynomial-time algorithm always returns }S\text{ with }B_I(S)\le\rho B_I^*\}\). If no finite factor is achievable, set \(\rho^*=+\infty\). Conditional hardness assumptions, the encoding model, and whether the infimum is attained are part of any claimed evaluation of \(\rho^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The threshold is the infimum of all worst-case polynomial-time approximation factors achievable for a specified bottleneck minimization family.
assumptions_latex: Every instance \(I\in\mathcal I\) has a nonempty feasible family \(\mathcal F(I)\).
All bottleneck costs are nonnegative and finitely encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho^*\) precisely records the boundary between achievable and excluded approximation factors.

notation.meaning: Optimal bottleneck value for instance I.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard multiplicative approximation-threshold definition specialized to bottleneck objectives.

children.title: Radius-Search Connections
children.top_down_role: Links between bottleneck thresholds and parametric radius search.

knowledge_statements.title: Radius-Search Connections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of finite-valued bottleneck minimization to ordered threshold feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=\{r_1<\cdots<r_m\}\) contain every possible bottleneck value, and suppose feasibility is monotone: if a solution exists with value at most \(r_i\), then one exists for every \(r_j\ge r_i\). Query a threshold oracle by binary search on \(R\), maintaining an infeasible lower interval and a feasible upper interval. Stop at the least declared-feasible radius \(\widehat r\) and output the oracle's solution. An exact oracle yields \(\widehat r=r^*\). More generally, if feasibility at radius \(r\) makes the oracle return a solution of value at most \(\alpha r\), the output has value at most \(\alpha r^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary search over candidate radii converts monotone threshold feasibility into exact or approximate bottleneck optimization.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is finite, ordered, and contains the optimum \(r^*\).
The threshold oracle runs in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search uses \(O(\log |R|)\) oracle calls and returns an \(\alpha\)-approximate solution.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Monotone binary search and its dilation guarantee follow directly from the stated oracle contract.

children.title: Metric-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of center or bottleneck landmarks on metric structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of constant-factor approximability when the triangle inequality is removed from center instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider discrete \(k\)-center with a symmetric dissimilarity \(d\) satisfying \(d(v,v)=0\), but not necessarily the triangle inequality, and let \(1\le k<|V|\). Given a graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(M>1\), set \(d(u,u)=0\), set \(d(u,v)=1\) for distinct adjacent vertices \(u,v\), and set \(d(u,v)=M\) for distinct nonadjacent vertices. A center set of size at most \(k\) has radius at most \(1\) exactly when \(G\) has a dominating set of size at most \(k\); otherwise every such center set has radius \(M\). Consequently, a polynomial-time approximation with factor strictly below \(M\) would decide Dominating Set. Allowing polynomially encoded \(M\) excludes every fixed approximation factor unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without the triangle inequality, graph-derived center instances have an arbitrary 1-versus-M gap, destroying every fixed approximation guarantee unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: Dissimilarities are symmetric and nonnegative, have zero diagonal, and may violate the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No constant-factor polynomial-time approximation exists for unrestricted-dissimilarity \(k\)-center unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Arbitrarily large dissimilarity assigned to distinct nonadjacent vertices.

review_flags: An authoritative source for the graph-gap reduction and unrestricted-dissimilarity boundary is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Covering Integrality-Gap Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case gap of the standard unweighted set-cover linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) contain \(n\) elements and let \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\). For the relaxation \(\min\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}x_S:\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\ge1\ \text{for all }e\in U,\ x_S\ge0\}\), write \(\mathrm{LP}(U,\mathcal S)\) for its value and \(\mathrm{OPT}(U,\mathcal S)\) for the minimum integral cover size. Every instance satisfies \(\mathrm{OPT}/\mathrm{LP}\le H_n\), where \(H_n=\sum_{i=1}^n1/i\). Moreover, there are set systems with \(n\to\infty\) for which \(\mathrm{OPT}/\mathrm{LP}\ge(1-o(1))\ln n\). Hence this relaxation has worst-case integrality gap \(\Theta(\log n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard set-cover LP has logarithmic worst-case integrality gap, bounded above by the nth harmonic number and matched asymptotically by explicit families.
assumptions_latex: Every element belongs to at least one set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{(U,\mathcal S)}\mathrm{OPT}(U,\mathcal S)/\mathrm{LP}(U,\mathcal S)=\Theta(\log n)\).
review_flags: Authoritative source needed for both the harmonic upper bound and asymptotically matching gap family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The harmonic upper bound and asymptotically logarithmic lower-bound family fit this complexity-bound topic, but both are substantive results requiring an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Packing Integrality-Gap Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projective-plane family giving an unbounded gap for the basic set-packing relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a projective plane of order \(q\) have point set \(P\) and line set \(L\), with \(|P|=|L|=q^2+q+1\), every line containing \(q+1\) points, and every two lines intersecting. For set packing, use lines as sets and the relaxation \(\max\{\sum_{\ell\in L}x_\ell:\sum_{\ell\ni p}x_\ell\le1\ \text{for all }p\in P,\ x_\ell\ge0\}\). The integral optimum is \(1\). The assignment \(x_\ell=1/(q+1)\) is feasible and has value \((q^2+q+1)/(q+1)=q+1/(q+1)\). Thus the relaxation's integrality gap is unbounded as available projective-plane orders grow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite projective planes make the basic set-packing LP arbitrarily weaker than integral packing: only one line is integral, while a large fractional packing exists.
assumptions_latex: A finite projective plane of order \(q\) exists.
The relaxation uses only point-capacity inequalities and nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The gap is at least \(q+1/(q+1)\), and is therefore unbounded over prime-power orders.
review_flags: Source needed for projective-plane parameters and their use as a set-packing gap family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projective-plane calculation is internally consistent and the counterexample kind fits, but the projective-plane parameters and existence over unbounded prime-power orders require a source.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated-Location Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded gap of the basic hard-capacitated facility-location relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For hard-capacitated facility location, let \(y_i\) denote opening facility \(i\) and \(x_{ij}\) the fraction of client \(j\) assigned to it. The basic relaxation imposes \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\), \(x_{ij}\le y_i\), \(\sum_j d_jx_{ij}\le u_i y_i\), and \(0\le x_{ij},y_i\le1\), while minimizing \(\sum_i f_i y_i+\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\). There are finite metric instance families for which the ratio of the optimal integral cost to this relaxation's optimum grows without bound. Hence this LP alone cannot certify any uniform constant-factor approximation without strengthening inequalities or capacity augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The natural hard-capacitated facility-location LP has unbounded integrality gap, so constant-factor methods require stronger constraints or relaxed capacities.
assumptions_latex: Facility capacities are hard and may not be violated.
Opening and connection costs are nonnegative.
Connection costs form a metric instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_I \mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)/\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)=+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Fraction of client j assigned to facility i.

review_flags: A precise published gap construction is required to certify the metric and hard-capacity version.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed unbounded gap for this particular hard-capacitated metric facility-location LP is formulation-sensitive and cannot be certified without a precise published construction.

children.title: Partitioning Symmetry Classes
children.top_down_role: Recurring symmetry patterns in set-partitioning formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning Symmetry Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit classes of labeled partition encodings under objective-preserving relabelings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^N\) encode feasible labeled partitions, and let a finite permutation group \(G\) act on coordinates such that \(gx\in X\) and \(c^\top gx=c^\top x\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\). The symmetry class of \(x\) is its orbit \(Gx=\{gx:g\in G\}\). Two encodings \(x,y\in X\) represent symmetry-equivalent partitions exactly when \(y\in Gx\). The orbit-stabilizer identity gives \(|Gx|=|G|/|G_x|\), where \(G_x=\{g\in G:gx=x\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-preserving label permutations partition feasible encodings into group orbits; each orbit is one partitioning symmetry class.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and the objective are invariant under \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equivalence classes are precisely the orbits \(Gx\), with \(|Gx|=|G|/|G_x|\).

notation.meaning: Orbit, or symmetry class, of x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard group-action orbit definition and orbit-stabilizer identity.

children.title: Symmetry-Induced Search Redundancy
children.top_down_role: Search duplication caused by equivalent partition representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Induced Search Redundancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity of equivalent integer solutions encountered by symmetry-unaware exhaustive search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a finite symmetry group \(G\), a feasible encoding \(x\) has \(|Gx|=|G|/|G_x|\) distinct objective-equivalent encodings. Any exhaustive search that enumerates every feasible labeled encoding and performs no orbit pruning therefore processes every member of \(Gx\), although one representative suffices to determine the orbit's objective value. Relative to retaining one representative, this creates \(|Gx|-1=|G|/|G_x|-1\) redundant encodings. In particular, when the action is free on a family of solutions, each underlying unlabeled partition appears \(|G|\) times, of which \(|G|-1\) copies are redundant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry-unaware exhaustive search processes every member of each orbit; relative to one representative, an orbit of size m creates m minus one redundant copies.
assumptions_latex: The search enumerates all labeled feasible encodings without orbit pruning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each orbit contains \(|G|/|G_x|\) equivalent encodings, of which \(|G|/|G_x|-1\) are redundant relative to one representative.

notation.meaning: Number of distinct symmetric copies of x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The redundancy count follows directly from orbit-stabilizer under exhaustive labeled enumeration.

children.title: Partitioning Relaxation Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate relaxation behavior in partitioning models.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning Relaxation Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal-face degeneracy of a linear relaxation for a partitioning formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^N:Ax\le b\}\) be a nonempty bounded relaxation of a partitioning formulation, and let \(z^*=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\). Its optimal face is \(F^*=\{x\in P:c^\top x=z^*\}\). The relaxation is optimal-face degenerate when \(\dim(F^*)>0\), equivalently when it has distinct optimal points and therefore a nontrivial optimal line segment. This notion concerns multiplicity in the relaxation and is distinct from basis degeneracy, where a vertex admits a basic representation containing a zero basic variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partitioning relaxation is optimal-face degenerate when its LP optimum occupies a positive-dimensional face rather than a unique point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimal-face degeneracy holds exactly when \(\dim(F^*)>0\).

notation.meaning: Face containing all optimal relaxation points.

source_refs.locator: 5.1.3 Dealing with Degeneracy p. 183

children.title: Symmetry–Degeneracy Interaction
children.top_down_role: Ways symmetry amplifies or obscures degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry–Degeneracy Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant optimal orbits generate nontrivial optimal faces in convex relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act linearly on a convex polytope \(P\), with \(gP=P\) and \(c^\top gx=c^\top x\) for all \(g\in G\). If \(x\in P\) is optimal, then every point in \(Gx\) is optimal, so \(\operatorname{conv}(Gx)\subseteq F^*\). The orbit average \(\bar x=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}gx\) is also optimal and is fixed by every group element. Consequently, if the orbit contains affinely independent points, the optimal face has dimension at least \(\dim\operatorname{aff}(Gx)\); any nontrivial orbit forces nonuniqueness of the relaxation optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant relaxation contains the convex hull and average of every optimal symmetry orbit, so nontrivial orbits create optimal-face degeneracy.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a convex polytope invariant under finite group \(G\).
The linear objective is invariant under \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(Gx)\subseteq F^*\) and \(\dim(F^*)\ge\dim\operatorname{aff}(Gx)\).

notation.meaning: Optimal face of the invariant relaxation.
Group average of an optimal point.
Affine hull of the symmetry orbit.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Convexity, objective invariance, and group averaging directly imply the stated containment and dimension bound.

children.title: Symmetry-Breaking Formulations
children.top_down_role: Formulation families that reduce equivalent partition representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Breaking Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lex-leader restriction selecting one encoding from every finite symmetry orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^N\) be invariant under a finite permutation group \(G\), and fix a total lexicographic order \(\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}\). Define the lex-leader restriction \(X^{\mathrm{lex}}=\{x\in X:x\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}gx\ \text{for every }g\in G\}\). Every orbit \(Gx\) has a unique lexicographically maximal vector, hence intersects \(X^{\mathrm{lex}}\) exactly once. If the objective is \(G\)-invariant, then optimizing over \(X^{\mathrm{lex}}\) has the same optimal value as optimizing over \(X\). Any exact linear encoding of these lex-leader predicates is therefore a valid symmetry-breaking formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lex-leader constraints retain exactly one binary encoding from every symmetry orbit while preserving the optimum of an invariant objective.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite binary set invariant under \(G\).
\(G\) is finite and acts by coordinate permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each orbit meets \(X^{\mathrm{lex}}\) once, and \(\min_{x\in X^{\mathrm{lex}}}c^\top x=\min_{x\in X}c^\top x\).

notation.meaning: Lex-leader representatives of feasible symmetry orbits.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Every finite orbit has one maximal element under a fixed total order, and invariant objectives are constant on orbits.

knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Threshold Cliffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discontinuity of threshold-coverage value under arbitrarily small radius or distance perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite demand set with weights \(w_i\ge 0\), let \(S\) be a nonempty set of open facilities, and define \(C_r(S)=\sum_{i\in I}w_i\mathbf 1\{\min_{j\in S}d_{ij}\le r\}\). The map \(r\mapsto C_r(S)\) is a step function whose jumps occur at distances \(\min_{j\in S}d_{ij}\). Indeed, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(W>0\), an instance with one demand of weight \(W\) at distance \(r+\varepsilon\) from \(S\) satisfies \(C_r(S)=0\) and \(C_{r+\varepsilon}(S)=W\). Thus no instance-independent continuity bound in the threshold perturbation exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Threshold coverage changes discontinuously: an arbitrarily small increase in the service radius can add demand of arbitrarily large total weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_r(S)\) can jump by an arbitrarily large amount under an arbitrarily small change of \(r\).

notation.meaning: total demand covered by facilities S within radius r
distance from demand i to facility j

children.title: Demand Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Location-model failures caused by inaccurate demand inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Demand Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive location-cost error caused solely by incorrect demand weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite demand set, \(S\ne\varnothing\) an open-facility set, and \(D_i(S)=\min_{j\in S}d_{ij}\). For true weights \(w_i\ge0\) and modeled weights \(\widehat w_i\ge0\), demand misspecification is the replacement of \(F(S;w,d)=\sum_{i\in I}w_iD_i(S)\) by \(F(S;\widehat w,d)\). For fixed \(S\), its objective error satisfies \(F(S;\widehat w,d)-F(S;w,d)=\sum_{i\in I}(\widehat w_i-w_i)D_i(S)\), and hence \(\lvert F(S;\widehat w,d)-F(S;w,d)\rvert\le\sum_{i\in I}\lvert\widehat w_i-w_i\rvert D_i(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Demand misspecification replaces true demand weights by modeled weights; its fixed-location cost error is bounded by weighted absolute demand errors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert F(S;\widehat w,d)-F(S;w,d)\rvert\le\sum_i\lvert\widehat w_i-w_i\rvert D_i(S)\).

notation.meaning: distance from demand i to its nearest open facility

children.title: Distance Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Location-model failures caused by inaccurate distance or travel-cost inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Location-cost error caused solely by replacing true demand–facility distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite demand and facility sets \(I,J\), let \(S\subseteq J\) be nonempty and let \(w_i\ge0\). Distance misspecification replaces true distances \(d_{ij}\) by modeled distances \(\widehat d_{ij}\) in \(F(S;w,d)=\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min_{j\in S}d_{ij}\). If \(\max_{i\in I,j\in S}\lvert\widehat d_{ij}-d_{ij}\rvert\le\varepsilon\), then \(\lvert F(S;w,\widehat d)-F(S;w,d)\rvert\le\varepsilon\sum_{i\in I}w_i\). This bound permits the identity of a nearest facility to change and therefore does not assume a fixed assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform distance error of at most epsilon changes any fixed facility set’s nearest-assignment cost by at most epsilon times total demand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert F(S;w,\widehat d)-F(S;w,d)\rvert\le\varepsilon\sum_iw_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform perturbation bound is correct for a fixed nonempty facility set and allows nearest-facility changes, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Coupled Demand–Distance Error
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes where demand and distance errors reinforce one another.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Demand–Distance Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interaction term for simultaneous demand and distance errors under a fixed assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a:I\to S\) be a fixed assignment and define \(L(a;w,d)=\sum_{i\in I}w_i d_{i,a(i)}\). Write \(\Delta w_i=\widehat w_i-w_i\) and \(\Delta d_i=\widehat d_{i,a(i)}-d_{i,a(i)}\). Simultaneous misspecification obeys the exact decomposition \(L(a;\widehat w,\widehat d)-L(a;w,d)=\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(\Delta w_i d_{i,a(i)}+w_i\Delta d_i+\Delta w_i\Delta d_i\bigr)\). The final bilinear term is the coupled demand–distance error and is absent from a first-order additive treatment of the two perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed assignment, simultaneous demand and distance errors include a bilinear cross-term beyond the two separate first-order effects.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and \(a:I\to S\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta L=\sum_i(\Delta w_i d_{i,a(i)}+w_i\Delta d_i+\Delta w_i\Delta d_i)\).

notation.meaning: cost of assignment a under demand w and distances d

children.title: Misspecification Robustness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of solution stability under input misspecification.

knowledge_statements.title: Misspecification Robustness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions separating uniformly bounded location-cost error from unbounded sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(S;w,d)=\sum_{i\in I}w_i\min_{j\in S}d_{ij}\), suppose \(\sum_iw_i\le W\), \(\sum_i\lvert\widehat w_i-w_i\rvert\le\eta\), \(0\le d_{ij}\le D\), and \(\max_{i,j}\lvert\widehat d_{ij}-d_{ij}\rvert\le\varepsilon\). Then every nonempty \(S\) satisfies \(\lvert F(S;\widehat w,\widehat d)-F(S;w,d)\rvert\le D\eta+\varepsilon(W+\eta)\). No uniform bound depending only on \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\) exists if either the distance scale \(D\) or total demand scale \(W\) is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded total demand and bounded distances yield a uniform perturbation bound; removing either scale restriction permits unbounded cost error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert F(S;\widehat w,\widehat d)-F(S;w,d)\rvert\le D\eta+\varepsilon(W+\eta)\), with no scale-free analogue when \(D\) or \(W\) is unbounded.

notation.meaning: upper bound on total true demand

children.title: Capacity Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by discrepancies between modeled and realized service capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of assignment feasibility when modeled facility capacities exceed true capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{ij}\in[0,1]\) assign demand \(w_i\ge0\) to facilities and define facility load \(\ell_j=\sum_iw_ix_{ij}\). Modeled capacities \(\widehat u_j\) certify modeled feasibility when \(\ell_j\le\widehat u_j\) for every \(j\), whereas true feasibility requires \(\ell_j\le u_j\). Capacity mismatch occurs whenever some \(j\) satisfies \(u_j<\ell_j\le\widehat u_j\). More generally, if \(\widehat u_j-u_j\le\delta_j\), a modeled solution with reserve \(\widehat u_j-\ell_j\ge\delta_j\) remains truly feasible; without this reserve, arbitrarily small capacity overestimation can invalidate feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A modeled assignment can be feasible yet truly overloaded; a reserve covering the capacity error is sufficient to preserve feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat u_j-\ell_j\ge\delta_j\ge\widehat u_j-u_j\) for all \(j\) implies \(\ell_j\le u_j\) for all \(j\).

children.title: Congestion Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by omitted or inaccurate congestion effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Congestion Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective error produced by using an incorrect load-dependent congestion function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For facility load \(\ell_j\ge0\), let \(h_j(\ell_j)\) be the true congestion cost and \(\widehat h_j(\ell_j)\) its modeled counterpart. Congestion mismatch on a load domain \(L_j\subseteq\mathbb R_+\) is measured by \(\epsilon_j=\sup_{z\in L_j}\lvert\widehat h_j(z)-h_j(z)\rvert\). If a feasible assignment induces \(\ell_j\in L_j\) for each used facility, then its total congestion-cost error satisfies \(\left\lvert\sum_j\widehat h_j(\ell_j)-\sum_jh_j(\ell_j)\right\rvert\le\sum_j\epsilon_j\). This bound concerns evaluation at fixed loads and does not control assignment changes caused by misspecified marginal congestion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform errors in facility congestion functions bound cost-evaluation error at fixed loads, but do not bound assignment changes.
assumptions_latex: Each induced load satisfies \(\ell_j\in L_j\subseteq\mathbb R_+\).

children.title: Capacity–Congestion Feedback
children.top_down_role: Feedback between capacity usage and congestion severity.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity–Congestion Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point representation of assignments whose congestion depends on the loads they induce.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X(u)=\{x:\sum_iw_ix_{ij}\le u_j\text{ for all }j\}\), let \(\ell_j(x)=\sum_iw_ix_{ij}\), and let perceived assignment costs be \(c_{ij}(x)=d_{ij}+q_j(\ell_j(x);u_j)\). Capacity–congestion feedback is represented by a fixed point \(x^*\in B(x^*)\), where \(B(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in X(u)}\sum_{i,j}w_iy_{ij}c_{ij}(x)\). Thus capacities restrict feasible loads, loads determine congestion, congestion changes assignment costs, and the resulting best-response assignment must reproduce the loads used to calculate those costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feedback-consistent assignment is a fixed point: capacity limits loads, loads determine congestion costs, and those costs regenerate the assignment.
assumptions_latex: The feasible assignment set \(X(u)\) is nonempty.
Each best-response set \(B(x)\) is defined using costs evaluated at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feedback-consistent assignment satisfies \(x^*\in B(x^*)\).

children.title: Overload Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where capacity or congestion mismatch produces overload.

knowledge_statements.title: Overload Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Queue-stability cliff at equality of arrival rate and service capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a facility modeled as an \(M/M/1\) queue with arrival rate \(\lambda\ge0\) and service rate \(\mu>0\). A stationary workload distribution exists exactly when \(\rho=\lambda/\mu<1\). In that regime, the expected sojourn time is \(1/(\mu-\lambda)\), which diverges as \(\lambda\uparrow\mu\). If \(\lambda\ge\mu\), the queue is not positive recurrent and has no finite stationary mean sojourn time. Hence the capacity boundary \(\lambda=\mu\) separates stable finite-delay operation from overload, and errors that move estimated utilization across one can qualitatively invalidate a location-service evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an M/M/1 facility, delay diverges as demand approaches service capacity; at or above capacity, no finite stationary mean delay exists.
assumptions_latex: Arrivals form a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\).
Service times are independent exponential variables of rate \(\mu\).
The queue uses one work-conserving server.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite stationary mean sojourn time holds exactly for \(\lambda<\mu\), with value \(1/(\mu-\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: utilization ratio lambda divided by mu

children.title: Facility Failure Fragility

knowledge_statements.title: Facility Failure Fragility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case loss of covered demand after deletion of open facilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq J\) be the open facilities, let \(r\ge0\), and define \(C_r(S)=\sum_{i\in I}w_i\mathbf 1\{\min_{j\in S}d_{ij}\le r\}\), with \(C_r(\varnothing)=0\). For an integer \(k\ge1\), the facility-failure fragility of \(S\) is \(\Phi_k(S)=\max_{F\subseteq S,\,|F|\le k}\bigl(C_r(S)-C_r(S\setminus F)\bigr)\). It is the largest covered-demand loss caused by at most \(k\) facility failures. The normalized fragility is \(\Phi_k(S)/C_r(S)\) when \(C_r(S)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facility-failure fragility is the maximum covered-demand loss caused by deleting at most a prescribed number of open facilities.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq J\) and \(k\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_k(S)=\max_{F\subseteq S,\,|F|\le k}(C_r(S)-C_r(S\setminus F))\).

children.title: Network Disruption Fragility
children.top_down_role: Location-system sensitivity to disrupted travel or service networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Disruption Fragility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case location-cost degradation caused by deletion or impairment of network elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite network with nonnegative edge lengths, let \(S\subseteq V\) be nonempty, and let \(d_{G-R}(i,S)\) be the shortest surviving path length after removal of \(R\subseteq E\), taking value \(+\infty\) if disconnected. For an admissible disruption family \(\mathcal R\), network-disruption fragility is \(\Psi_{\mathcal R}(S)=\sup_{R\in\mathcal R}\sum_{i\in I}w_i\bigl(d_{G-R}(i,S)-d_G(i,S)\bigr)\). It is infinite precisely when some admissible disruption disconnects a positive-weight demand from every facility; otherwise it measures the worst aggregate distance increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network-disruption fragility is the worst aggregate increase in demand-to-facility shortest-path distance, becoming infinite when positive demand is disconnected.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) and the demand set \(I\subseteq V\) are finite.
Edge lengths and demand weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Psi_{\mathcal R}(S)=+\infty\) exactly when some \(R\in\mathcal R\) disconnects a demand \(i\) with \(w_i>0\) from \(S\).

notation.meaning: post-disruption shortest-path distance from i to S

children.title: Correlated Outage Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fragility arising from dependent facility or network outages.

knowledge_statements.title: Correlated Outage Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginal outage probabilities do not determine the reliability of redundant facilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one demand point served by either of two open facilities, and let \(Y_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate outage of facility \(i\). Suppose \(\mathbb P(Y_1=1)=\mathbb P(Y_2=1)=p\), where \(0<p<1\), and service is lost exactly when \(Y_1=Y_2=1\). Under independent outages, the expected unit loss is \(p^2\). Under perfectly correlated outages satisfying \(Y_1=Y_2\) almost surely, it is \(p\). Thus identical marginal outage data permit a loss ratio \(p/p^2=1/p\), which is unbounded as \(p\downarrow0\); a model based only on marginals cannot guarantee a bounded approximation to correlated-outage loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two outage models with identical facility marginals can have expected service losses differing by an unbounded factor, so marginal probabilities alone cannot validate redundancy.
assumptions_latex: Either operational facility can serve the demand at unit service value.
The model specifies outage marginals but not their joint distribution.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically coherent, notation is defined, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. However, no citation or inspectable locator supports the correlated-outage interpretation or resulting modeling limitation.

children.title: Failure–Disruption Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined effects of facility loss and network impairment.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure–Disruption Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facility and network survivability considered separately need not imply joint survivability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a demand vertex \(u\) have two candidate facilities \(f_1,f_2\), with direct service edges \(e_i=uf_i\), and open both facilities. With no edge disruption, failure of either single facility leaves service through the other facility. With no facility failure, deletion of either single edge likewise leaves service through the other edge. However, the joint event consisting of failure of \(f_1\) and deletion of \(e_2\) disconnects \(u\) from every operational facility. Hence separate feasibility under one facility failure and under one edge disruption does not imply feasibility under their simultaneous occurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A placement can survive every single facility failure and every single edge disruption separately yet lose all service when one of each occurs together.
assumptions_latex: Service requires a path to an operational facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\)-facility-failure resilience and \(1\)-edge-disruption resilience do not imply joint \((1,1)\)-resilience.

notation.meaning: Direct service edge from the demand to facility i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated graph example correctly separates individual facility-failure and edge-disruption resilience from joint (1,1)-resilience, and failure_boundary is appropriate. No cited source or locator supports the resilience definitions or taxonomic claim.

children.title: Location Resilience Gaps
children.top_down_role: Differences between nominal location performance and disrupted-system performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Location Resilience Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The cost ratio between nominal and single-failure-resilient location can be unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(M>1\), consider one demand point and two colocated candidate facilities \(f_1,f_2\) with opening costs \(1\) and \(M\), respectively, and zero assignment cost. Nominal feasibility requires one open facility, so its optimum value is \(1\). Resilient feasibility requires the demand to remain served after failure of any one open facility. Consequently both facilities must be opened, giving resilient optimum \(M+1\). The multiplicative resilience gap is therefore \((M+1)/1=M+1\), which tends to infinity with \(M\). Thus nominal cost supplies no uniform multiplicative bound on the cost of single-facility-failure resilience.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with two colocated facilities, requiring service after any single facility failure can increase optimal opening cost by an arbitrarily large factor.
assumptions_latex: Opening costs are \(1\) and \(M\), with zero assignment cost.
Every demand must retain an open operational facility after any single open-facility failure.

notation.meaning: Opening cost of the expensive backup facility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed unbounded cost gap is internally correct under the stated resilience definition, and failure_boundary matches the container. A source with a specific locator is required for that resilience model and its interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Equity–Efficiency Conflict
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax distance equity can have an unbounded price relative to total-distance efficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(D>0\) and place \(n\ge2\) unit demands at \(0\) and one unit demand at \(D\) on the interval \([0,D]\). A single facility may be located at any \(x\in[0,D]\). Total-distance efficiency minimizes \(F(x)=n x+(D-x)\), whose unique minimizer is \(x=0\) with value \(D\). Minimax equity minimizes \(G(x)=\max\{x,D-x\}\), whose unique minimizer is \(x=D/2\). At that equitable location, \(F(D/2)=(n+1)D/2\). Hence enforcing minimax equity has efficiency ratio \((n+1)/2\), which is unbounded as \(n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one-facility location on a line, the minimax-equitable site can have arbitrarily worse total distance than the efficiency-optimal site.
assumptions_latex: One facility can be placed anywhere in \([0,D]\).
